Kuczynski 001 — PASS
Question: Does logic require the existence of non-spatiotemporal entities? Give the property-based argument.
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 6
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Causality; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology
Word count: 266

EXACT ANSWER
Yes. Logic requires non-spatiotemporal entities, and the argument is embarrassingly simple.

Start with an indisputably correct inference: "Sally and Fred are both intelligent." This is not controversial. It follows that "there is something that they have in common; that is, that there exists some property P such that Fred is an instance of P and Sally is an instance of P."

Now ask where that property lives. "Instances of intelligence are in space-time. Einstein was in space-time; so was Keynes. But intelligence itself is not in space-time." You will "never encounter intelligence per se and it would make no sense to assign any spatiotemporal location to it."

So the inference forces us to grant non-spatiotemporal entities. "Thus, to validate the rather rudimentary inference... it is necessary to grant the existence of non-spatiotemporal entities and thus to do a bit of ontologizing."

The anti-Platonist will try to collapse the property into its instances. That fails. "Consider the property of having a perfectly triangular shape. Nothing has this property." If we say it doesn't exist because it has no instances, we are saying "there exists a property, viz. that of triangularity, such that, because nothing has it, it doesn't exist. Which is absurd."

Hence: "The property of having a perfectly triangular shape exists even though nothing has this property."

The doctrine that properties don't exist, or exist only as spatiotemporal entities, is nominalism or anti-Platonism. It is false. And note the deeper problem: "words are themselves universals," so the nominalist's own tool refutes him.

Logic traffics in properties. Properties are not in space-time. Therefore logic requires non-spatiotemporal entities.

Kuczynski 002 — PASS
Question: What is a property, and why is a property not identical with any of its instances?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 12
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Part II; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Causality
Word count: 330

EXACT ANSWER
A property is a way that things can be. Equivalently, a property is a possibility. If you are jogging, as opposed to watching t.v., that simply means that there are two possibilities only one of which was actualized; two paths or "ways of being", only one of which was taken; two properties, only one of which was instantiated.

So a property is not some pink elephant in the sky. "It's just a way something would have to be to be a pink elephant." And for there to be no instances of that property is simply for nothing to be that way.

Now, why is a property not identical with its instances? Because properties are modally elastic, whereas their instances are not. "The property of being a pink elephant exists, but is currently uninstantiated. If there were to come into being a single pink elephant, which promptly died, the property wouldn't go out of existence. It would still be around. But if it were identical with instances, then it would go out of existence the moment its one instance did."

The same point refutes identifying a property with a scattered object composed of its instances. "Even though that 'scattered object' is always undergoing changes (in, for example, the location of its outer boundary), the property of being a rock does not undergo corresponding changes, which would not be possible if that property were identical with that object."

Properties can also be thought of as conditions. "The property of being a pink elephant is a condition a thing must fulfill in order to be a pink elephant." And "properties that aren't instantiated are just unfulfilled conditions." Mary's impossible suitor—genius, always friendly, never sleeps, a billionaire—fulfills no condition anyone meets, yet the condition plainly exists.

Hence: "given that there are unfulfilled conditions, it follows that there are uninstantiated properties. And given that properties exist, even when they have no instances, it follows that, when they do exist, they aren't identical with their instances."

Kuczynski 003 — PASS
Question: Can a non-spatiotemporal entity have causal powers?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 11
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Do We Think in Words?; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8
Word count: 272

EXACT ANSWER
No. A non-spatiotemporal entity cannot have causal powers. This is not a limitation I lament—it is a structural feature of what causation is.

To be a cause is to induce change. "Causes are necessarily in space and time. To be a cause is to induce change. Changes and their causes are ipso facto in space-time." My pounding the table breaks it; my not destroying Jupiter does nothing to Jupiter or to anything else. The first has a place in the causal tapestry; the second is nowhere in it.

This matters because it exposes a confusion in the argument from causal impotence against properties. The objection runs: properties lack causal powers, therefore they are explanatory deadwood, therefore we should not posit them. I grant the premise. "Properties do indeed lack causal powers." But the conclusion does not follow.

The error is the assumption that all explanation is causal. It is not. "Not all explanation is causal explanation. Some explanation is what we call analytic or conceptual." That there are as many even numbers as whole numbers is not explained by anything pushing anything. It is explained by a one-one correspondence.

So the Platonist need not make properties into causes. "Ways things can be are not spatiotemporal. A way that something can be is simply a possibility as to how it can be, and such a possibility obviously isn't a constituent of space-time." Properties are ways things can be. They explain by being the structures in terms of which things are intelligible—not by shoving them around.

The demand that everything explanatory be causal is itself the dogma. Drop it, and the causal-impotence objection collapses.

Kuczynski 004 — PASS
Question: Why does the existence of properties follow from meaningful predication?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 3
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Part II; Causality; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6
Word count: 315

EXACT ANSWER
The existence of properties follows from meaningful predication because predication itself presupposes them. Consider the inference from "John and Bill are both tall" to "there is something that John and Bill have in common." This inference obviously goes through, and it presupposes the existence of a property (namely, tallness), since the term "something" in the second statement is obviously shorthand for "some property."

Attempts to eliminate properties fail. "Attempts have been made to replace statements about properties with statements about their instances, but such attempts inevitably fail." The reason is that predication carries modal and structural content that instances alone cannot supply. "The statement 'one can have most of the properties of a great businessman without being a great businessman' cannot be translated into a statement that does not presuppose the existence of properties."

Nor can properties be reduced to their instances. "As for the idea that properties are identical with or composed of their instances, that too is a non-starter." Suppose someone identifies the property of being a rock with a scattered object consisting of all rocks. "But this move fails, since even though that 'scattered object' is always undergoing changes... the property of being a rock does not undergo corresponding changes, which would not be possible if that property were identical with that object."

The upshot generalizes: "Analogous reasoning refutes any attempt to identify any property with any spatiotemporal entity." Properties are not located in space and time, and they do not change as their instances change.

Even Plato obscured this. "Plato himself mischaracterized his own theory, by assuming that properties must in some way or other 'resemble' their own instances." Resemblance is the wrong model. The property of being tall does not resemble a tall man; it is what the man instantiates.

So: meaningful predication requires properties. Deny properties, and you cannot even state the inference from shared predicates to shared features.

Kuczynski 005 — PASS
Question: What are propositions?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 20
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Part II; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Causality; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 233

EXACT ANSWER
Propositions are sets of properties. That is the core of my view. "By a 'proposition,' I mean what is meant by an utterance of a sentence." If I point at Smith and say "that man is a scoundrel," the meaning of my utterance is a proposition.

They are not sentences. "Propositions are not themselves sentences. That is why different sentences (e.g., 'schnee ist weiss' and 'snow is white') can express the same proposition." Nor are they psychological. "Propositions are not psychological entities; they are mind-independent entities." The believing is mental; the believed is not.

They are also the things toward which attitudes are directed. "Propositional attitudes: Propositions are the things we affirm. They are also the things towards which belief, doubt, fear, and all other attitudes are directed."

And they are the primary bearers of truth. "Propositions are thus 'non-derivatively true,' whereas beliefs and sentences are 'derivatively true.'" A sentence is "true" only derivatively, by association with a true proposition.

Structurally, they are digital. "It follows that propositions consist of discrete parts; it also follows that those discrete parts correspond to discrete parts of the sentences that express them."

They are also properties. "Since sets can, in the way just described, be identified with properties, it follows that propositions are properties." And they are not human creations: "Propositions, when true, are truths. Thus, propositions have existed as long as there have been truths."

Kuczynski 006 — PASS
Question: What makes a proposition true?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 20
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Part II; Causality; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 240

EXACT ANSWER
A proposition is true just in case the properties that are its members are instantiated. That is the whole of it.

I hold that "propositions are sets of properties; and a proposition is true just in case the properties that are members of it are instantiated—so what it is for a proposition to be true is for the members of the set with which it is identical to be jointly instantiated." Roughly, truth is instantiatedness.

Consider Tommy is smoking. The proposition is a set of properties. It is true iff each member of that set is instantiated in the world.

This is why I say that "for a proposition to be true is for it to fit the facts." The facts are not sentences. They are ways the world is. And "the world's being a certain way is identical with its having a certain property."

So truth is not a property of sentences in the first instance. "For a sentence to be 'true' is for it to encode a true proposition." The sentence is a human artifact; the proposition is not.

This matters because "propositions are not human creations." The moon was less massive than the Earth before we arrived. That proposition was true then, and it will be true after we are gone.

Truth, then, is instantiatedness. A proposition is true when the properties it contains are jointly instantiated—when the world is the way the proposition says it is.

Kuczynski 007 — PASS
Question: Can truth be reduced to correspondence between a proposition and a fact?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 4
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Part II; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Causality; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 273

EXACT ANSWER
Truth is correspondence, but not between a proposition and a fact. It is correspondence between a proposition and the facts.

The distinction matters. When a sentence is described as "true," the property being attributed to it isn't the same as the property that is attributed to a proposition that is so described. For a sentence to be "true" is for it to encode a true proposition. But this isn't what it is for a proposition to be true, since propositions don't encode anything.

So what is it for a proposition to be true? The obvious answer, though imprecise, is the right one; namely, for a proposition to be true is for it to fit the facts.

This is why the term "statement" is ambiguous; it has three distinct meanings. Sometimes it refers to propositions, sometimes it refers to the sentences used to affirm them, and sometimes it refers to the act of using a sentence to affirm a proposition.

The confusion between these three is what generates the pseudo-problem. Wittgenstein didn't countenance the existence of propositions, and this obviously had a hand in his erroneously believing that philosophy is the analysis of sentences, when the truth is that philosophy is the analysis of propositions.

Even Frege's analyses of sentences such as "someone snores" and "nothing is a square circle" fail to conform to Wittgenstein's conception of what philosophy is supposed to do, since they're analyses of propositions that involve analyses of sentences and, therefore, are not themselves analyses of sentences.

Correspondence is the right account. But the relata are propositions and facts—not sentences and facts. Get the relata right and the theory holds.

Kuczynski 008 — PASS
Question: Why are propositions not sentences or mental events?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 13
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Part II; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Causality; Do We Think in Words?; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means
Word count: 237

EXACT ANSWER
Propositions are neither sentences nor mental events because they are the *meanings* that sentences express and the *objects* that mental acts grasp—and neither of those things is identical with the vehicle that carries it.

Start with sentences. "Propositions are not themselves sentences. That is why different sentences (e.g., 'schnee ist weiss' and 'snow is white') can express the same proposition." A sentence is a human artifact—"the sentence 'the moon is less massive than Earth' is a human artifact; it didn't exist until a few centuries ago." But "the truth it expresses is in a different category. That truth exists independently of us." The moon was less massive than the Earth before anyone wrote the sentence down. So the thing meant cannot be the thing that means it.

Now mental events. When Smith believes that the inventor of bifocals is six feet tall, "Smith's having that belief is indeed a psychological condition. But the thing believed is not. The believing is mental; the believed is not." Why? Because "whatever it is, that thing is something that others grasp"—and a private mental episode in Smith's head cannot be the shared object that you and I both believe.

So what are propositions? "They're properties." And truth is instantiatedness: "propositions must be identified with properties and a proposition's being true must be identified with its being instantiated." A proposition is a way the world can be—mind-independent, spatiotemporal-free, and graspable by anyone.

Kuczynski 009 — PASS
Question: What is wrong with treating possible worlds as the basis of counterfactual truth?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 20
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?
Word count: 263

EXACT ANSWER
The problem is that possible worlds can't do the work Lewis assigns them. We have no epistemic access to them independent of the modal knowledge they're supposed to explain.

As I've argued, "We obviously can't see or otherwise sense-perceive what is going on in other worlds; nor can we can sense-perceive evidence of what is going on in such worlds. Any knowledge that we have of what is going on in them is parasitic on our knowledge of counterfactual truths." This is fatal. Our knowledge of counterfactual truths has nothing to do with other worlds.

Lewis himself concedes the point: "we don't know about alternative worlds by taking a tour of them. We know about them by considering materials that are available to us here and 'employing a principle of recombination.'" But then "the worlds answer to us, not us to them." The explanatory order is inverted.

Worse, the analysis fails on its own terms. Given that x occurs in our world, "a world W in which x doesn't occur will bear so little resemblance to our world that it won't be able to validate the target-counterfactual." To rescue the analysis, Lewis must posit miracles—"if Smith had not shot Jones, then a miracle would have happened"—which is "obviously a preposterous counterfactual." As I put it, "A theory that only doctored data supports is a bad theory, and Lewis' analysis of counterfactuals is untenable."

The deeper issue: if worlds are sets of statements, "counterfactuals merely register interpropositional relations"—and once that relation is identified, "it won't be necessary to talk about other worlds at all."

Kuczynski 010 — PASS
Question: How should counterfactual conditionals be understood?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 14
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Part II; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6
Word count: 270

EXACT ANSWER
Counterfactuals are disguised causal or logical assertions. They are not reports about what happens in other universes.

My analysis is straightforward: "counterfactuals are just disguised causal or logical assertions and that, consequently, alternative worlds have no place in any decent analysis of them." When I say "Kennedy's assassination prevented an otherwise reelection bound Kennedy from being reelected," I am not describing a distant world. I am stating a causal fact about this one.

The same holds for logical counterfactuals. "Anything that is half the height of something that is six-feet tall is three-feet tall" is not a report about a possible world. It is a logical truth wearing hypothetical clothing.

Lewis and his followers have it backwards. "We don't know anything about other universes, let alone whether Smith and Kennedy exist in them or, therefore, what their situations there are." Our knowledge runs the other way: "our knowledge of counterfactuals precedes our knowledge of other worlds."

This means CF is viciously circular. It "assumes that the concept of counterfactual truth is not itself to be explained in terms of the concept of causality. But that may well be false." Consider: "Falling off the building caused an otherwise unthreatened Smith to die" is equivalent to "If Smith hadn't fallen off the building, he wouldn't have died."

So the correct order is: causality and logic first, counterfactuals second. "Counterfactuals hold in virtue of the logical and causal structure of our world, as opposed to other worlds."

There is no reason to posit other worlds at all. "There is no reason at all to posit their existence or therefore to accept Lewis's analysis."

Kuczynski 011 — PASS
Question: Are laws of nature invariant with respect to every region of space?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 2
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism
Word count: 326

EXACT ANSWER
No. Not all laws of nature need to be spatiotemporally invariant.

Some philosophers of science have taken the term "general principle" to mean "spatiotemporally invariant principle," and they have thus taken the position that the laws of nature must be spatiotemporally invariant. A principle is spatiotemporally invariant if, "given any two regions of space-time, it holds no less for the one than the other."

But many of the dependence-relations on which scientists depend are undefined, and therefore neither true nor false, for almost all regions of space-time. That is the decisive point. If a dependence-relation is undefined across nearly every region of space-time, it cannot be a candidate for spatiotemporal invariance in the first place.

So the demand for invariance misdescribes what many scientific laws actually are. They are context-specific. They hold where their relata are defined, and they say nothing where those relata are not.

Consider how I treat law more generally. "Laws of nature are not perfect concomitances: for it to be a law of nature that instances of phi bring about instances of psi is not for each and every phi to be followed by an instance of psi." A law can obtain "even if no phi ever brought about any psi." What makes it a law is that instances of phi are "dispositive, for reasons of a relatively non-context-specific nature, of the occurrence of instances of psi."

Note the phrase: relatively non-context-specific. Not absolutely invariant. Even paradigm laws like "nothing exceeds the speed of light" sit in the same category as principled but defeasible generalizations, so long as science has work to do.

The scope of natural law is also not confined to actual objects. "Laws of nature are not restricted to this or that object; they hold with respect to entire classes of objects," and "those classes sometimes comprise merely possible objects."

Invariance across every region of space-time is therefore the wrong criterion. Laws are principled, defeasible, class-governing, and often context-specific.

Kuczynski 012 — PASS
Question: What distinguishes a law of nature from an accidental regularity?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 5
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 258

EXACT ANSWER
The distinction is not statistical. It is dispositional and grounding-based.

A law of nature is not a perfect regularity. As I argue, "for it to be a law of nature that instances of phi bring about instances of psi is not for each and every phi to be followed by an instance of psi." There "could be such a law even if no phi ever brought about any psi." What makes it a law is that "instances of phi [are] dispositive, for reasons of a relatively non-context-specific nature, of the occurrence of instances of psi."

This is why I insist that "the difference between (a) x is human→x is cyanide-intolerant and (b) x is human→x is shellfish-intolerant is not to be understood in statistical terms." Both could hold universally, yet only (a) is a law. The reason is that "it is inherent in what it is to be physiologically human (or otherwise mammalian) that a human being be cyanide intolerant." The law is "rooted in his having a distinctively mammalian physiological make-up."

Contrast this with shellfish-intolerance. Even if "everyone happened to be shellfish-intolerant," none of those instances "would be rooted in what it is to have a distinctively human physiology." A deviation would be "a singularity only in some emptily statistical sense."

So the mark of lawhood is support for predictions and counterfactuals. As I put it, "each of (a) and (c) supports predictions and counterfactuals; (b) does not do so, and neither does an accidental, albeit place- and time-invariant, generalization."

Accidental regularities are inert. Laws are dispositive.

Kuczynski 013 — PASS
Question: Why is causation a relation between events rather than objects?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 12
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 265

EXACT ANSWER
Because only events can be causes. Objects are not causes. This is not a stylistic preference—it is a logical constraint on the concept of causality.

Consider the rock and the window. "The rock is not a cause. The rock didn't cause the window to break. What did so was some event involving the rock (e.g., the rock's striking the window at a certain time)." The rock has causal properties—its mass, its velocity—but having a causal property is not the same as being a cause. "Non-causes may have causal properties."

When we say "Hitler was the cause of World War II," we speak elliptically. Such statements are shorthand for "such and such events involving Carter (Hitler) were responsible for the recession in the late '70s (World War II)." The object drops out; the events remain.

There is a further distinction I insist on. "We must also distinguish conditions from events. A condition is a relatively persistent state (e.g., the room's having a certain temperature)." Conditions are not causes either—they are the standing backdrop against which causal events occur.

Why does this matter? Because dependence-relations, which is what causation fundamentally is, "don't hold between objects. They hold between events or between statements, depending on whether they're of a causal or a logical nature." Objects persist through change; they cannot stand in the asymmetric, productive relation that causation requires.

The concept of efficient causality is coherent precisely because events—not substances—are its relata. "The concept of efficient causality clearly is a coherent one. There is such a thing as efficient causality." That coherence depends on getting the relata right.

Kuczynski 014 — PASS
Question: Can we observe causal connections?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 8
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 261

EXACT ANSWER
Yes. We observe causal connections whenever we observe anything at all.

Hume's error was to assume we only observe discrete events and then hunt for some additional "tie" between them. But that assumes we could observe events that don't persist. We can't. "Anything that persists is, for that very reason, a causal process; and anything that is seen as persisting, which is everything that is seen, is, for that very reason, seen as a causal process."

The concept of persistence is itself a causal notion. So the very act of seeing something as enduring is already an act of seeing it as causal. There is no observation of a bare, non-causal event to which a causal tie would then need to be added.

Hume's own analysis collapses under this. He analyzes causality in terms of spatial occupancy, but "a given thing's occupying a given region R ipso facto alters the trajectories and velocities of other would-be and soon-to-be occupants of that region." Occupancy is causal through and through. So "Hume's analysis analyzes causality in terms of itself and therefore doesn't analyze it at all."

Nor is this an attenuated, theoretical observation. "We don't observe them only in the attenuated sense in which we are observing H2O molecules when we look with the naked eye at bodies of water." We see causal processes directly, and we see them as causal.

The empiricist demand for a non-causal observation of causation is incoherent. There is nothing instantaneous to observe. "We see nothing instantaneous." Every observation is an observation of persistence, and persistence is causation.

Kuczynski 015 — PASS
Question: Why is persistence itself a causal notion?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 13
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism
Word count: 255

EXACT ANSWER
Persistence is a causal notion because to endure is already to be caught up in a causal sequence. There is no such thing as an inert, causally neutral fact of remaining in existence.

As I argue, "The concept of persistence is itself a causal notion, and anything that persists is, for that very reason, a causal sequence." So we do not first observe bare persistence and then, separately, infer causation. "We observe causal sequences whenever we observe anything."

Consider what persistence actually involves. "Every case of persistence is a case of continuous change." The chair you sit on is the paradigm of persistence, yet it is changing along every dimension at once. What we call "staying the same" is really a stable pattern of continuous alteration.

This is why Hume's picture collapses. He treats space and time as an array of discrete boxes, each permutation-friendly, so that "the permutation-friendliness definitive of spatio-temporal location... is identical with the absence of causal connections between distinct states of affairs." But that conception "cannot be sustained."

The deeper point: "Spatio-temporal continuity is a form of persistence. Consequently, continuity is a causal phenomenon." And "motion and persistence are themselves causal phenomena. To say that x has endured for a certain period of time, or has moved from A to B, is to make a causal claim."

Hence "no state of affairs can be described by a non-causal proposition." Even X's rolling is causal, and so is Y's standing still. Persistence is not a stage on which causation happens—it is causation.

Kuczynski 016 — PASS
Question: Why does spatial occupancy imply causal power?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 10
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Do We Think in Words?
Word count: 315

EXACT ANSWER
Spatial occupancy is a causal concept. To occupy a place is already to exert causal influence on what else can occupy that place.

My argument is this: "the concept of spatial occupancy is a causal concept. What is it for me to be occupying this place? It is for it to be harder than it would otherwise be for you to enter this place." There is no such thing as a thing sitting in a region while making no difference to anything else. "To occupy a place is to make it harder, other things equal, than it would otherwise be for other things to enter that place."

This is why Hume's analysis collapses. He treats space and time as a grid of independent boxes, each fillable without ramification for the others. But "the very notion of spatial occupancy is a causal notion, since a given thing's occupying a given region R ipso facto alters the trajectories and velocities of other would-be and soon-to-be occupants of that region."

The consequence is that Hume's definition of causation is circular. He defines causation in terms of spatiotemporal adjacency, but adjacency is itself causal. "E1 and E2 are simultaneous iff it isn't possible for a signal beginning with either to be sent to the other. Order in time is thus to be understood in causal terms." And in space: "x and y are in different places exactly if something affecting the one may fail to affect the other."

So the answer is not that occupancy *implies* causal power as an extra fact. Occupancy *is* causal power. "If one says that x and y occupy distinct but adjacent places, or that they occupy some one place, one is ipso facto making a causal statement." Strip away the causal relations and there is no residual "pure" position left over. "There is no 'pure' change in position underlying all the causal changes."

Kuczynski 017 — PASS
Question: What is wrong with Aristotle's notion of formal causes?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 7
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?
Word count: 266

EXACT ANSWER
The concept of a formal cause is incoherent. That is the short answer.

Aristotle tells us that "x is the formal cause of y if x is y's form." But this trades on an ambiguity. Sometimes he means shape. Sometimes he means essence—"those properties that are essential to a given thing."

The problem is that dependence-relations, properly understood, don't hold between objects at all. They "hold between events or between statements, depending on whether they're of a causal or a logical nature."

So-called formal causes "don't hold between events (or states of affairs) or statements; they hold between things. Thus, the concept of a formal cause is an incoherent one."

Consider his own example. "It is essential to a thing's being triangle that it have three sides. But a given triangle-shaped object's continued existence needn't depend on its continuing to have three sides. Things change shape."

The same collapse occurs with water. "It is essential to a thing's being water that it consist of H2O molecules. But a given puddle's continuing to exist needn't depend on its consisting of such molecules. Things undergo chemical changes without ceasing to exist."

What Aristotle wants is a logical relation—entailment—but he locates it in the wrong place. "To say that x's having three sides is essential to x's being a triangle is to say that 'x is a triangle' entails that 'x has three sides.'"

That is a relation between statements, not between things. And "the concept of a material cause" falls for the same reason.

Only efficient causality survives. "The concept of efficient causality clearly is a coherent one."

Kuczynski 018 — PASS
Question: Can goals themselves be causes?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 5
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means
Word count: 266

EXACT ANSWER
No. Goals per se are abstract objects—propositions—and abstract objects do no causal work.

This is the heart of my analysis of so-called final causes. "Goals per se do nothing. Goals are abstract objects and therefore do no causal work." What does causal work is a person's *having* a goal. My having the goal that I get in shape "obviously does causal work; it causes me to jog around the block for hours on end." But the goal itself, the proposition, does nothing.

So when Aristotle speaks of final causes, he is caught in a dilemma. "In saying there are such things as 'final' causes, Aristotle is either making the trivial point that a person's having a goal can have effects or he is making the deeply confused point that goals per se can have effects." There is no third option.

The mechanism is straightforward. "My having that goal is my intending to make that proposition come true. But my having a goal is a garden-variety efficient cause." Nothing exotic is required. "In general, goals per se, being propositions, aren't causes at all. A given person's (or creature's) having a given goal is a cause. But it's a garden-variety efficient cause."

This matters because it dissolves the apparent need for a distinct category of causation. "There is such a thing as efficient causality... it's the most fundamental one." Final causation, properly understood, collapses into it. The goal is the content of an intention; the intention is the cause.

So: goals themselves cannot be causes. Only the having of goals—an efficient cause like any other—can bring anything about.

Kuczynski 019 — PASS
Question: Why does Hume's analysis fail to distinguish causation from epiphenomenal succession?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 10
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?
Word count: 233

EXACT ANSWER
Hume's analysis fails because it cannot distinguish a genuine causal connection from a mere sequence of effects produced by a common cause. His conditions are satisfied by both.

Take my earthquake example. Fido barks hysterically; an earthquake strikes. "Hume's analysis entails that Fido's antics causes the earthquake to strike." All three conditions hold: the antics immediately precede, are adjacent with, and are regularly followed by earthquakes. Yet the antics obviously did not cause the quake.

The reason is that "some one thing was responsible both for Fido's antics and for the earthquake." The two effects formed a sequence that "mimicked a bona fide causal connection." Hume's machinery cannot tell the difference.

This is the general defect. As I put it, "HC doesn't distinguish actual from epiphenomenal causality." Let e1 cause both e2 and e3, with e2 immediately preceding and adjacent to e3. Hume's analysis then falsely declares that e2 causes e3. The rotation of the Earth makes day follow night—but "day doesn't cause night."

The deeper failure is that Hume's conditions are purely external. Real causation involves a mechanism, a continuity. "It's the mechanism, the continuity, that is the sine qua non of causality." Pseudo-causal processes, on inspection, "prove to involve discontinuities not involved in their real counterparts."

So the analysis is not merely incomplete—it is untenable. It mistakes constant conjunction for connection, and thereby licenses every epiphenomenal sequence as a causal one.

Kuczynski 020 — PASS
Question: What is the relation between causation and explanation?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 3
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Causality; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 240

EXACT ANSWER
Causation is a relation between events, and explanation is the identification of causes. The two are not merely related—explanation just is causal identification.

As I put it: "To explain is to find causes; to explain an event is to identify its cause." That is the platitude from which everything else follows.

So when a vase breaks, we explain it by locating the collision that preceded it. I write: "A vase breaks at time t*. Let B be that event. This vase collided with the ground at t, this being right before it." The explanation is the cause.

But here is where it gets interesting. Knowing *what* killed Tim is not the same as knowing *how*. I address this directly: "I can know what killed Tim (he ate fish), but not know how it did so." The resolution: "knowledge of the how is knowledge of the what. How-knowledge is high-resolution what-knowledge."

Explanation, then, is causal knowledge at resolution. And what drives the search for it? One principle: "causal anomalies must be minimized." Everything is explained "when and only when it is known, for any given state of affairs, what caused that state of affairs to obtain."

And how do we minimize anomalies? "The elimination of causal anomalies consists in the elimination of discontinuities."

Explanation and prediction almost always consist in the identification of program-causes—stable conditions that predetermine specific events. That is the machinery. Causation supplies the relation; explanation supplies the resolution.

Kuczynski 021 — PASS
Question: Do people think in natural language?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 8
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Do We Think in Words?; Part II; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6
Word count: 238

EXACT ANSWER
No. We do not think in natural language, and we do not think in any innate code either.

The thesis that we think in language comes in two versions. The first holds that "English speakers think in English; Albanian speakers think in Albanian; etc." The second holds that we think in some innate, universal code. Both are false.

Consider what it would mean for my thought that snow is cold to be identical with the sentence "snow is cold" flashing through my mind. It isn't. "Understanding a sentence is different from its flashing through your mind." I can have the sounds of a language I don't understand pass through my head without grasping anything.

Then there's the digital/analogue distinction. "Sentences are 'digital' structures, meaning that they decompose into a finite number of distinct parts. Sense-perceptions are non-digital; they are 'analogue' structures." Much of my thinking is imagistic, and images don't decompose into discrete parts the way sentences do.

And consider monolinguals. "People who speak different languages can have the same thoughts." A Spanish speaker and an English speaker both believe 1 + 1 = 2. If thought were identical with a sentence, they couldn't share that belief.

So why does it feel like we think in words? Because language enhances cognition enormously—like icons on a desktop that let you manipulate underlying processes they only schematically resemble. The voice in my head is a tool, not the thought itself.

[Do We Think in Words?] We can obviously have thoughts that we are incapable of putting into words. This shows that we grasp those thoughts in some way other than by grasping the English sentences that express them. Kuczynski 022 — PASS
Question: Why must thought be possible before language can be learned?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 12
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Do We Think in Words?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Part II; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible
Word count: 311

EXACT ANSWER
Language learning is parasitic on thought. You cannot learn that certain sounds have certain meanings unless you can already make judgments about what means what.

My third reason states it directly: "In order to learn a language, one must already be able to think. To learn English is to learn that certain sounds have certain meanings; and in order to be able to do this, you already have to be able to synthesize information—to make judgments, on the basis of experience, as to what sounds have what meanings." So "knowledge of a language presupposes the ability to think."

The same point holds for understanding. "Understanding sentences involves thought. You must be able to think to understand what is meant by 'if snow is cold, then snow is not hot.'" A sentence can flash through your mind without your grasping it—"If I hear a sentence of a language that I don't understand, it may pass through my mind later... but I won't know what it means." Grasping meaning is not the same as undergoing a sentence.

This is why Version #1 of the language-of-thought thesis fails. We "can obviously have thoughts that we are incapable of putting into words," and often "thinking is a prerequisite to using language, which in turn shows that at least some thinking is non-linguistic."

Against Wittgenstein, Blackburn, and McDowell—who insist "If you can't say it, you don't know it"—I hold that "a given person's beliefs can be expressed in many ways, and many of them don't depend on that person's being able to use words." Their view "presupposes that what we believe is expressed only in the words we utter. But that's not the case."

Wittgenstein's claim that "thinking consists of manipulating expressions" is inconsistent with the fact that "unless one can think, one cannot use expressions meaningfully." Barking sounds without knowing their meaning is not speech.

Kuczynski 023 — PASS
Question: Can a person have a sophisticated thought that cannot yet be put into words?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 11
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Do We Think in Words?; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism
Word count: 269

EXACT ANSWER
Yes. And the existence of such thoughts is precisely what refutes the thesis that we think in language.

My argument is straightforward. "We can obviously have thoughts that we are incapable of putting into words. This shows that we grasp those thoughts in some way other than by grasping the English sentences that express them." If thinking were identical with the manipulation of linguistic items, this would be impossible. It is not impossible. Therefore thinking is not linguistic through and through.

Consider the second reason I give. "Some kinds of information (e.g., visual information) seem inherently incapable of being fully expressed by sentences of English or of any other natural language." A painter who captures the precise difference between two shades of red knows something—but the knowing is in the brushstroke, not in a sentence.

The Wittgensteinian rejoinder is that no genuine knowledge is involved here. I reject this flatly. "A person's knowledge of the differences between x and y may be expressed in that person's drawings of x and y; or it may be expressed in that person's movements while he is in the vicinity of x and y; or it may be expressed in some other non-linguistic manner." And the denial is self-undermining: "it overlooks the fact that, but for this 'pseudo-knowledge,' we couldn't know anything about language, since it is only through our ability to differentiate noises, ink-marks, etc., on the basis of their perceptible properties that we can learn, or use, language."

So the sophisticated wordless thought is not an anomaly. It is the norm from which articulate thought is a late and effortful achievement.

Kuczynski 024 — PASS
Question: What is wrong with the language-of-thought hypothesis?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 7
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Do We Think in Words?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Causality
Word count: 297

EXACT ANSWER
The language-of-thought hypothesis fails because it cannot account for how we understand the sentences it posits. If thought is conducted in an innate code, then understanding that code requires knowing its rules—but knowing those rules would itself require thought, which is viciously circular.

I put the point this way: "if one's thought is entirely dependent on such a language, then one can't know those rules, or anything else for that matter, without understanding those expressions. Therefore it is viciously circular to hold that we think in an innately known code."

The defender's escape is to deny that we understand the code at all—we are merely "built to conform" to it. But this collapses. As I argue, "If a sentence isn't understood by so and so, then from so and so's viewpoint it is not functioning as a sentence."

My book analogy makes this vivid: a book thrown at a roommate "is not in this context functioning as a book and, for all intents and purposes, is not a book." Likewise, sentences nobody understands "aren't really functioning as sentences anymore."

There are further problems. "People who speak different languages can have the same thoughts"—a Spanish speaker and an English speaker both believe 1+1=2, but they use different sentences, so the thought cannot be identical with either sentence.

And crucially, "understanding sentences involves thought." You must be able to think to grasp what a sentence means; a sentence merely "flashing through your mind" is not understanding.

Finally, much thought is simply non-linguistic. Some information—visual information, for instance—"seem[s] inherently incapable of being fully expressed by sentences of English or of any other natural language."

So we may "tentatively conclude that we don't think in language, even though, undeniably, knowledge of language enormously enhances at least some of our cognitive capabilities."

Kuczynski 025 — PASS
Question: How does Russell's theory of descriptions improve on Frege's semantics?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 9
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Do We Think in Words?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Part II; Causality
Word count: 246

EXACT ANSWER
Russell's theory of descriptions solves a problem Frege's semantics cannot: the failure of substitutivity in intensional contexts. Frege treats "the inventor of bifocals" and "the first postmaster general" as referring terms. But then, "given that those expressions co-refer, replacing the one with the other should preserve truth-value. But it doesn't." Sentence 1 may be false while 3 is true, and vice versa. That is the hard data any adequate theory must explain.

My theory of descriptions—TD—handles this directly. According to TD, the meanings of the problematic sentences become: "Smith believes that something uniquely invented bifocals, and any such thing is 6 ft tall" and "Smith believes that something was a unique first postmaster general and any such thing is 6 ft tall." The description is not a referring term at all. It is a quantifier.

This is the crux. "We must suppose that the phi is a quantifier of the kind just described." Once we do, the entailments fall out correctly: "1 doesn't entail 3, and 1 is compatible with 4." TD is compatible with the hard data. Frege's theory is not.

Frege saw the problem and "added an epicycle to his theory that he hoped would save it. It did not." His intensional contexts were a patch, not a solution.

The deeper virtue is systematic. The theory of descriptions accounts for why certain D-sentences are "systematically ambiguous"—the wide-scope/narrow-scope distinction—and "accounts for the exact way in which they are ambiguous." Frege's semantics has no comparable machinery.

Kuczynski 026 — PASS
Question: Why is a definite description not a singular term?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 14
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Do We Think in Words?; Part II; Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 257

EXACT ANSWER
A definite description is not a singular term because it does not refer to anything at all. "Definite descriptions aren't referring terms. No definite description refers to anything."

The reason is that the semantics of a description cannot be given denotatively. Consider "the inventor of Velcro." If its meaning were fixed by who it refers to, then in a world where Bob invents Velcro, the description would refer to Bob. But "there is no individual x such that, to know the semantics of 'the inventor of Velcro' is to know that it refers to x."

What a description does instead is encode an existence-claim. "The inventor of Velcro has psi" says that "something uniquely invented Velcro, and any such person has psi." That is a quantified structure, not a name.

This is why "the inventor of bifocals snored" is true iff "exactly one thing invented bifocals, and any such snored." The description contributes a condition on properties, not an individual.

So descriptions are quantifiers. "The position, first advocated in 1905 by Bertrand Russell, that definite descriptions are not devices of reference and are instead quantifiers." A singular term picks out an object; a description says that a property is uniquely instantiated.

The consequence for belief reports is immediate. "Ponce de Leon believes that the fountain of youth exists" does not relate Ponce to a fountain. Reparsed, it becomes "Ponce de Leon believes that the property of being a fountain of youth is uniquely instantiated." No object is the target of his belief—only a property and its instantiation.

Kuczynski 027 — PASS
Question: What does the sentence 'The present King of France is bald' logically assert?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 1
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Part II; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Causality; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible
Word count: 233

EXACT ANSWER
The sentence asserts a quantified generalization, not a mere subject-predicate pairing. According to my Theory of Descriptions, "the king of France is bald" has for its meaning a quantified generalization that is either identical or equivalent with: something x is uniquely a king of France; moreover, x is bald.

So unpack the logical form. There exists an x such that x is a king of France; there is at most one such x; and that x is bald. The definite article carries existential and uniqueness commitments that the surface grammar conceals.

This is the whole point. "The king of France is bald" means a quantified generalization according to Russell's Theory of Descriptions. It does not name a nonexistent object and then predicate baldness of it. It says, in effect, that exactly one thing satisfies the description "king of France" and that thing is bald.

The consequence is decisive. Since France is presently a republic, the existential conjunct fails. The sentence is therefore false, not meaningless. That is the virtue of the analysis: it explains why we can understand and evaluate the sentence without positing a subsistent King of France.

The same machinery handles any definite description. "The present King of France is bald" is not about a shadowy entity; it is a claim about how the world would have to be arranged for the description to be satisfied. It isn't. Hence falsehood, cleanly.

Kuczynski 028 — PASS
Question: Why can grammatical form conceal logical form?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 20
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Part II; Do We Think in Words?; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Causality
Word count: 261

EXACT ANSWER
Grammatical form conceals logical form because certain expressions—quantifiers and contextually defined terms—make sentences appear to be about objects when they are really about properties.

Take "whales are mammals." Its grammar suggests it picks out whales. It doesn't. As I put it, "WM makes a statement, not about whales, but about the property of being a whale." The perspicuous rendering is that "the property of being a whale has the property of being instantiated only by mammals." Grammatical and logical form diverge.

The mechanism is the quantifier. "Given any statement of English, or any other non-artificial language, that contains quantifiers, the logical and grammatical forms of that sentence diverge." A quantifier is an expression such that "if a sentence contains it, that sentence is ipso facto to the effect that the extension of one property has a certain degree of overlap... with the extension of some other property."

So quantified sentences are "pseudo-objectual statements. They appear to be about objects, but are really about properties." That is precisely why "they must be reparsed if their logical forms are to be exposed."

Contextual definition does the same work. "Someone" refers to no one. Its meaning is given by the rule that "‹Someone has psi› is true just in case the property of being a psi is instantiated." Grammar hides this.

Frege saw it first. "Frege was the first to see clearly that logical and grammatical may diverge—he was the first to grasp the very idea of such a divergence." And with that insight, "Frege discovered both facts and, therewith, created modern analytic philosophy."

Kuczynski 029 — PASS
Question: What is a desire?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 3
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Why Does Alcoholics Anonymous Work?; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Causality; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?
Word count: 312

EXACT ANSWER
A desire is a belief. Specifically, it is a judgment as to how to achieve gratification of a certain kind.

I want to eat that piece of cake. If I believed that cake to be made of chalk-dust or mud, I wouldn't want to eat it. The reason: I'd believe that eating it would not be a source of gratification. By the same token, since I believe that eating that piece of cake would be exquisitely pleasurable, I do want to eat it. My desire to eat that piece of cake, I therefore submit, is identical with a judgment on my part: a judgment to the effect that eating it would be pleasurable.

The same logic governs aversion. I don't currently want to drink the contents of that bottle of dishwashing detergent. The reason: I believe that it would bring me no joy and much distress. But I would want to drink from that bottle if I thought it to contain a non-addictive, side-effect-free elixir that induced a state of euphoria. Conclusion: My desire to abstain from consuming the contents of that bottle is a judgment: a judgment to the effect that failing to so abstain would bring me much grief.

This has a crucial consequence. One doesn't have to have a belief to be in an unpleasant state. But one does have to have a belief if one is to have a desire to alleviate or otherwise respond to that state. One doesn't have a desire to take a pill unless one has a belief as to what taking that pill will do. And if one has such a belief, one has the corresponding desire.

So a desire is not a raw urge. It is a belief about what will bring gratification—and, at a higher level, "a desire is a belief as to how to achieve gratification of a certain kind."

Kuczynski 030 — PASS
Question: Why is an intention not identical with one's strongest desire?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 9
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Do We Think in Words?; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8
Word count: 289

EXACT ANSWER
The empiricist identification of intention with strongest desire is false. Davidson holds "that what one intends to do in a given context C is identical with what one most wants to do in C," and that "one's C-intention is one's strongest C-desire." This is a mistake.

Consider the gunman. "A man sticks a gun in my face and says: 'Your money or your life.'" Do I want to give him my money? The empiricist says yes, since I want to live. But "I want to live. But that doesn't mean I want to do all the things that are involved in staying alive." Someone may need a leg amputated to survive, but they don't want to lose the leg. "What they want is to live."

So too here: "I don't want to give the gunman my money." I have no desire to hand it over. I see it as "a grim concession I must make to circumstances that I wholeheartedly wish I didn't have to make."

What is my intention, then? "My intention to give the gunman my money is not a desire. It is a judgment." Specifically, "a judgment that I'll be better off if I give the gunman my money than if I don't."

This is not ambivalence. Ambivalence is wanting both to do and to refrain from X—as when I love my mother and want to give her a present, but am angry and also want not to. That is not the robbery case. There, I simply lack the desire altogether.

The deeper error is treating all motivated behavior as desire-driven. Much of it is judgment-driven. Even Frankfurt's higher-order desires often turn out to be judgments in disguise: "Many a so-called HOD is really a judgment."

Kuczynski 031 — PASS
Question: Can a desire remain present when it is outweighed by another desire?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 4
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Why Does Alcoholics Anonymous Work?; Causality; Do We Think in Words?
Word count: 298

EXACT ANSWER
Yes. A desire does not vanish simply because it is outweighed. This is the central error in the empiricist conflation of intention with desire.

Consider the armed robbery. A man sticks a gun in my face and says: "Your money or your life." I hand over the money. Does that mean I want to give him my money? No. "I want to live. But that doesn't mean I want to do all the things that are involved in staying alive."

The empiricist—Davidson, for instance—holds "that what one intends to do in a given context C is identical with what one most wants to do in C." This is false. What actually happens is that I judge "that, if I am to gratify a relatively strong desire (my desire to live) I must forego gratification of a relatively weak one (my desire to hold on to my money)."

But here is the crucial point: "Desires don't cease to exist when they are outweighed." The desire for my money remains fully present. If the gunman dropped dead of a heart attack, "I couldn't be happier." That reaction is only intelligible if the desire was still there, still operative, still mine.

The objection will come: "One can both want to not do something and also to do it. One can be ambivalent." Yes—but that is not what is happening here. Ambivalence is wanting both to do and to refrain. What I am describing is different: I want to live and I want my money, and one outweighs the other without extinguishing it.

This distinction matters for ethics too. When I steal from Smith to save my children, my obligation not to steal "did not cease to exist. It was merely outweighed." Remorse remains appropriate precisely because the outweighed thing was real.

Kuczynski 032 — PASS
Question: How are values related to agency?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 20
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Causality; Why Does Alcoholics Anonymous Work?; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 286

EXACT ANSWER
Values are not merely related to agency—they constitute it. To value something is to see it as conducive to the consolidation or enlargement of one's agency. This is the core of my position.

I hold that "to value something, I propose, is to see it as conducive to the consolidation or enlargement of one's agency." We value reading Mill over Harlequin romances because the former fortifies our agency. We value Bach over hip-hop for the same reason.

But there is a deeper norm beneath all others. "That norm is given by the proposition that what we should value is the extension and consolidation of agency. This particular value is the ur-value - the value underlying all values."

Why does agency occupy this foundational role? Because "it is only to the extent that one's behavior is guided by superstructure-specific desires that one is acting, rather than reflexively reacting. Therefore, it is only to that extent that one is an agent."

The connection runs both ways. Agency requires value-sensitivity, and value-sensitivity requires agency. "Value-drivenness is the glue that makes a multiplicity of otherwise disconnected mental states constitute a single subject." Without it, there is no subject at all—only "a sequence of mental states that, although associated with some body, don't jointly form a single mind."

This is why "the essence of subjecthood is sensitivity to value and, therefore, to a kind of proto-morality, if not a bona fide morality." Morality has far deeper roots than we typically acknowledge.

The practical upshot: "If you see values as yours to accept or reject, you are less likely to be duped by moralistic propaganda into reducing yourself." Values are the nucleus of agency. To surrender them is to void the self.

Kuczynski 033 — PASS
Question: Why must an agent value truth in order to value anything?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 3
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Causality
Word count: 301

EXACT ANSWER
The agent must value truth because valuing anything at all presupposes it. "To value X is to believe it a truth that X has some virtue or other. If one doesn't value the truth, one can't see X as inherently better than non-X."

This is not a moral exhortation. It is a structural fact about agency. Consider the person who retreats into fantasy. "His very own mind is the virtual reality machine. So he isn't aware of the difference between fact and fiction. He sees them as interchangeable. This means he no longer has the concept of truth and therefore cannot value the truth. This means that he values nothing."

The inhabitant of virtual reality is a different case entirely. "The inhabitant of virtual reality is all too aware of the distinction between fact and fiction; it is because he is aware of it that he chose to live in virtual-reality." He retains the concept of truth, and therefore retains the capacity to value. The fantasist loses both at once.

Now consider what this means for connection. "The ability to have such a connection presupposes the ability to have values; and it thus presupposes that one values the truth, since one must value the truth to value anything." So even a criminal meaningfully connected to but one other human being "has values and thus has the psychological architecture needed to mediate value-driven ideation. This, in turn, means that he is an agent."

The psychopath is the limiting case. "The fact that the psychopath can't value anyone or anything means" he lacks the architecture of agency itself. This is why "only agents can be evil and only agents can be criminals." Evil is not mere harm; it is "generalized, rigidified hate" — and hate, like any valuation, requires the truth-concept it presupposes.

Kuczynski 034 — PASS
Question: What distinguishes evil from hatred?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 2
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Why Does Alcoholics Anonymous Work?
Word count: 325

EXACT ANSWER
Evil is generalized, rigidified hate. Hatred is person-specific; evil is not.

"Everyone hates someone, but not everyone is evil. But the concept of evil must be understood in terms of that of hate. Evil is generalized, rigidified hate. So whereas your hatred is person-specific, its target being Jerry, Stalin's was not, its target being humanity itself."

That is the core distinction. Your hatred has a face. You hate Jerry because Jerry wronged you, or because Jerry is contemptible, or because Jerry stands in your way. The target is bounded, particular, and — crucially — finite. Evil has no such boundary. Its target is humanity itself.

This matters because it tells us what evil is not. Evil is not merely intense hatred. Intensity is a matter of degree; generality is a matter of kind. A man who hates his brother with murderous intensity is not thereby evil. A man whose hatred has been abstracted from every particular person and redirected at the category "human" — that man is evil.

The distinction also tracks agency. "Only agents can be evil and only agents can be criminals, and a given agent can be both." Wickedness and criminality are not mutually exclusive. But neither is identical to evil. The criminal may act from greed, passion, or necessity. The evil agent acts from a hatred that has lost its object and found a species.

There is a further point about psychological architecture. The capacity to value anything presupposes the capacity to value the truth. "The ability to have such a connection presupposes the ability to have values; and it thus presupposes that one values the truth, since one must value the truth to value anything." The evil agent retains this architecture — he is still an agent — but his valuations have been captured by a generalized negation.

Hatred can be rational. Evil cannot. Hatred responds to a perceived wrong; evil responds to nothing in particular and therefore to everything.

Kuczynski 035 — PASS
Question: What makes unconscious mental activity necessary for explaining conscious thought?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 8
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Do We Think in Words?; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Causality; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 357

EXACT ANSWER
Unconscious mental activity is not a speculative add-on to psychology. It is a precondition of any coherent account of conscious thought whatsoever.

Consider what conscious episodes actually are. "Freud proposed that conscious psychological episodes are installments in sequences of events large portions of which are constituted by unconscious psychological activity." If that is right, "psychological reality is continuous and law-governed, notwithstanding the erratic and discontinuous nature of activity within the sphere of consciousness." The stream of consciousness is a surface phenomenon. The stream of psychology runs beneath it.

This is why the empiricist program collapses. "There is no way to understand the concept of repression in strictly empiricist terms, the same being true of the concept of rationalization." These are not empirical discoveries that could have gone otherwise. "These are definitional truths. Repressed ideation is by definition unconscious, and rationalizations by definition involve a bifurcation of mental activity into conscious and unconscious strata."

And the deeper point: "What is unconscious is by definition what is unintrospectible. The unconscious, by definition, can be known only through inference, so far as it can be known at all."

So the necessity is structural, not optional. "The hypothesis that there is unconscious mental activity is the ultimate deviation from the strictures of empiricism. But there is no way to explain conscious mental activity except on the assumption that there is unconscious mental activity."

Why? Because most of the work is already done before consciousness arrives. "Most data-synthesis occurs below the threshold of consciousness." When you walk into a room, "you automatically upload a mass of information and you automatically make many inferences from that data." The uploading "doesn't need your conscious cooperation. If it did, you'd know very little indeed."

Even your intentions betray this. My intention to build a trading platform "developed on the basis of judgments made in response to a wide range of situations and linked together by protracted and therefore largely unconscious thought-processes." It would be "extraordinarily odd if intentions of this kind were identical with constituents of consciousness."

Hence the sterility of empiricist psychology. The unconscious is not a rival to consciousness. It is its condition.

Kuczynski 036 — PASS
Question: How is repression possible?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 15
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Causality; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8
Word count: 236

EXACT ANSWER
Repression is possible because the mind is not a seamless unity. It is a composite of parts that communicate badly, and this imperfect architecture is what makes both repression and self-deception possible in the first place.

My position rests on three facts. First, "the mind is not a perfectly unified entity; it consists of various parts that communicate with each other only very imperfectly. The right hand doesn't always know what the left is doing." Second, there are two ways of being aware of a thing—knowledge by acquaintance and knowledge by description. Third, there are two senses in which a mental content can be conscious: it can be a constituent of consciousness, or it can be something of which one is conscious.

Given this, repression splits into two kinds. Repression1 "involves inaction"—it is "a failure to perform the operations by which one customarily generates one's beliefs." One suspects, but declines to verify. Repression2 "does involve already formed beliefs. The essence of repression2 is dissociation."

The conventional picture is incoherent. It claims the subject "knowingly drives it into his unconscious" while the repressed content "is constantly struggling to break into consciousness." But if he knows what he is keeping out, he is conscious of it, and "it is ipso facto unrepressed."

So repression is possible precisely because knowing is not the same as attending, and because a mind with parts can keep its own contents from itself.

Kuczynski 037 — PASS
Question: What is the difference between having a belief and knowing that one has it?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 1
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Why Does Alcoholics Anonymous Work?; Part II; Causality
Word count: 267

EXACT ANSWER
Having a belief and knowing that one has it are distinct. "One must distinguish having a given propositional attitude (or, more generally, mental content) from knowing that one has it."

The first is simply being in a state. The second is a judgment about that state. "Knowing that one feels that way involves making a judgment about one's mental state."

This distinction matters because propositional attitudes do not present themselves directly. "Propositional attitudes never make an appearance in consciousness in propria persona---or, rather, they do so, but only in the indirect sense in which rocks and trees do."

What is in consciousness is at best a representative or derivative of the attitude. "What is in consciousness; i.e., what is constitutive of consciousness, is at best some representative or derivative of a propositional attitude."

So you can feel anger without recognizing it as anger. You can want something without knowing you want it. The attitude is present; the meta-cognition about it is not.

This is not mere ignorance. "Self-deception seems to presuppose that, at some level, one has knowledge of the thing of which one lacks conscious knowledge."

That is the crucial point. Self-deception requires that the attitude be present and operative while remaining unrecognized at the level of judgment. "Given only that one can fail to recognize some one propositional attitude in two different conscious expressions of it, all that follows is that one is not completely transparent to oneself."

Opacity to oneself is the condition of possibility for self-deception. It is not a failure of introspection but a structural feature of how attitudes relate to consciousness.
