Kuczynski 038 — PASS
Question: Why can rationalization preserve a belief while concealing its real basis?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 7
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Why Does Alcoholics Anonymous Work?; Causality
Word count: 281

EXACT ANSWER
Rationalization preserves a belief by systematically preventing the rationalizer from seeing what he already knows. The mechanism is decontextualization.

As I argue, "the essence of rationalization is decontextualization. The very purpose of rationalizing is to isolate bodies of information that, if allowed to commingle, will lead to an awareness of the very thing one doesn't want to know."

This is why rationalizing is not lying. "To rationalize is to suppress one's own knowledge of some truth and to choose to replace it with a belief that one knows to be false (or, if true, is so only by accident) but is more comforting than its predecessor." The liar knows the truth and deceives another. The rationalizer knows the truth and deceives himself.

The trick requires two operations: "Lying to oneself" and "Inventing a story to make the lie believable." Hence the maxim: "No fraud without a fairy tale." That saying "goes double for the frauds one perpetrates on oneself."

But rationalization only works under a specific condition. "One can rationalize only if one has conflicting beliefs." If I knew RA was spurious, RA wouldn't work. The rationalization must be "largely true" — people do need breaks, people do need to cool off — but the truth is "taken out of context."

And it is never a clean success. "Few rationalizations are complete successes... But seldom are they complete failures." I don't fully accept RA, but I accept it enough to have the cigarette.

The real basis stays concealed because each cover-up demands another. "Each instance of repression2 creates a hole in one's body of knowledge that one must explain away." The result is "a loss of both ratiocinative and ethical integrity."

Kuczynski 039 — PASS
Question: Why does self-deception not require a mind divided into separate persons?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 3
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Why Does Alcoholics Anonymous Work?; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism
Word count: 297

EXACT ANSWER
Self-deception requires only that one fail to recognize a propositional attitude one actually has—not that the mind house two distinct persons. The divided-mind picture is a fiction, and a lazy one.

The first move is to separate having a mental content from knowing one has it. "One must distinguish having a given propositional attitude (or, more generally, mental content) from knowing that one has it." This distinction alone does enormous work. "One can feel a certain way towards so and so but not know it." Knowing that one feels that way "involves making a judgment about one's mental state." No second person is needed—only a missing judgment.

The second move concerns how attitudes appear in consciousness. "Propositional attitudes never make an appearance in consciousness in propria persona." What is in consciousness is "at best some representative or derivative of a propositional attitude." So the anger Smith feels toward his dad shows up as a surge, not as a labeled datum.

Now the crucial point. Self-deception is not mere ignorance. "Self-deception seems to presuppose that, at some level, one has knowledge of the thing of which one lacks conscious knowledge." That is why the divided-mind model tempts us. But the presupposition is satisfied by the structure I've described: one has the attitude, one fails to recognize it, and one's conscious expressions of it are indirect.

What follows is only that "one is not completely transparent to oneself." It does not follow that "there can be some sort of internal conflict---between what one knows and what one wants to know, between what is unconscious (because repressed) and what is conscious (because countenanced)." The conflict is between an attitude and a judgment about it, not between two persons.

Self-deception is possible because consciousness traffics in derivatives, not in attitudes themselves.

Kuczynski 040 — PASS
Question: What role does anxiety play when repression breaks down?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 3
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Why Does Alcoholics Anonymous Work?; Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8
Word count: 281

EXACT ANSWER
Anxiety is not the return of the repressed. It is the signal that the machinery of repression is failing.

When repression breaks down, the subject does not suddenly confront a fully formed piece of forbidden knowledge. What happens is subtler. As I argue, "the anxiety that the subject feels when the forces of repression1 break down isn't the result of some hitherto unconscious knowledge entering consciousness. It is the result one's own thought- processes, despite one's attempt to stymie them, following up on clues that it had good reason to believe would lead to a belief that one doesn't want to have."

The subject suspects where the inference is heading. That suspicion is not knowledge. "Suspicion isn't knowledge; and there's nothing paradoxical about not wanting to pursue suspicions that one suspects would, if pursued, lead to knowledge one would rather not have."

This is why anxiety has its peculiar quality. It is dread without an object, because the object is precisely what one refuses to let oneself identify. "One can know what sort of thing something is without knowing which thing it is."

The panic attack is the limiting case. "People have panic attacks when they are in a situation in which they are actually threatened but where they cannot admit as much without having to forfeit an inflated self-concept."

The anxiety is the price of the lie. The subject is "seriously in over his head" and "could not admit that fact to himself without his self-concept being shattered."

So anxiety plays a diagnostic role. It marks the point where the stream of thought-processes, "despite one's attempt to stymie them," keeps yielding "the very judgments that you don't want it to."

Kuczynski 041 — PASS
Question: What does Libet's experiment actually show about free will?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 18
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Why Does Alcoholics Anonymous Work?; Causality
Word count: 254

EXACT ANSWER
Libet's experiment does not show that we lack free will. It shows something more radical and more specific: that "what we thought were choices aren't."

The experiment demonstrates that the conscious event we identify with our decision—call it W—is not the intention itself. As I argue, "W is not the intention; it is an awareness of the intention." The readiness potential is the proximal psychological cause of the action, and since "an intention is the proximal psychological cause of the action," the intention precedes our conscious awareness of it.

This is the crucial point. "The Libet Experiment is not just an iteration of the very old idea that choices have causes. It is proof that we what we thought were choices aren't." It is "also proof that the center of consciousness that a person regards as the nucleus of his very self, and of his agency in particular, isn't."

What makes this so damaging is that it strikes at the compatibilist too. "By the time you make an appearance, the decision has already been made." The choices "are yours to behold, LE shows us, but not to make."

This is why I insist that "the idea that neuroscientific research 'dovetails nicely' with compatibilist views of agency is misleading." And it goes further than Freud: "Freud was not saying that your conscious decisions, or what you believe to be your conscious decisions, are lame ducks." Libet shows precisely that.

So the answer is: not that you are determined, but that you are "on the sidelines."

Kuczynski 042 — PASS
Question: Why does neural activity preceding conscious awareness not disprove agency?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 8
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Do We Think in Words?; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Causality; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism
Word count: 269

EXACT ANSWER
The neural activity preceding conscious awareness does not disprove agency because it is not a separate cause of the action. It is the early phase of a single process.

My argument turns on the structure of the event-chain. As I put it, "the suite events that Libet is studying---the event-chain comprising RP and W---does not consist of 'parts'. We therefore cannot say that some early 'part' of it is responsible for some later 'part' of it." The readiness potential is not a hidden agent that decides before you do. It is "simply the first part of a single, indivisible unit of a process that is temporally indissoluble but only the last part of which rises above the level of conscious awareness."

This is why the standard reading misfires. Some have claimed the brain-activity "is not causative of W and, therefore, that W is indeed the operative intention." I find that move unnecessary. The deeper point is that most philosophers "have taken the position that, even if that data is legitimate, it doesn't warrant a revision of any of frameworks within which philosophers have traditionally attempted to understand the nature of human 'freedom'."

Consciousness still does work. The data are "certainly consistent with, though not probative of, the supposition that W 'polices' the subject's intention to move." In general, "our 'conscious intentions'—in other words, our conscious awareness of our intentions—have the power to check and possibly otherwise modify the execution of those intentions."

So the subject who called his decision "utterly 'free'" was not deluded. He was reporting the last, conscious phase of a process that was his all along.

Kuczynski 043 — PASS
Question: What is wrong with identifying a decision with awareness of deciding?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 6
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Causality; Do We Think in Words?; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 321

EXACT ANSWER
The identification is false, and the Libet data prove it. What you experience as your decision to move your finger is not your decision to move your finger.

The reasoning is straightforward. "RP is obviously the proximal psychological cause of the action. An intention is the proximal psychological cause of the action. Therefore, RP is the intention; therefore, W is not the intention; it is an awareness of the intention." W is the conscious event you mistake for the decision itself. It isn't.

By the time W occurs, RP is nearly complete. So even if W contributed something, it would be subordinate—at most "a facilitating function." But intentions are supposed to play "a decisive role in the genesis of the corresponding actions, and W clearly does not have such a role." To insist otherwise is to take "the incoherent view that intentions did not have a decisive role in the genesis of the corresponding actions."

This is more radical than Freud. Freud held that consciousness is "like a monarch whose power, though considerable, is limited"—a weak ruler, but still a ruler. Libet shows the ruler is a puppet. "The Libet Experiment is not just an iteration of the very old idea that choices have causes. It is proof that we what we thought were choices aren't."

So what is W actually doing? It is approving or disapproving of decisions already made. "What consciousness does do, though, is either approve or disapprove of decisions already made." These approvals are experienced as decisions—"decisions to green-light an existing intention"—but that is a phenomenological disguise. If we saw them as they are, awareness would be "overburdened," since "one makes innumerably many choices within the space of a single minute."

The error, then, is mistaking the awareness of a decision for the decision itself. The "center of consciousness that a person regards as the nucleus of his very self, and of his agency in particular, isn't."

Kuczynski 044 — PASS
Question: How does unconscious preparation relate to a conscious action?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 1
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Do We Think in Words?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism
Word count: 289

EXACT ANSWER
The conscious decision is not the cause of the action. It is the last event in a chain that began elsewhere.

"What we believe to be choices that are initiated in consciousness are not initiated in consciousness; they are initiated prior to any conscious awareness of them and also far outside any such awareness." This is the core of my position. The will does not originate the act; it registers an outcome already determined beneath the threshold of awareness.

Consider what this requires. There are "two kinds of awareness: propositional and objectual." I can be aware of the tightness in my shoes without possessing the concept *tight* or *shoe*. The same architecture governs action. The unconscious processes that generate a choice are objectual — they operate without conceptual articulation — while the conscious "decision" arrives as propositional knowledge of something already underway.

This is why "knowledge requires conceptual articulation, whereas awareness does not necessarily require concepts." The unconscious prepares; consciousness reports.

The mechanism is not mysterious. "Mind-cure works by relaxing the barrier between the unconscious and unconscious minds." When that barrier is rigid, "it prevents the conscious mind from drawing on the power in the unconscious mind." When relaxed, the conscious mind draws on it — but it does not command it.

The religious analogue confirms the structure. "The religious person hasn't discovered God so much as he has projected him." The conscious experience of receiving grace is the afterimage of an unconscious production. "Religious sentiment is possible only when the barrier between consciousness and unconsciousness is relaxed."

So the relation is this: unconscious preparation is the cause; conscious action is the symptom. The feeling of having chosen is real, but it is a feeling — not an origin.

Kuczynski 045 — PASS
Question: Why does Alcoholics Anonymous work?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 20
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Why Does Alcoholics Anonymous Work?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Causality; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible
Word count: 320

EXACT ANSWER
Alcoholics Anonymous works because it achieves what the alcoholic cannot achieve alone: an entire psychic change. The alcoholic's will is shattered. As I've written, "The alcoholic's will has been completely shattered. He is internally divided: one part of him wants to drink; the other wants to live."

This internal division is the core of the disease. The alcoholic knows he cannot drink safely, yet he deceives himself into believing he can. "The two defining facts about the alcoholic's condition are his complete lack of self-control with respect to drinking and his ability to deceive himself about this fact." Will and self-knowledge—the two cornerstones of self-determination—are useless here. "Consequently, will and self-knowledge—the two cornerstones of self-determination—are useless."

The solution is surrender. "The only remaining path is to find a higher power and surrender to it." This is not a metaphor. The transformation required is so radical that "no person could possibly carry it out on his own, and a higher power is therefore necessary to effectuate this change."

Here is my secular model of what actually happens. "The alcoholic's higher power is a projection of his superego. By surrendering to it, he realigns himself with his superego, and the resulting internal unity gives him peace of mind and strength of will." The alcoholic has spent years rationalizing his conduct, so he cannot find moral guidance by looking inward. He must project his superego outward and then surrender to it.

The mechanism is realignment. "Prior to surrendering to it, this person was ashamed of his drinking and drinking-related conduct and was therefore on the wrong side of his own conscience." After surrender, "he becomes less internally conflicted and his will is strengthened."

The steps operationalize this through action, not mere belief. "The Steps are operationalized through constant action, as opposed to mere intellectual acceptance." And crucially, the alcoholic must help others. "To avoid relapsing, the alcoholic must help others with their alcoholism."

Kuczynski 046 — PASS
Question: What psychological function is served by admitting powerlessness in Alcoholics Anonymous?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 15
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Why Does Alcoholics Anonymous Work?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8
Word count: 273

EXACT ANSWER
Admitting powerlessness serves a precise psychological function: it deflates the ego and thereby makes the alcoholic less egocentric. That is the core of my analysis.

The mechanism is straightforward. "Acknowledging his own powerlessness is itself a way of making him less narcissistic and, therefore, less egocentric." The ego is the faculty of control, and the alcoholic's ego has been running the show—badly. "The ego, after all, is about control, and surrendering is forfeiture of ego."

So what is being surrendered, and to whom? My hypothesis is that "the higher power to which the alcoholic is surrendering is his idealized self---his ego-ideal." This is why the move works psychologically rather than merely theologically. "The alcoholic's higher power is a projection of his superego. By surrendering to it, he realigns himself with his superego, and the resulting internal unity gives him peace of mind and strength of will."

The surrender is not self-annihilation. It is a realignment. The alcoholic has spent years rationalizing, so he "must project his superego in order to surrender to it owing to the fact that he has spent years justifying his degenerate conduct to himself."

Note the exchange being made: "The alcoholic is surrendering indolent, childish ego in exchange for action-positive, adult non-ego." He trades passive wallowing for agency. "The recovering alcoholic's shift from a passive to an active relationship to the world also serves to keep his ego in check."

This is why the transformation must be radical. Recovery requires "an entire psychic change," and "the necessary transformation is so radical that no person could possibly carry it out on his own." Powerlessness is the doorway, not the destination.

Kuczynski 047 — PASS
Question: Why is surrendering to a higher power essential in Alcoholics Anonymous?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 20
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Why Does Alcoholics Anonymous Work?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8
Word count: 259

EXACT ANSWER
Surrendering to a higher power is essential because the alcoholic's will has been shattered and cannot repair itself. As I put it, "The alcoholic's will has been completely shattered. He is internally divided: one part of him wants to drink; the other wants to live." The part that wants to drink keeps winning until the choice is quit or die. At that point, "he must acknowledge that his will is defunct and surrender to a higher power."

But here is the mechanism that matters. The higher power is not an external deity—it is a projection of the alcoholic's own superego. "In surrendering to a higher power, the alcoholic is really surrendering to some part of himself." By surrendering, "he realigns himself with his superego, and the resulting internal unity gives him peace of mind and strength of will."

Why must it be projected outward rather than confronted directly? Because the alcoholic has spent years justifying his conduct. He has made it "impossible for him to find anything other than rationalizations when he looks inwards for moral guidance." The superego must be externalized before he can submit to it.

The surrender also serves a second function: it dismantles ego. "The ego, after all, is about control, and surrendering is forfeiture of ego." Acknowledging powerlessness is itself "a way of making him less narcissistic and, therefore, less egocentric."

This is why the leap of faith is justified—not by its truth, but by its consequences. The surrender produces internal unity, peace of mind, and the strength of will required to stay sober.

Kuczynski 048 — PASS
Question: What is the difference between changing oneself and changing one's self?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 2
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Why Does Alcoholics Anonymous Work?; Part II; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 223

EXACT ANSWER
The difference is between how one is and who one is. Changing oneself is possible. Changing one's self is not.

I put it plainly: "A person can change himself, but he cannot change his self." The self is fixed. "One's identity is predetermined. Experience doesn't determine who one is; it determines how one is who one is."

This is why the distinction matters. Changes to oneself, if they are not to render one's self defunct, "must occur within limits set by one's inborn biological structure." You can alter your habits, your skills, your circumstances—the how. You cannot alter the underlying identity—the who.

The twin studies confirm this. Identical twins raised in radically different environments—"one twin would be raised in a mansion, the other in a hovel"—remained "identical in respect of their IQs, degree of spirituality, and to what degree, and in what manner, they were social or anti-social." Environment shaped the expression, not the essence.

Sally's case illustrates the failure mode. She attempted to change who she was, not how she was. "Sally is committing psychological suicide. She is trying to change who she is, not how she is." In doing so, she operated outside the limits set by her native endowment, and lost its support.

The practical upshot: self-improvement is real, but self-replacement is not. Work within your structure, not against it.

Kuczynski 049 — PASS
Question: Why is psychological identity constrained by inborn biological structure?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 5
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Do We Think in Words?
Word count: 281

EXACT ANSWER
Psychological identity is constrained by inborn biological structure because your emotional architecture is not something you chose and cannot be rebuilt at will. The range of value systems you can accept is fixed by facts about your wiring, not by preference or effort.

I put the point this way: "the range of admissible value systems is limited by immutable facts about our psychology (and biology)." This is not a soft empirical generalization. It is a structural claim about what kind of creature you are.

The Chomsky analogy makes the mechanism clear. Just as "any humanly learnable language satisfies rather narrowly defined formal constraints," so too "the range of psychologically (and biologically) admissible values is limited." You are hardwired for certain value structures the way you are hardwired for certain grammars.

The consequence is severe. "If your emotions reflect your actual values, then you don't really accept a value system that brings you misery." You can comply outwardly with a foreign value system, but compliance is not acceptance. The self does not migrate.

This is why I say "a person can change himself, but he cannot change his self." Experience determines *how* you are who you are, never *who* you are. The twin studies confirm it: identical IQs, identical spirituality, identical sociability across radically different environments.

Sally's case is the limit case. "She is trying to change who she is, not how she is. But one can't change who one is." In internalizing a sociopathic value system, she was "not operating within those limits," and so she lost "the support of her own native endowment."

The identity is the endowment. Sever it and you do not become someone else—you become no one.

Kuczynski 050 — PASS
Question: Why is the attempt to empiricize psychology not identical with making psychology scientific?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 6
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Causality; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 328

EXACT ANSWER
The attempt to empiricize psychology is not identical with making it scientific because empiricism is not science. Empiricism is a philosophical doctrine about the source and scope of knowledge; science is a practice of modeling data by positing hidden structures. Confusing the two is the central error I diagnose.

As I argue, "science is not about sticking to the facts. It is about organizing the facts, and it is therefore about positing hidden structures to restore to nature the continuities of which observation strips it." The empiricist's injunction to "stick to the facts" is "either the triviality that correct theories are fact-consistent or it's the absurdity that one can model data without extrapolating."

So when psychologists equate being scientific with being empirical, they commit a fallacy. They think "science is not about sticking to the facts"—no, they think it *is*, and thereby strip psychology of its theoretical resources.

The consequence is sterility. I speak of "the sterility of attempts to empiricize psychology and the erroneousness of attempts to identify the empiricization of psychology with the scientization of it." This is the legacy: psychology becomes "nothing but a series of disjoint ex nihilo obtrusions into an otherwise integrated, explanatorily well-behaved world."

Worse, empiricism cannot even handle introspection. "Introspection" is "an act of conceptualization, and not of theoretically innocent reportage." Hume overlooks this; Husserl tries to empiricize introspection by "stripping introspection of its conceptual component"—but "since introspection is conception, this approach is doomed to fail."

The genuine scientific question is whether psychological data admit of models. "It is a datum that there are psychological data." The scientist's job is "to model the data that he's given," not "to prejudge the significance of that data." Denying psychological data because they resist physics-friendly modeling is not science—it is "the a priori, and therefore non-empirical, assumption that physics is the only legitimate discipline."

Empiricizing psychology, then, damages it. Scientizing it requires the opposite: taking its data seriously and building theories adequate to them.

Kuczynski 051 — PASS
Question: Are there any genuinely non-extensional contexts?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 5
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Part II; Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Do We Think in Words?; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 295

EXACT ANSWER
No. There are no genuinely non-extensional contexts. Every context is substitution-tolerant.

My argument is straightforward. When two expressions that appear to refer to the same individual cannot be inter-substituted, they actually refer to different propositions. That is the whole of it. "Thus, there are no intensional contexts. (In other words, all contexts are substitution-tolerant.) Whenever two expressions that appear to refer to the same individual cannot be inter-substituted, they actually refer to different propositions."

Consider the apparent counterexamples. Take the sentence about the woman prettier than every other woman. What looks like a failure of substitution is really a shift in what is being referred to. "The real meanings of those sentences are, respectively: (3*) it is necessarily the case that any woman who is prettier than every other woman is prettier than every other woman. and (4*) it is necessarily the case that any woman who is prettier than every other woman is also more evil than every other person."

These attribute the property of being necessarily true to two distinct propositions. "Since those propositions are distinct, the fact that the one proposition is necessarily true doesn't entail that the same is true of the other; and there is thus violation of Leibniz's Law."

So the so-called intensional context is a fiction. What we actually have is reference to propositions rather than to individuals. "Thus used, an 'intensional context' in which expressions that otherwise refer to individuals (e.g., 'Benjamin Franklin') refer to propositions."

The terminology remains useful only as shorthand. "Nonetheless, the term 'intensional' is useful as a way of abbreviating otherwise hard-to-state truths."

But it names no genuine feature of the world. "A context that isn't intensional is extensional, and expressions occurring in it do so extensionally." Every context, properly understood, is extensional.

Answer type: indirect

EXACT ANSWER
The indexed corpus does not contain a direct answer to this question. I have no passage in which I define or distinguish "semantics" from "presemantics," and I will not manufacture a position on that distinction.

What the corpus does contain is adjacent material about how differences among generalizations are to be understood. I argue that "the difference between (a) and (c) is one of degree: (a) is more approximate than (c) and (a) also has less scope than (c)," yet each still "serves as a generalization on the basis of which specific situations can be evaluated." I also insist that certain differences are not statistical: "the difference between knowledge and mere belief is not statistical," and the difference between a lawlike generalization and an accidental one "is not to be understood in statistical terms" but rests on whether the connection is "rooted in his having a distinctively mammalian physiological make-up."

I further distinguish causal series by structure: "the difference between immanent and transeunt causation is that immanent causation is, whereas transeunt causation is not, structure-preserving," and in the mental case, "the differences between the Gus-caused electrical activity and its JM-caused counterpart led to no differences between the Gus-caused software activity and its JM-counterpart."

These passages concern kinds of difference—degree versus kind, statistical versus inherent, structure-preserving versus not. They do not address semantics versus presemantics. I cannot responsibly convert them into an answer to that question.

Kuczynski 053 — PASS
Question: Does the necessary a posteriori survive the semantics/presemantics distinction?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 2
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Part II; Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Do We Think in Words?
Word count: 290

EXACT ANSWER
No. The necessary a posteriori does not survive the distinction between semantics and presemantics.

My argument is straightforward. "Kripke's arguments for these views appear probative only so long as one fails to distinguish between semantics and presemantics—between the literal meanings of sentences, on the one hand, and the information on the basis of which one identifies those literal meanings, on the other."

This is the crux. Kripke argues for necessary a posteriori truths, and this view is widely accepted—but only because the distinction goes unnoticed. Once you separate the literal meaning of a sentence from the information by which you identify that meaning, the appearance of a posteriori necessity dissolves.

Consider what the necessary a posteriori requires. It requires that a truth be necessary—holding in all possible worlds—yet knowable only through experience. But necessity attaches to the proposition, to the semantics. The a posteriori character attaches to how we identify that proposition, to the presemantics. These are different registers.

"The acceptance of necessary a posteriori truths relies on a failure to distinguish semantics from presemantics." Conflate them, and necessity seems to leak into the epistemic. Separate them, and it doesn't.

The same failure runs through other cases. "What led Kant astray was a failure to distinguish the..."—and here the pattern repeats. Kant thought we have a priori knowledge of the phenomenal world, that "parallel lines don't meet in it, triangles have interior angles adding up to 180°." But "on Kant's account, even this knowledge turns to be a posteriori." The confusion is structural, not incidental.

So the necessary a posteriori is an artifact. It trades on an equivocation between what a sentence means and how we come to know what it means. Once that equivocation is exposed, the category collapses.

Kuczynski 054 — FAIL
Question: Does Frege's puzzle require a theory of sense?
Answer type: indirect
Direct evidence count: 0
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Do We Think in Words?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Causality
Word count: 260
Failure reason: The diagnostic does not accept fluent output based on indirect or absent source material.

EXACT ANSWER
No. Frege's puzzle does not require a theory of sense. It requires a theory of dependence-relations.

The puzzle is usually framed as a problem about cognitive significance: how can "a=a" and "a=b" differ in informativeness if they concern the same object? The standard move is to posit senses—modes of presentation—as intermediate entities. I reject that move. My framework treats analytic truths as expressing dependence-relations, and the Fregean cases fall under that treatment.

Consider my examples. "If P, then either P or Q" obviously expresses a dependence-relation. But so do the non-obvious cases: "There are infinitely many primes," "1+1=2," "1+1≠3." As I put it, "Analytic truths, even when not obviously so, express dependence-relations." The informativeness of "a=b" is not a matter of grasping a sense; it is a matter of grasping a dependence-relation between the identity of a and the identity of b.

And how are such truths known? Not by positing a third realm. As I argue, "Some dependence-relations are known, not through sensory observation, but through conceptual analysis," and "Analytic truths, which involve dependence-relations, are known through conceptual analysis rather than sensory observation."

So the puzzle dissolves. What Frege called "sense" is a placeholder for a dependence-relation we have not yet articulated. The work is to articulate it, not to reify it.

I have no need for senses. I need only the causal and logical structure of our world—"It is by examining the causal and logical structure of our world, not other worlds, that we know whether or not a given counterfactual is true." The same principle applies here.

Kuczynski 055 — PASS
Question: Is indirect referentialism coherent?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 1
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Part II; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Do We Think in Words?; Causality; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible
Word count: 299

EXACT ANSWER
Indirect referentialism is coherent. The apparent paradox that motivates descriptivism rests on a fallacy about communication, not a genuine problem about meaning.

The descriptivist's argument runs: "‘Hesperus is identical with Phosphorous’ communicates a significant astronomical discovery. ‘Hesperus is identical with Hesperus’ is an empty truism." From this, they conclude that "it is very hard to see how ‘Hesperus’ and ‘Phosphorous’ could be mere labels." But this inference is invalid.

My position is that "‘Hesperus has phi’ has the same literal meaning as ‘Phosphorous has phi,’" and likewise "‘Hesperus is identical with Phosphorous’ has the same literal meaning as ‘Hesperus is identical with Hesperus.’" If proper names are mere labels, then "the literal meaning of sentences with co-referring names is the same."

So where does the felt difference come from? Not from literal meaning. "Those differences are to be explained not by supposing that those sentences differ in respect of literal meaning. Rather, those differences are to be explained in terms of facts about how people ascertain the literal meanings of the sentences that they encounter."

The key insight is this: "What an occurrence of a sentence communicates to somebody isn’t always confined to its literal meaning. Isn’t necessarily even inclusive of its literal meaning." Communication and meaning come apart.

The supposed paradox dissolves once we see that "to hear a sentence is not to hear a proposition. One must make one’s way from the physical noise that one hears." The route from noise to proposition varies with the hearer's epistemic situation—but the destination, the literal meaning, does not.

Therefore, "communicative differences arise from how people ascertain meanings, not from literal meaning differences." Indirect referentialism "can account for communicative differences without denying that co-referring names have the same literal meaning." The fallacy that underlies this supposed paradox is easily exposed.

Kuczynski 056 — PASS
Question: Does Russell's Theory of Descriptions correctly analyze definite descriptions?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 9
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Part II; Causality; Do We Think in Words?; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism
Word count: 231

EXACT ANSWER
Yes. Russell's Theory of Descriptions correctly analyzes definite descriptions, and the proof lies in negative existentials.

Consider "the monster under little Timmy's bed doesn't exist." This sentence is true. But if "the monster under little Timmy's bed" referred to something, "it wouldn't be true, since there would then exist some monster under little Timmy's bed to which that definite description referred." Russell's insight is that we must reparse. The needed reparsing yields: "the property of being a monster under little Timmy's bed isn't instantiated." That property exists—"there is a way something would have to be in order to be such a monster"—but nothing has it. Problem solved.

The same machinery handles "the fountain of youth exists." Its grammatical form is not to be trusted. "Appropriately reparsed, that sentence becomes: 'the property of being a fountain of youth is uniquely instantiated.'" Ponce de Leon's belief is not about an object but about a property's instantiation.

This is why "definite descriptions aren't referring terms. No definite description refers to anything." The meaning of "the inventor of Velcro" isn't given denotatively but contextually—by saying what whole sentences containing it mean. In general, "for any property phi, ‹the phi› is defined, not denotatively, but contextually."

The word "the" itself signals this: it "obviously indicates existence (unlike the word 'no') and also uniqueness (unlike the word 'a')." Descriptions are quantifiers, not singular terms. Russell was right.

Kuczynski 057 — PASS
Question: Are proper names rigid designators?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 9
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Part II; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Causality; Do We Think in Words?
Word count: 263

EXACT ANSWER
Yes. Proper names are rigid designators, and the reason is semantic, not metaphysical.

My criterion is this: "E 'rigidly designates' x if there is no possible world that is semantically just like ours where E fails to designate x." A proper name satisfies this because its reference is fixed by a semantic rule that picks out its object directly, regardless of what properties that object happens to have.

Consider "Barack Obama." "Given that 'Barack Obama' refers to Barack Obama, it couldn't possibly fail to refer to him in a world that is semantically like ours." It could fail only in a world where the semantic rules themselves differ.

Contrast this with definite descriptions. "'The inventor of bifocals' refers to Bob Denver in some possible worlds, to Walt Disney in others, and so on." Descriptions are non-rigid because they pick out whatever satisfies them.

The same holds for "Venus." "If x is what 'Venus' in fact refers to, x is what 'Venus' would refer to in any world semantically like ours." But "'the LMS,' like 'the current U.S. President,' is not a rigid designator; it refers to different things in semantically identical situations."

So I conclude: "In general, proper names are rigid designators." "Hesperus" and "Phosphorous" are proper names, hence rigid. This is why "Hesperus is Phosphorous" expresses a non-analytic necessary truth.

The mechanism is direct reference. "Hesperus" picks out its object "not because it has this or that property," but because "the semantic rule for 'Hesperus' is to the effect that, no matter what properties O has, 'Hesperus' is to pick it out."

Kuczynski 059 — PASS
Question: Do substitution failures in belief contexts prove intensionality?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 5
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Causality; Part II; Do We Think in Words?; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means
Word count: 321

EXACT ANSWER
No. Substitution failures in belief contexts do not prove intensionality—they prove that the expressions in question refer to different propositions.

My argument is straightforward. "Whenever two expressions that appear to refer to the same individual cannot be inter-substituted, they actually refer to different propositions." The apparent failure is not a failure of substitutivity at all; it is a failure of co-reference. The expressions only appeared to refer to the same thing.

Consider the classic case. Take "it is necessarily the case that any woman who is prettier than every other woman is prettier than every other woman" and "it is necessarily the case that any woman who is prettier than every other woman is also more evil than every other person." The first attributes the property of being necessarily true to one proposition; the second expresses that same property to a different proposition. "Since those propositions are distinct, the fact that the one proposition is necessarily true doesn't entail that the same is true of the other."

So there is no violation of Leibniz's Law here. Leibniz's Law is not breached when two expressions fail to inter-substitute, because they were never referring to the same individual in the first place.

My conclusion is uncompromising: "Thus, there are no intensional contexts. (In other words, all contexts are substitution-tolerant.)" Every context—modal, moral, causal, doxastic—behaves the same way. "Given any context—modal, moral, causal, etc.—an argument exactly similar to the one just given shows that replacing a name occurring in that context with a co-referring name cannot possibly lead from truth to falsity, at least not at the level of semantics."

The word "intensional" remains useful, but only as shorthand. "An 'intensional context' in which expressions that otherwise refer to individuals (e.g., 'Benjamin Franklin') refer to propositions." That is all it means. It is not a distinct semantic phenomenon; it is a convenient label for cases where we have misidentified what the expressions refer to.

Kuczynski 060 — PASS
Question: Is conceptual atomism true?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 4
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Causality; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Do We Think in Words?; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means
Word count: 277

EXACT ANSWER
No. Conceptual atomism fails for the same reason logical atomism fails: there are no non-composite truths.

The atomist needs "atoms" of nature in a logical sense—simple truths out of which complex ones are built. But "any given truth is entailed by infinitely many others and itself entails infinitely many truths." Since "a statement's entailment-relations (what it entails and what it entails it) reflect its structure, there are no 'ultimate', foundational truths."

So the atomist's building blocks don't exist. "Consequently, there are, in this sense, no 'atoms' of nature—no non-composite truths out of which other truths can be constructed or from which they can be derived."

Even granting minimal units of physical composition doesn't rescue the view. "Given only that these entities are physically simple (or at least relatively so), it doesn't follow that the truths that describe them, and in terms of which we are to understand them, are correspondingly simple." In fact, "because these entities are known in a such a theory-mediated way, those truths are exceptionally complex."

The consequence is stark: "even if there are 'atoms' (minimal building blocks) of nature, they are not building blocks in a logical sense—on the contrary, they are, in that respect, at the opposite extreme of the epistemological pyramid."

Consider "1+1=2." It "could function as an axiom (an accepted truth that neither requires nor admits of justification) or (as is the case in set theory), it could function as the end-result of a long chain of reasoning." Which role it plays "depends on the dialectical context." That context-relativity is fatal to atomism.

Summary: "Atoms, in the sense in which the philosophy of logical atomism requires them to exist, don't."

Kuczynski 061 — PASS
Question: Is meaning determined by use?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 15
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Part II; Do We Think in Words?
Word count: 285

EXACT ANSWER
No. Meaning is not determined by use, and Wittgenstein's doctrine that "meaning is use" is incoherent on multiple levels.

Start with the simplest point. "A meaningless burst of noise isn't an expression." If I cough or guffaw, that noise has no linguistic meaning at all. So there can be no expression-use until after there is expression-meaning. As I put it, "since there can be no expression-use until after there is expression-meaning, it makes no sense at all to say that expression-use determines expression-meaning." The slogan inverts the actual order of dependence.

The deeper error is conflating two very different claims. There is all the difference in the world between saying that an expression's meaning is *causally determined* by its use, and saying that its meaning *is identical with* its use. The first is innocuous—"probable" once meant "capable of being definitively established," and enough people used it otherwise that its meaning shifted. The second is false: "An expression E's having meaning M cannot possibly be constituted by its being used in such and such a manner, since E isn't an expression and, therefore, isn't an expression to be used until it has a meaning."

Meaning guides use, not the reverse. "I know what 'hug' means; I also know what 'discuss' means. That's why, when talking to my students, I say 'I want to discuss the exam,' and not 'I want to hug the exam.'" If meaning were use, meaning couldn't guide use. But it obviously does.

This is why the Wittgensteinian exhortation to study concepts by studying word-use collapses. "One can't learn about C by studying E unless one can grasp C, and can therefore examine it, without E's help." Conceptual role semantics fares no better.

Kuczynski 062 — PASS
Question: Is linguistic understanding a body of knowledge or an ability?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 4
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Do We Think in Words?; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Part II; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism
Word count: 288

EXACT ANSWER
Linguistic understanding is both—but not in the way the dichotomy suggests. It is knowledge-how that is constituted by knowledge-that.

The argument that skill and propositional knowledge are "fundamentally different things" fails. Consider: "No matter how much I know about the physics and geometry of bike-riding, I may not be able to ride a bike at all; and no matter how good I am at riding a bike, I may not be able to tell you the first thing about the geometry or physics involved." This shows bike-riding is procedural all along—it never was declarative. But language is different.

"Knowledge of a language is knowledge-how. To be able to speak English is to have a skill. But that skill involves having knowledge-that, for you must know various syntactic and semantic truths (e.g., the truth that 'snow' picks out snow) to speak English." The skill is real, but it is not free-floating.

My thesis is precise: "Knowledge of a language is operationalized semantic and syntactic knowledge. In general, procedural knowledge is operationalized declarative knowledge." The declarative content is not something you consult before speaking—it is built into the procedure itself.

This is why "one has no conscious access to the declarative knowledge internal to one's procedural knowledge." You do not recite rules before uttering a sentence. But the rules are there, operative.

The competence/performance distinction clarifies this. "Competence is ability"—but ability grounded in grasp of principles. When I grasp a semantic rule, "knowledge of how to apply SR is built into knowledge of SR. Knowledge of secondary principles is no part of the story."

So linguistic understanding is an ability. But it is an ability that is knowledge of truths, operationalized. Not one or the other—both, in the right relation.

Kuczynski 063 — PASS
Question: Is the computational theory of mind true?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 1
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Do We Think in Words?; Causality; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?
Word count: 241

EXACT ANSWER
The computational theory of mind is false, and it fails for the same reason functionalism fails: it strips awareness of its causal efficacy.

My argument is direct. "Functionalizing one's awareness of P strips that awareness of causal efficacy, and functionalism is therefore false." The computational theory of mind is functionalism in machine form—it identifies mental states with their functional roles, their input-output profiles, their position in a computational architecture. If functionalism is false, so is its computational variant.

Here is the deeper problem. A theory can be "extensionally correct but intensionally incorrect if the facts are consistent for the wrong reason." The computational theory may predict the right outputs while misdescribing what is actually happening. It gets the behavior right for the wrong reason.

I distinguish intensional from extensional correctness sharply. "A theory is intensionally correct if there are no counterexamples to it and the reason there are no counterexamples to it is that it is a correct description of what it's supposed to describe." Computation describes the wrong thing.

The analogy to my Martian case is exact. A theory that "there will be at least 10 articles of furniture in Olin 310 on Thursday due to an invisible Martian" can be extensionally correct while intensionally bankrupt. The computational theory of mind is that Martian. It predicts, but it does not explain.

Consciousness has causal efficacy. Computation, as a formal structure, does not. Therefore computation cannot be what the mind is.

Kuczynski 064 — PASS
Question: Is any mentation subpersonal?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 14
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Do We Think in Words?; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8
Word count: 311

EXACT ANSWER
Yes. Subpersonal mentation exists, and it is the foundation of everything we call thinking.

I distinguish two strata of mind. The personal stratum is "the totality of mental events within one's own mind that could in principle fall within the scope of introspective awareness." The subpersonal stratum is everything else—the cognitive processes that mediate perception, language-comprehension, and inference. As I put it, "the cognitive processes mediating language-comprehension, perception, etc., are not done by you, even though they happen in your mind. There is thus a sense in which they are impersonal (or subpersonal)."

This is not a minor architectural detail. It has a striking consequence: "Subpersonal mentation is inherently intelligent. Personal mentation is inherently unintelligent." Consciousness, on its own, traffics only in pictures and sensations. "Consciousness qua consciousness is not intelligent; to the extent that it mediates thought, it mediates picture-thought, which is the lowest form of thought." And: "whatever intelligence is to be found in the personal stratum of awareness is bequeathed to it by the subpersonal."

So the intelligence you experience as your own thinking is borrowed. It originates below the threshold of introspection.

Chomsky deserves credit for first delineating this concept and putting it to scientific use. But the idea has deeper roots. "There are allusions to the subpersonal in Chapter VII of Freud's work The Interpretation of Dreams," and "The main contention of Kant's Critique of Pure Reason presupposes its existence."

Two unconsciousnesses must therefore be distinguished: "the personal (Freudian) unconscious and the impersonal (Chomskyan) unconscious." The Freudian unconscious is recoverable through psychoanalytic intervention; the Chomskyan one never is. "No amount of psychoanalytic intervention could make you introspectively aware of them, and they are therefore 'deeply' unconscious."

Rationality, finally, is personal intelligence deployed to one's advantage. Dogs have subpersonal intelligence but are sub-rational—not irrational, since "irrationality is corrupted rationality; so irrationality is a prerogative of rational beings."

Kuczynski 065 — PASS
Question: Are propositional attitudes relations to sentences?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 1
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Part II; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Causality
Word count: 247

EXACT ANSWER
No. Propositional attitudes are not relations to sentences.

My argument against them is straightforward. "The belief that there are propositional attitudes is part of folk-psychology." And "We don't put any stock in folk-physics or folk-physiology." So "Ceteris paribus, we shouldn't put any stock in folk-psychology." The conclusion follows: "Propositional attitudes don't exist."

If they don't exist, they can't be relations to anything—sentences included.

But suppose we grant the framework for a moment. Even then, the relation couldn't be to sentences. Consider what a sentence is. "No series of noises is a sentence-type: an ink-deposit is, at most, a sentence-token." And "Given some ink-deposit, which sentence-type it tokens is a function of what it means." That's the crucial point: "A series of noises acoustically just like utterances of the English sentence 'snow is white' could mean anything." So "Sentence-types are not individuated by the physical properties of their tokens."

Meaning comes first. The sentence is downstream.

This is why I hold that "Logical dependence-relations hold among propositions," and "A proposition is a truth or a falsehood." Propositions are the relata—not sentences, not tokens, not noises.

So the question misfires twice. First, propositional attitudes don't exist to stand in any relation. Second, even if we posited them, sentences are the wrong relatum—they're individuated by meaning, not the other way around.

Speaking personally, it was only after trying to defend the negation of that view, and finding that it was impossible to do so, that I came to accept it.

Kuczynski 066 — FAIL
Question: Is intentionality reducible to causal covariation?
Answer type: indirect
Direct evidence count: 0
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Causality; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 242
Failure reason: The diagnostic does not accept fluent output based on indirect or absent source material.

EXACT ANSWER
No. Intentionality cannot be reduced to causal covariation, and my work on the Counterfactual Analysis of Causality shows exactly why the reduction fails.

The covariation theorist needs causal truths to convert cleanly into counterfactual truths. But "in general, where there is causal redundancy, causal truths cannot be converted into counterfactual truths." That is the core problem.

Consider my hunter case. Suppose it is true that "The bird died because Smith shot it." Now suppose Smith was part of a pack of hunters, each of whom would have shot the bird had Smith not done so. Then "If Smith hadn't shot it, the bird would not have died" is not a consequence of the causal truth. The covariation is broken precisely where the causal relation holds.

This matters for intentionality because mental content exhibits the same structure. A belief can be about its object even when the counterfactual covariation fails—when other mechanisms would have produced the same state, or when the state would have occurred regardless of the specific antecedent.

My broader argument is that "CAC is intensionally false." The theory is not merely incomplete; it misdescribes what it purports to describe. And "CACD fails to account for causal redundancy and the non-contingency of event identity on specific causes in multiple scenarios."

Intentionality inherits this failure. Content is not a covariation relation. It is a normative, aboutness-constituting relation that survives the collapse of counterfactual dependence.

This topic warrants deeper exploration—consider increasing word count.

Kuczynski 067 — PASS
Question: Can a machine mean anything by what it outputs?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 1
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Part II; Do We Think in Words?; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6
Word count: 284

EXACT ANSWER
No. A machine cannot mean anything by what it outputs, because meaning is not use, and it is certainly not mere production of tokens.

My argument against the use theory of meaning applies with full force here. "Meaning cannot be use. One reason is there are meaningful expressions that are never used literally and infinitely many that aren't used at all." A machine's output is just such a case—it may be produced, but production is not use in the sense that matters.

Consider the coffee machine. "If, by some freak accident, a coffee machine were to produce noises homophonic with a token of 'I'm badly hurt; please send an ambulance'; it wouldn't be saying anything." The same holds for any computational system. Homophony with a meaningful sentence is not meaning.

The deeper point concerns what meaning attaches to. "What can be inferred from a given token of it obviously depends on the circumstances, and not just on its literal meaning." But circumstances only matter because there is a fixed, circumstance-invariant meaning to begin with. "The right conclusion to draw about 'I'm in the room right next door to yours' is that it has a fixed, circumstance-invariant meaning, but that the meaning of that meaning is circumstance-dependent."

A machine has no fixed meaning to be circumstance-dependent on. It has no semantic anchor.

Wittgenstein's inference from context-sensitivity to meaning-as-use is already a mistake. "On the basis of the fact that any given sentence can be used to convey anything, given the right circumstances, Wittgenstein infers that expressions don't have fixed meanings." That inference is as bad as concluding a rock got lighter because X lifted it after Y failed.

Machines produce outputs. They do not mean.

Kuczynski 068 — PASS
Question: Is thought prior to language or language to thought?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 17
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Do We Think in Words?; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Part II; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology
Word count: 228

EXACT ANSWER
Thought is prior to language. Language is a tool that thought uses, not the medium in which thought consists.

My position is straightforward: "whatever one can grasp through language, one must be able to grasp independently of language." This is counterintuitive, I grant. But I came to it only after trying to defend the negation and finding it impossible.

The first reason is decisive. "We can obviously have thoughts that we are incapable of putting into words." If grasping a thought required grasping the sentence that expresses it, this would be impossible. It isn't. Moreover, "there are occasions where, although we can put into words what we are thinking, doing so requires great effort." That effort proves thinking precedes articulation.

Wittgenstein, Blackburn, and McDowell deny this. "If you can't say it, you don't know it," they say. This is false. "A given person's beliefs can be expressed in many ways, and many of them don't depend on that person's being able to use words."

Consider that "people who speak different languages can have the same thoughts." A monolingual Spanish speaker and a monolingual English speaker both believe 1 + 1 = 2. Different sentences, same thought. So thought cannot be identical with any sentence-token.

Wittgenstein held that "one can't think unless one knows a language." He was wrong. Language enormously enhances cognition, but it does not constitute it.

Kuczynski 069 — PASS
Question: Is skepticism refutable?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 4
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism
Word count: 273

EXACT ANSWER
Skepticism about the external world is refutable, but only if we get the logic of explanation right. My central claim is that "skepticism about the external world is actually an extravagant and irrational position." It is not the cautious, conservative stance it pretends to be.

The reason is analytic. Given two otherwise comparable theories, "the one that leaves us with fewer anomalies is the one that ought to be preferred." This is not an inductive generalization; it is an analytic truth about what it means to explain. And the skeptic's denial of this "embodies an analytically false conception of explanation."

Run the machinery. Your sensory experience is full of discontinuities. "Every time you open your eyes or turn your head, you are flooded with sensory experiences that are totally unlike those that you were experiencing a moment earlier." The non-skeptic says these are links in causal chains whose other links you don't perceive. The skeptic says they "come into existence ex nihilo." The first theory explains the discontinuities; the second multiplies them. So the first is rationally preferable.

This refutes Hume's argument. "Hume is wrong; Hume's argument fails. This is a direct consequence of Step 5."

But I must be honest about the limits. I have written that "Speaking frankly, I'm not 100% that I believe what I'm saying in this passage." The refutation of Hume's analysis of induction is cogent; the analysis of scientific explanation is cogent. What I don't fully believe is "my attempt to base a refutation of skepticism on that attempt." So skepticism is refutable in principle—but my own execution of the refutation is not adequate as it stands.

Kuczynski 070 — FAIL
Question: What is the relation between knowledge by description and knowledge by acquaintance?
Answer type: indirect
Direct evidence count: 0
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Do We Think in Words?; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible
Word count: 236
Failure reason: The diagnostic does not accept fluent output based on indirect or absent source material.

EXACT ANSWER
The relation is one of presupposition, not parity. Knowledge by description is parasitic on knowledge by acquaintance, and the dependency runs in one direction only.

My argument turns on information-transmission. "Knowledge is initially acquired through information-transmission series—our thoughts inherit their structures from our perceptions, which inherit their structures from the corresponding externalities." Acquaintance is that first link: the perceptual inheritance of structure from what is encountered. Description is what we build afterward, when we "acquire knowledge of non-information-transmissive evidential relations."

The consequence is strict: "Knowledge of non-information-transmissive evidential relations presupposes knowledge of information-transmissive series." You cannot describe your way into a first encounter. Every descriptive chain terminates in something that was, at some point, simply met.

This is not a psychological claim about learning order. It is a structural one. Description traffics in propositions; acquaintance traffics in objects. As I put it, "Logical dependence is interpropositional, while causal dependence is objectual and pertains to space-time entities." Descriptive knowledge is interpropositional—it relates claims to claims. Acquaintance is objectual—it relates a knower to an occupant of the manifold.

So the two are not two species of one genus. Description is a network of propositions whose warrant ultimately rests on contact. Strip away acquaintance and description has nothing to be about.

Inference: this asymmetry also explains why descriptive knowledge can be transmitted between minds while acquaintance cannot. I can hand you a proposition. I cannot hand you my perception.

Kuczynski 071 — FAIL
Question: Must a justified believer be able to state his reasons?
Answer type: indirect
Direct evidence count: 0
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Why Does Alcoholics Anonymous Work?; Causality; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Part II
Word count: 244
Failure reason: The diagnostic does not accept fluent output based on indirect or absent source material.

EXACT ANSWER
No. A justified believer need not be able to state his reasons.

My account of knowledge runs: "If you know it, then (i) You believe it, (ii) It is true, and (iii) Your reasons for believing it are legitimate." That is the knowledge relation. But justification is a distinct matter, and I have argued that "All knowledge justified true belief but not vice versa." The asymmetry is the whole point.

The broken clock case makes this vivid. "Given only that it's true and that you are justified in believing it, it doesn't follow that you know it." A man glancing at a stopped clock at noon holds a true, justified belief. He cannot state his reasons—there are none worth stating—yet the belief is justified by the read-out. "If your belief that it's noon is based on the read-out of a broken clock, it isn't knowledge, even if that clock happens to be right."

So the capacity to articulate reasons is not a condition on justification. It is at most a condition on a certain kind of knowledge—the kind where the believer can marshal his grounds.

Testimony sharpens the point. "A belief based on the testimony of a dishonest person is knowledge, so long as the testimony in question was information-transmissive." The recipient may be unable to state why he trusts the speaker. What matters is the transmission, not the recitation.

Justification tracks the legitimacy of the grounds, not the believer's ability to voice them.

Kuczynski 072 — PASS
Question: Is the Gettier problem a real problem?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 4
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Causality; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible
Word count: 257

EXACT ANSWER
Yes. The Gettier problem is a real problem, and it demolishes the traditional definition of knowledge.

The traditional account held that knowledge is justified true belief. Gettier showed this is false. As I put it, "There can be justified true beliefs that are not knowledge, as shown by the Smith-Jones example." That is the whole game. If you can have a justified true belief that still fails to be knowledge, then justification, truth, and belief together are not sufficient.

The structure of the counterexample is precise. "For something to be knowledge, it is necessary that it be true, a belief, and justified." Those three conditions are necessary. But necessity is not sufficiency. Gettier's cases prove the gap: "It shows that, for something to be knowledge, it is not sufficient that it satisfy conditions (1)–(3), even though, for the reasons discussed earlier, it is necessary."

Russell saw the same thing earlier. "Bertrand Russell's example shows that a belief can be true and justified but not knowledge due to the fluke nature of its truth." The truth arrives by accident, not by the epistemic route that justification is supposed to guarantee.

So the conclusion is unavoidable: "The traditional definition of knowledge as justified true belief is inadequate." And more sharply, "This shows that there can be justified true beliefs that are not knowledge."

The lesson is not that knowledge is impossible. It is that justification must do more work than the tradition assumed—it must connect the belief to the truth in the right way, not merely make it probable.

Kuczynski 073 — PASS
Question: Are perceptual beliefs inferential?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 4
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Part II; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Do We Think in Words?; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Causality
Word count: 288

EXACT ANSWER
Yes. Perceptual beliefs are inferential, and the inference is usually invisible to you.

Take the stop sign. "If you look at X from a certain distance—from, say, a hundred feet away—it will appear a certain way to you." From that appearance alone, "you cannot tell whether you are looking at an object that is around 8-feet tall and a hundred feet away or an object that is 1,000-feet tall and much further away or an object that is 6 inches tall and very nearby." Yet you do know its height. So something beyond the appearance must be doing the work.

That something is background knowledge. "It is your background knowledge that, in conjunction with how X appears to you under the circumstances described, enables you to assign the right height to X." The appearance plus the background knowledge yields the belief. That conjunction is an inference, whether or not it feels like one.

This is why I say perceptual knowledge is theoretical. "You can just see how tall, approximately, X is. But, for the reasons just given, it seems that background knowledge of the kind just described seems to be involved in, and to some degree to constitute, your seeing this." The inference is baked into the seeing itself.

The consequence is epistemic. "Any belief about the external world involves an element of inference, an element of theoretical extrapolation, and is to that extent precarious: after all, the more inferences you make, the more likely you are to be wrong." By contrast, "one's knowledge that one is sad doesn't involve any inference and is thus not precarious."

So perceptual beliefs rest on inference, and that is precisely what makes them less secure than beliefs about one's own mind.

Question: Does the success of AI bear on the dispute between empiricism and rationalism?
Answer type: indirect
Direct evidence count: 0
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?
Word count: 257
Failure reason: The diagnostic does not accept fluent output based on indirect or absent source material.

EXACT ANSWER
The success of AI bears on the dispute, but not in the way most people assume. It does not settle whether knowledge derives from sense-experience or from reason alone. It sharpens the distinction.

My framework turns on what can and cannot be sense-perceived. I hold that "you cannot see (or otherwise sense-perceive) principles" and that "principles are general and express dependence-relations, which cannot be apprehended by senses." This is the crux. An AI system is trained on data — sensory input, in effect — yet what it manipulates are general dependence-relations. That gap is exactly the rationalist's point.

But empiricists will object: the system learned those relations from data. Fair. Yet I distinguish kinds of knowledge. "Empirical knowledge can be either direct or indirect; the same is true of analytic knowledge." AI complicates the picture because its outputs look analytic while its training is empirical.

Here is where I draw the line. "Empiricists don't believe in uninstantiated properties." An AI that reasons about properties never instantiated — counterfactuals, unbuilt structures — is operating with something empiricism cannot easily house. And "anyone who does believe in such properties, or who believes that properties are not spatiotemporal entities, is a rationalist."

So: AI's success is evidence that general principles are graspable and deployable, but it does not show they are sense-perceived. It shows the empiricist's "confusion that has stymied intellectual progress for centuries" persists. The machine learns from data, but what it learns are principles — and principles are not seen.

This topic warrants deeper exploration—consider increasing word count.
