Kuczynski 075 — PASS
Question: Is empiricism defensible in any form?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 10
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Causality; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8
Word count: 281

EXACT ANSWER
Empiricism is not defensible in its strictest form. I argue this directly: "empiricism is not in its strictest form a defensible doctrine and that, consequently, at least some knowledge has a non-perceptual basis."

The doctrine holds "it's inherent in the nature of knowledge that all knowledge be strictly observation-based." My refutation turns on a single structural point: "it cannot be known through observation that (2) is correct." Observation cannot adjudicate consistency between statements—"observation cannot tell you whether one statement is consistent with some other statement."

From this it follows that "any body observational data is consistent with the assumption that empiricism is false." So "there cannot be strictly observational grounds for believing empiricism correct." The self-undermining result is exact: "so far as empiricism is correct, there are no grounds for believing it correct; and so far as there are such grounds, empiricism is false."

The likelihood of empiricism is therefore "inversely proportional to the degree of probability that the information at our disposal confers on it." And so: "if it's a certainty that empiricism is correct, it's a certainty that it's false. Therefore, empiricism, if true, is false; therefore it's false."

Two corollaries follow. First, "many commonsense-based views about the internal (psychological) and external (physical) worlds must be jettisoned." Second, "sober scientific methodology actually demands an acceptance of principles that would strike common sense as decidedly unscientific."

What survives? Empiricism as a regulative standard, not a description of thought. It "doesn't describe how we actually think or how we should think. But it does describe a standard with respect to which it is appropriate to evaluate the thoughts we have had." It is "a touchstone of thinking, not its propelling force."

Kuczynski 076 — PASS
Question: Are properties abstract objects?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 6
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Part II; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Causality; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?
Word count: 264

EXACT ANSWER
Properties are not abstract objects in the sense of being spooky copies floating in some Platonic heaven. They are simply ways things can be. My position is that "a property is simply a way that things can be. Equivalently, a property is a possibility."

This dissolves the standard resistance. People recoil from Platonism because they imagine that "the property of being a cat is a cat-in-the-sky, the same mutatis mutandis being true of the property of being a square." That is a caricature. When you are jogging rather than watching television, there are simply "two possibilities only one of which was actualized; two paths or 'ways of being', only one of which was taken; two properties, only one of which was instantiated."

So properties exist, but not in space-time. "Everything that is in space-time is an instance of at least one property, and properties are not themselves in space-time." I like to play tennis; I am an instance of that property. But "no matter how thoroughly one searches the universe, one will never encounter the property of liking to play tennis. One will, at most, encounter its instances."

Nor can we eliminate them. There is "no way to validate even so rudimentary an inference as 'John and Tom are both smart; therefore, there is something that they have in common', since 'something' in this context means 'some property.'"

Properties themselves have properties. "The property of being a square circle has the property of being uninstantiated." Such higher-order properties are themselves non-spatiotemporal. The upshot: "Everything that exists is either a property or is in space-time."

Kuczynski 077 — PASS
Question: Are counterfactuals to be understood in terms of possible worlds?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 18
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means
Word count: 294

EXACT ANSWER
No. Counterfactuals are not to be understood in terms of possible worlds. They are disguised causal or logical assertions.

I have examined David Lewis's analysis in detail. According to him, "if kangaroos didn't have tails, they would fall over" means "given any world W where kangaroos don't have tails, kangaroos fall over, provided that W is as much like our world as is permitted by the fact that, in it, kangaroos don't have tails." This analysis "obviously assumes that other 'worlds' exist."

But this is backwards. As I wrote, "I find this analysis completely preposterous. We don't know anything about other universes, let alone whether Smith and Kennedy exist in them or, therefore, what their situations there are."

The fatal problem is epistemic. "We obviously can't see or otherwise sense-perceive what is going on in other worlds; nor can we can sense-perceive evidence of what is going on in such worlds. Any knowledge that we have of what is going on in them is parasitic on our knowledge of counterfactual truths."

So the dependency runs the wrong way. "This shows that we know (i) to be true because we know of some fact in our world that coincides with the fact registered by (i). Which, in its turn, shows that other worlds have nothing to do with counterfactual truth. Which shows that LA is false."

The correct analysis: "counterfactuals are just disguised causal or logical assertions and that, consequently, alternative worlds have no place in any decent analysis of them." Thus "Kennedy's assassination prevented an otherwise reelection bound Kennedy from being reelected."

If the worlds are mere sets of statements, then "counterfactuals merely register interpropositional relations" — and once that relation is identified, "it won't be necessary to talk about other worlds at all."

REPRESENTATIVE SOURCE-LINKED QUOTATIONS

Kuczynski 078 — PASS
Question: Are laws of nature necessarily invariant with respect to all regions of space?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 1
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?
Word count: 309

EXACT ANSWER
No. Not all scientific laws need to be spatiotemporally invariant.

Some philosophers of science have taken the term "general principle" to mean spatiotemporally invariant principle, and they have thus taken the position that the laws of nature must be spatiotemporally invariant. A principle or law is spatiotemporally invariant if, given any two regions of space-time, it holds no less for the one than the other.

But that demand is too strong. Many of the dependence-relations on which scientists depend are undefined, and therefore neither true nor false, for almost all regions of space-time. A law governing the behavior of copper, for instance, is silent about regions where no copper exists—and such regions are the overwhelming majority of space-time.

This does not demote such principles to mere accidents. Even though the class of space-time regions in which there are people is a vanishingly small sub-class of the total class of space-time regions, a generalization about people is nonetheless ultimately in the same category as a paradigm-case of a law, such as that nothing exceeds the speed of light. Each supports predictions and counterfactuals.

Laws of nature are not restricted to this or that object; they hold with respect to entire classes of objects. And those classes sometimes comprise merely possible objects. Many laws of nature hold only with respect to classes all of whose members are merely possible.

Nor do laws require perfect concomitance. For it to be a law of nature that instances of phi bring about instances of psi is not for each and every phi to be followed by an instance of psi. There could be such a law even if no phi ever brought about any psi.

So long as there is a need for science, principled but defeasible generalizations are to be co-categorized with principled, non-defeasible generalizations—they are to be categorized as laws of nature.

Kuczynski 079 — PASS
Question: Is causation a relation between events or between facts?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 9
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?
Word count: 231

EXACT ANSWER
Causation is a relation between events, not facts. Events cause other events to occur. Facts are not the relata.

My position is unambiguous: "it is only events that can be causes. Objects are not causes." The rock is not a cause. What caused the window to break was an event—the rock's striking the window at a certain time.

This is not a trivial distinction. When we say "Hitler was the cause of World War II," we speak elliptically. Such statements are shorthand for events involving Hitler being responsible for the war. The person is not the cause; the events are.

I also distinguish causes from conditions. "A condition is a relatively persistent state (e.g., the room's having a certain temperature)." Conditions differ from events, and this matters for how we parse causal claims.

Further, I separate something's being a cause from its having causal properties. "Non-causes may have causal properties." The rock isn't a cause, but its having a certain mass is a causal property—its having that mass is, or can be, a partial cause.

So the answer is clear: events are the relata of causation. Objects and facts are not. When ordinary language suggests otherwise, it is elliptical.

The empiricist worry that we never observe causal ties is, I argue, incoherent. "The more it's scrutinized, the more incoherent it proves to be." Causation is real, and its terms are events.

Kuczynski 080 — PASS
Question: Are there natural kinds?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 1
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Part II; Causality; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Do We Think in Words?; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 249

EXACT ANSWER
Yes. Natural kinds exist, and they are grounded in micro-structure, not in surface resemblance.

My criterion is explanatory and predictive power. "Properties that don't have those virtues (e.g., person who drives a green car, edible substance on Larry's table) don't generate natural kinds." The property of driving a green car is a gerrymandered mess—no laws track it, no inductions project from it. But "the property of being H2O generates a natural kind." Why? Because things sharing that property cannot diverge in their causal powers.

Contrast this with macro-characteristics. "Two things that are explanatorily and predictively very different can, at least within the narrow horizons within which non-experimentalists typically operate, be indistinguishable in respect of their macro-characteristics." Twin Earth scenarios make this vivid: identical appearance, different essence. So "the property of having such and such macro-characteristics does not determine a natural kind."

Micro-characteristics are different. "Two things that are indistinguishable in respect of their micro-characteristics (e.g., their chemical compositions) cannot be explanatorily and predictively different. Thus, the property of having such and such micro-characteristics generates a natural kind."

This yields a necessary but non-analytic identity. "It can't be known a priori what chemical composition water has. But, for the reasons just given, its having that composition, whatever it turns out to be, is essential to it." So "water is H2O" expresses a "necessary, but non-analytic truth."

Natural kinds, then, are not our categories. They are the joints reality cuts on its own—chemical, physical, structural. Our job is discovery, not stipulation.

Kuczynski 081 — PASS
Question: Is classical logic ampliative or merely transformative?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 3
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Do We Think in Words?; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Part II; Causality
Word count: 255

EXACT ANSWER
The claim that deduction is non-ampliative is false—and it is false for two entirely different reasons, depending on which kind of entailment you mean.

Take model-theoretic entailment. "Triangles are shapes model-theoretically entails Socrates is identical with Socrates, but there is nothing in the content of the first that has anything to do with Socrates." The consequent introduces content the antecedent never contained. That is amplification, not transformation.

Formal entailment behaves the same way. "'Smith is tall' formally entails 'either Smith is tall or grass is green,' but there is nothing about grass in 'Smith is tall.'" Again, the conclusion says something the premise did not.

So the slogan that "if P entails Q, there is nothing in Q that is not also in P" collapses on contact with either notion. It is "obviously false where model-theoretic entailment is concerned" and "obviously false where formal entailment is concerned."

But there is a deeper point. Purely syntactic inference cannot even get you from P1 to Q1. "P1 is syntactically just like P3, and Q1 is syntactically just like Q3. But there is no legitimate inference from P3 to Q3." Since the sentences are formally identical, "it follows there is no legitimate, purely syntactic inference from P1 to Q1."

Yet P1 does entail Q1—"P1 also entails Q1 in some other, much more robust sense." That robust sense is the ampliative one. In Kuczynski (2007) I put forth a theory of exactly this entailment.

Classical logic is ampliative. It is not a mere reshuffling of what you already had.

Kuczynski 082 — PASS
Question: Can deduction yield new knowledge?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 3
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Do We Think in Words?; Causality; Part II; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means
Word count: 290

EXACT ANSWER
Deduction is ampliative. It increases knowledge. The textbook claim that it doesn't is simply false.

The absurdity is easy to expose. If deduction didn't increase knowledge, "it would follow that people who draw inferences know no more than those who don't and just live in the moment—that our Pleistocene ancestors are as knowledgeable as we are. But that's absurdities."

The conception of entailment underlying Moore's argument, as well as Hume's, generates precisely these absurdities. On their view, deduction merely unpacks what's already contained in the premises. But that picture cannot survive scrutiny.

Consider what happens when I learn a mathematical theorem by reading a proof. "If one learns some complex mathematical theorem by reading a proof of it, one learns that theorem through observations of ink-deposits; but it isn't by observing such deposits that one learns it." The observations merely "occasion or 'trigger' the purely logical ratiocinative activity that does lead to a genuine knowledge of that principle."

This is decisive. "Somebody with 20/20 vision who has carefully studied those ink-deposits... may completely and utterly fail to understand the corresponding proof; whereas somebody whose vision is just good enough to see some of the key lines of the proof may, on the basis only of those observations along with the thoughts they precipitated, understand it extremely well."

The same point holds for auditory learning. "Somebody who has heard the proof stated but hasn't read it may, on the basis only of those auditory observations along with the thoughts they precipitated, thoroughly understand the proof." And note: "Ink-deposits bear no physical resemblance to noises. Therefore, it isn't by studying ink-deposits that one learns the proof."

So deduction is ampliative. My argument in the Appendix establishes this against the standard textbook treatment.

Question: Is defeasible inference a species of deduction?
Answer type: indirect
Direct evidence count: 0
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Do We Think in Words?; Causality; Part II; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible
Word count: 273
Failure reason: The diagnostic does not accept fluent output based on indirect or absent source material.

EXACT ANSWER
No. Defeasible inference is not a species of deduction. It is a distinct genus of legitimate inference, governed by a different rule.

My framework treats legitimate inference as correspondence to dependence-relations. As I put it: "Inferences, when legitimate, are made in accordance with legitimate rules of inference. | Rules of inference, when legitimate, correspond to dependence-relations." And: "Legitimate inferences correspond to dependence-relations."

Deduction is one such correspondence. "Given two propositions P and Q, P entails Q iff Q is a logical consequence of P. | If P entails Q, then, if P is true, it follows that Q is true and therefore that Q may be inferred from P." So the deductive rule is non-defeasible: once P entails Q, no further premise can sever the inference.

Defeasible inference runs on a different rule. "Supposing that P confirms Q, Q may legitimately be inferred from P if, and only if, (a) The supposition that P is true and Q is false has fewer unexplainable consequences than the supposition that P and Q are both true, and (b) The supposition that P is true has fewer unexplainable consequences than the supposition that P is false."

Note the structure. Deduction turns on entailment; defeasible inference turns on comparative explanatory cost. These are not the same dependence-relation, and the rules do not reduce to one another.

This is why I treat principled but defeasible generalizations as laws of nature alongside non-defeasible ones: "As long as there is a need for science, low-grade but principled generalizations like (a) should be categorized as laws of nature alongside non-defeasible laws like (c)."

Defeasible inference is its own species. Not deduction.

Question: What is System L and what does classical logic fail to do that it does?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 1
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6
Word count: 272

EXACT ANSWER
System L is a radically different kind of logical system—one that actually helps us reason rather than merely cataloging known-valid inferences. It represents a decisive break from classical logical frameworks.

Classical logic fails at competence-demanding inferences. "Classical logic can assist with performance-demanding inferences (though often inefficiently). But it offers no help with competence-demanding inferences—the very kind that most require logical assistance." This limitation isn't accidental; it's inherent in classical logic's fundamental nature as a system of formalization rather than discovery.

System L's key innovation lies in its approach to those competence-demanding inferences—those requiring genuine insight rather than mere computational power. "It employs a semantic network that represents concepts not as atomic symbols but as nodes in a vast web of relationships." These relationships capture not just formal logical connections but also probabilistic associations, causal links, and analogical mappings.

System L also incorporates defeasible reasoning, allowing it to make provisional inferences that can later be revised in light of new information. When evaluating a question like whether emotional intelligence requires empathy, System L might initially infer yes based on typical cases—but then revise this upon considering edge cases like highly functioning individuals with autism who display emotional intelligence through learned rules rather than empathy. This better mirrors actual human reasoning while providing more practical utility than classical logic's requirement for absolute certainty.

Crucially, System L maintains a distinction between discovery and verification. "While it uses inductive methods to discover solutions, it employs deductive methods to verify them when working in deductive domains." Mathematicians rarely proceed by pure deduction; they notice patterns, draw analogies, and follow hunches—then verify. System L formalizes that actual practice.

Kuczynski 085 — PASS
Question: Is logical form a property of sentences or of propositions?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 3
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Part II; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Causality; Do We Think in Words?; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6
Word count: 241

EXACT ANSWER
Logical form is a property of propositions, never of sentences. This is not a stylistic preference—it follows from what sentences and propositions are.

A sentence is a string of symbols. What it means depends on convention. As I've argued, "It's up to us what our symbols mean. But it's not up to us whether those meanings are correct." We decide that "snow is white" means what it means. We do not decide whether that meaning holds.

A proposition, by contrast, is what a sentence expresses. And crucially, "Propositions are not themselves sentences." Different sentences—"schnee ist weiss" and "snow is white"—can express the same proposition. If logical form belonged to sentences, translation would destroy it. It doesn't.

So when we say a sentence is "logically true," we are speaking loosely. "What they mean is that, given what it is that it means, (4) must be true. So what they are in fact describing as logically true is the proposition that (4) couldn't be false, given what it is that it means." The logical truth is the proposition, not the marks on the page.

This is why LP fails. "LP identifies logical truth with conventional truth: truths of logic are sentences that are true by convention. But that's false." Conventions govern symbols. Logic governs what those symbols can correctly express.

The consequence is stark: "Logical truths are never sentences; they're always propositions, and propositions are never conventionally true." Form tracks meaning, not inscription.

Kuczynski 086 — PASS
Question: Is mathematics reducible to logic?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 3
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Causality; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Do We Think in Words?; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?
Word count: 336

EXACT ANSWER
No. Mathematics is not reducible to logic, and the failure is not a matter of insufficient cleverness—it is a structural impossibility.

The logicist program rested on a specific hope: that arithmetical truths could be paraphrased into a formal idiom, and that a single algorithm could then sort the true from the false. As I put it, "Logicists attempted to provide the requisite paraphrases. And, thanks to their paraphrases, it was possible to identify formal-decision procedures for huge classes of arithmetical truths." That was the promise.

Gödel destroyed it. "Kurt Gödel (1906–1978) showed that there is no way of paraphrasing or otherwise representing arithmetical truths that permits the construction of some one formal decision-procedure that decides the truth of any given arithmetical truth. He showed that logicism was doomed and also that any other attempt to formalize arithmetic was doomed."

Note the scope. Not merely logicism—"any other attempt to formalize arithmetic." The reduction fails because the formal apparatus cannot capture what it was meant to capture.

The set-theoretic analyses themselves survive. "There is nothing wrong with the (set-theoretic) analyses of number, and of number statements, put forth by Frege and Russell and other logicists." What died was the claim that "there is some one algorithm such that, given any statement of arithmetic, that algorithm can correctly say whether or not that statement is true or false."

The distinction matters. "Given any finite set of arithmetical statements, there is an algorithm that, given any statement falling into that set, correctly says whether or not that statement is true. But there is no one algorithm that, given any arithmetical statement, correctly says whether or not that statement is true."

So the reduction is local, not global. Numbers can still be identified with sets—"The number two can be identified with sets of all pairs, actual and possible." But identity of objects is not reducibility of truths. The truths outrun any formal net we can cast.

Mathematics is not logic. It is something logic can partially model and never fully contain.

Kuczynski 087 — FAIL
Question: Are numbers objects?
Answer type: indirect
Direct evidence count: 0
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Part II; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Causality; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Do We Think in Words?
Word count: 219
Failure reason: The diagnostic does not accept fluent output based on indirect or absent source material.

EXACT ANSWER
Numbers are not objects. They are propositions—or more precisely, the objects of knowledge are propositions, and numbers function as abstracta whose identity is exhausted by their role in true propositions.

My framework is this: "The objects of knowledge are propositions. It isn't known unless it's believed and it isn't believed unless it's a proposition." Numbers, then, are not rocks or trees. You cannot bump into the number seven. You can only know truths about it.

This matters because it blocks a common confusion. One can be aware of non-propositions—"rocks, trees, people"—but "one does not in the relevant sense know them. Rather, one knows truths about them." The same holds for numbers. Awareness of the numeral '7' is not knowledge of the number; knowledge of the number is knowledge of propositions in which it figures.

Nor are numbers causes. "Objects themselves are not causes, though they possess causal properties that contribute to events having effects." Numbers possess no causal properties at all. They do no work in the world.

So: numbers are not objects in the sense that rocks are objects. They are the constituents of propositions, and propositions are what we know. To treat numbers as things is to mistake the object of a truth for a thing in the world.

This topic warrants deeper exploration—consider increasing word count.

Kuczynski 088 — PASS
Question: Is mathematical knowledge a priori?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 14
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Do We Think in Words?; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 256

EXACT ANSWER
Mathematical knowledge is a priori. My position is unambiguous: "My own strongly held view is that there is a priori knowledge."

Consider 1+1=2. "To know that is it true, one doesn't do empirical work; one doesn't perform experiments or make observations. 1+1=2 is thus a priori." The same holds for 7+5=12. Kant classifies it as synthetic a priori, and I follow him on the a priority even where I press on the syntheticity.

The reason is not merely that we happen to learn arithmetic without lab coats. It is that empirical grounding cannot generate mathematical knowledge at all. "Even one's knowledge that 1 + 1 = 2 isn't known empirically." Observation "reveals facts, not norms." And mathematical truths carry normative force: if two people enter a house and three leave, you do not revise 1+1=2—you revise your belief that the house was empty.

There is a deeper structural point. "Your knowledge of arithmetical truths is based on a grasp of non-empirical principles." Even if you watched one object placed atop another, that observation alone gives you no way to generalize to the other mathematical truths you know. "To make the needed inferences, you'd need access to rules of inference that you couldn't possibly know about if your knowledge were strictly sense-based."

So the a priority of mathematics is not a psychological curiosity. It is a precondition of mathematical inference itself. Knowledge "is coded into the very structures of our minds and therefore pre-exists any perceptions that we have."

This topic warrants deeper exploration—consider increasing word count.

Kuczynski 089 — PASS
Question: How should imaginary numbers be represented?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 1
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Do We Think in Words?; Causality; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Part II; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6
Word count: 232

EXACT ANSWER
Imaginary numbers should be represented as ordered pairs, not as mysterious entities. My view is that the imaginary unit *i* is identical with the ordered pair (0,1), and complex numbers generally are ordered pairs of reals with the familiar operations defined on them.

This dissolves the apparent mystery. There is nothing "imaginary" about *i* once we see it as a structured object. The same strategy I apply to the natural numbers applies here. Just as "+n is more accurately represented as an ordered triple ((n,0),+S, × S) rather than simply (n,0)," so too the complex numbers are best understood as structured tuples rather than as sui generis mathematical objects.

The deeper point is that "it is false to say that +n=(n,0)" in the strict sense. The identity only holds "relative to the assumption that + and × are defined in the just-described way." Representation is always relative to a chosen framework.

This matters because mathematical ontology is not about discovering what numbers "really are" in some framework-independent sense. It is about constructing precise structures that do the work we need.

So: represent *i* as (0,1). Represent *a+bi* as (a,b). Define addition and multiplication componentwise in the standard way. The imaginary vanishes into structure.

The lesson generalizes. Whenever a mathematical object seems metaphysically queer, look for the underlying structure. The queerness is usually an artifact of bad representation, not of the object itself.

Kuczynski 090 — PASS
Question: Explain why the concept of repression is coherent.
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 5
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Causality; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means
Word count: 290

EXACT ANSWER
The concept of repression is coherent because its denial is self-undermining. Those who claim repression doesn't exist are themselves performing an act of repression.

Consider what the denial of repression actually amounts to. As I've argued, "the denial of emotions is itself a thoroughly emotional position, and the denial of repression is itself an instance of repression." This isn't a rhetorical trick. It's a structural feature of the phenomenon.

The denier says he is being "scientific." But "it's hard to see how such dishonesty and obtuseness could deserve to be so characterized." Science requires honesty about the data. And the data here is overwhelming.

Look at the empirical record. "People don't see themselves for what they are." This is not controversial outside the discipline of psychology. It is, in fact, "the obvious and, outside of the discipline of psychology, universally acknowledged fact that people deceive themselves."

Why do they deceive themselves? Because they don't want to see. "People don't want to see themselves for who they are; so they don't."

Now consider the alternative explanation. Could this blindness be mere ignorance—lack of data, lack of intelligence, lack of effort? No. "Given the empirical fact that hyper-intelligent people are quite as prone to not seeing themselves for who they are as their less gifted brethren, it is de rigueur, from the viewpoint of scientific methodology, to suppose another factor to be operative."

That factor is motivational. The mind actively resists certain contents.

So the coherence of repression follows from a simple observation: "there's no coherent way to deny that repression is not only possible, but actual, and not only actual, but integral to the human condition."

The denier's position collapses under its own weight. To deny repression is to exercise it.

Kuczynski 091 — PASS
Question: Is a counternarrative necessary for repression?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 2
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Causality
Word count: 301

EXACT ANSWER
Yes. A counternarrative is necessary for repression.

My account distinguishes two forms of repression, and both require the construction of a narrative alternative to the one that describes reality as it really is. As I put it, "both forms of repression involve the construction and operationalization of a narrative alternative to the one that, supposing the repressed idea to be correct (which it typically is), describes reality as it really is."

That narrative alternative is what I call rationalization. And rationalization is not optional. "Without rationalization, it is hard, if not impossible, to repress an idea and also to keep it repressed."

Consider what repression actually does. "To repress2 an idea is to take its vote away; it is to decide to give it no weight." But you cannot simply strip an idea of its vote and leave a vacuum. The mind abhors a vacuum in the space of reasons. Something must occupy the deliberative slot the repressed idea would have filled.

That something is the counternarrative. It is the story you tell yourself instead.

Note the asymmetry I flag: "rationalization-construction is more heavily involved in ensuring that already repressed ideas stay repressed than it is in initially repressing them." So the counternarrative is most essential for maintenance. Initial repression may be cruder; sustained repression demands a coherent alternative.

Both forms of repression, I argue, "involve conflict between, on the one hand, forces within oneself of which one is aware and, on the other hand, forces within oneself of which one is unaware." The counternarrative is how the aware self manages that conflict without confronting it.

This is why I treat self-deception and repression as structurally linked. The counternarrative is the mechanism by which the repressed idea is kept from reasserting its vote.

This topic warrants deeper exploration—consider increasing word count.

Kuczynski 092 — PASS
Question: Is psychoanalysis an empirical theory or a hermeneutic one?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 1
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Causality; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Do We Think in Words?; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means
Word count: 268

EXACT ANSWER
Psychoanalysis is an empirical theory. The hermeneutic reading is a category error.

Freud's central claim is that "conscious psychological episodes are installments in sequences of events large portions of which are constituted by unconscious psychological activity." That is a causal-explanatory thesis, not an interpretive one. It says something about the structure of psychological reality—namely, that "psychological reality is continuous and law-governed, notwithstanding the erratic and discontinuous nature of activity within the sphere of consciousness."

The objection that positing unconscious mental activity is "categorically false" fails. Given what we know about "causation and explanation, Freud's analysis would seem to be an entirely logical, if not positively mandatory, application of sound scientific methodology." The inference to unconscious causes is the same inference we make everywhere else in science: we posit unobserved entities to explain observed regularities.

This is why the hermeneutic framing collapses. If psychoanalysis were merely a reading practice—a way of re-describing symptoms in narrative form—then its claims would be immune to empirical refutation. But Freud's claims are not immune. They stand or fall on evidence.

"Whether Freud's theories are to be accepted is a strictly empirical question that is to be resolved wholly on the basis of the accuracy of the specific contents of those theories."

That is the decisive point. The theory makes determinate predictions about mental architecture. Those predictions can be tested. They can be confirmed or falsified.

The hermeneutic interpretation mistakes the method of discovery for the method of justification. Yes, the analyst interprets. But so does the physicist when reading a cloud chamber. Interpretation is a route to hypothesis, not a substitute for evidence.

Question: Can a man consciously believe p and unconsciously believe not-p?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 2
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Part II; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?
Word count: 242

EXACT ANSWER
Yes. This is not a paradox but a structural feature of the mind.

My argument runs like this. "The mind is not a perfectly unified entity; it consists of various parts that communicate with each other only very imperfectly." Because of this fragmentation, "there are two very different ways in which one can be aware of a given thing," and "two very different senses in which a given mental content can be 'conscious.'"

So the man who consciously believes p is not thereby committed to the same belief at every level of his mental economy. "Beliefs can be isolated to prevent them from engaging with other beliefs," and once isolated, they "become inert at the level of consciousness."

This is the mechanism of repression. "Repression involves making a belief's conscious representation an innocuous shell." The shell is what he avows; the belief underneath persists. "Repression renders a belief's conscious representation inert, but the belief continues to exist and influence subconsciously."

Hence the answer to your question: "Self-deception and repression are possible due to the fragmented nature of the mind and the different ways of being conscious." The conscious p and the unconscious not-p do not collide, because they never meet. The isolation prevents the engagement that would force a contradiction into view.

This is why I insist the mind is not one thing but many, communicating badly. A unified mind could not believe p and not-p. A fragmented one does so routinely.

Kuczynski 095 — PASS
Question: Does the sorites paradox show that "rich" is vague?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 4
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Causality; Do We Think in Words?; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 282

EXACT ANSWER
No. The sorites paradox does not show that "rich" is vague. It shows that we have misread the predicate.

My solution is simple. Statements of the form "x is rich" are elliptical for statements of the form "x is rich compared to y," where y is either some person or some benchmark. Once the benchmark is identified, the paradox dissolves.

Consider the standard form. A sorites paradox "always consists of a base-clause (e.g., 'a person with zero dollars is poor'), an inductive clause (e.g., 'if a person with n dollars is poor, so is a person with n + 1 dollars), and an obviously false conclusion that seems to follow (e.g., 'a person with a billion dollars is poor')."

The inductive clause equivocates. It trades on an unstated benchmark. "When the benchmark is identified, the underlined sentence is seen to be false. If Frank is the person/benchmark in question, and Frank has $1,000,000, then there is a number n (namely, 999,999)" at which the induction breaks.

So the paradox is not evidence of vagueness. It is evidence of ellipsis.

Note what I am claiming. "Most attempts to solve this paradox reject some law of classical logic, usually the law of bivalence." I do not. "I show that this paradox can be solved while holding on to all the laws of classical logic."

The same treatment applies to "smart." A person with an IQ of 70 is not smart — compared to whom? The chain "a person with an IQ of n is not smart, then a person with an IQ of n+1 is not smart" only seems compelling because the comparison class is suppressed.

Vagueness is not the culprit. Unarticulated comparison is.

Kuczynski 096 — FAIL
Question: Is supervaluationism a solution to anything?
Answer type: indirect
Direct evidence count: 0
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Causality; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Why Does Alcoholics Anonymous Work?
Word count: 239
Failure reason: The diagnostic does not accept fluent output based on indirect or absent source material.

EXACT ANSWER
Supervaluationism is a solution to one problem and a source of several others. It earns its keep by preserving classical logic in the face of vagueness, but it does so at a cost that I think is rarely worth paying.

The core move is simple. A sentence like "Smith is bald" is neither true nor false when Smith is a borderline case. But we can say it is *supertrue* if it comes out true on every admissible precisification of "bald," and *superfalse* if false on every precisification. Truth is then defined as supertruth, and classical logic survives intact.

This is elegant. It lets us keep bivalence at the level of supertruth while admitting truth-value gaps at the level of ordinary truth. The law of excluded middle holds: "Smith is bald or Smith is not bald" is supertrue even when neither disjunct is true.

But the cost is real. The semantics requires us to quantify over precisifications—sharpenings of vague predicates—and it is not clear what these precisifications *are*. They are not states of affairs in space-time. They are not truths or falsehoods. They are abstract objects whose identity conditions are obscure.

My general worry about expanding formal machinery to cover every case is that it "risks theoretical vacuity by dissolving all meaningful distinctions." When everything becomes a matter of admissible precisification, the concept loses explanatory grip.

Supervaluationism solves the logical problem of vagueness. It does not solve the metaphysical one.

Kuczynski 097 — FAIL
Question: Is wealth a continuous scale?
Answer type: indirect
Direct evidence count: 0
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means
Word count: 238
Failure reason: The diagnostic does not accept fluent output based on indirect or absent source material.

EXACT ANSWER
Wealth is not a continuous scale. It is discontinuous, and the discontinuities are where the interesting action is.

My general framework distinguishes continuous from discontinuous change by threshold effects. "Discontinuous changes tend to involve threshold effects." A circuit breaker does nothing until overload, then snaps. A firm does nothing until it is "in the red by a certain amount, at which point it files the paperwork." Wealth behaves the same way. You do not slide smoothly from solvent to bankrupt; you cross a threshold and the state flips.

This is why I treat the world as having a dual structure: "to the extent that the world changes discontinuously, it has a digital structure, and to the extent that it changes continuously, it has an analogue structure." An analogue clock drifts; a digital clock snaps between states. Wealth snaps. Bankruptcy, insolvency, and default are digital events.

The underlying accumulation may look analogue—slow, gradual, continuous. But the transitions that matter are transeunt: "the essence of transeunt causation is the discontinuous alteration of object-constitutive causal-series." A creditor's demand, a market crash, a lawsuit—these are collisions. They immobilize one party and mobilize another, exactly as "Ball A collides with hitherto stationary Ball B."

So the scale is continuous in its substrate and discontinuous in its consequences. That is not a paradox. It is the structure of any system where immanent drift meets transeunt shock.

This topic warrants deeper exploration—consider increasing word count.

Kuczynski 098 — PASS
Question: Is a law a command or an assurance of protection of a right?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 4
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Why Does Alcoholics Anonymous Work?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Part II; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 338

EXACT ANSWER
A law is an assurance of protection of a right, not a command. The command theorist mistakes the surface grammar of legislation for its function.

I argue that "the purpose of a legal system per se is to serve the interests of those who are subject to it—even though that may not be the objective of all, or even any, of the individuals who created that legal system." This is the key move. A corrupt legislator may issue commands for his own benefit, but that tells us nothing about what law *is*. It tells us only about what *he* wants.

Consider the functional analogy. "Even if everyone alive suddenly succumbed to liver disease, and each person's liver stopped removing toxins from his bloodstream, there would still be a significant sense in which livers were to be understood as removers of toxins." The same holds for law. "Like hearts and livers, governments and the laws they issue are to be understood in functional, and not strictly statistical-empirical, terms."

This dissolves the command theory. "Even if every government were thoroughly corrupt and exploitative, there would still be a significant sense in which governments were to be understood as protectors of rights, and in which the laws issued by governments were to be understood as attempts to provide protections of rights."

So the answer is decisive. A law is not defined by the will that issues it. It is defined by the interest it is meant to serve. "In general, one fails as law-maker if one issues a law that hurts those who are subject to it." That is the standard. Not obedience. Protection.

The command theorist is blind to this because he accepts "a strictly fact-based frame of evaluation." He sees only the sovereign's utterance. He misses the function. And "one is not blind to it if one accepts a frame of evaluation that allows for functional categories."

Law is a functional kind. Its essence is protection of rights, not the imperative form in which it happens to be expressed.

Kuczynski 099 — PASS
Question: Is adjudication covert legislation?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 3
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Part II; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Do We Think in Words?; Why Does Alcoholics Anonymous Work?; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 247

EXACT ANSWER
No. Adjudication is principled interpretation, not legislation.

Blackstone said that judges identify, and do not create, law. John Austin described Blackstone's position as a "childish fiction." I agree with Austin that judges do not merely find pre-existing law lying around like buried treasure. But I reject the opposite extreme just as firmly.

The legal realists hold that "judicial interpretation is mere legislation, and isn't answerable to objective standards." That is nihilism dressed as realism. It is false.

Here is my argument. Judicial rulings are "principled extensions of the law—that is, they are delineations of it, and are not cases of law being created out of whole cloth." Delineation is not creation. When a judge extends a principle to a novel case, she is drawing out what was already implicit in the law's rationale.

Consider my analogy. Some delineations of the concept of temperature are truer to pre-theoretic data than others. "Heat is dephlogistinated matter" is a bad delineation. "A body's temperature is the sum of the velocities of its constituent molecules divided by the number of those particles" is a good one. Both are delineations. Only one is correct.

So it is with law. Some interpretations of law are "truer to existing law than others." That comparative standard is objective. It is not a matter of judicial whim.

Therefore adjudication is neither pure discovery nor pure legislation. It is principled extension answerable to objective standards. Austin was right about Blackstone. The realists are wrong about everything else.

Kuczynski 100 — PASS
Question: Is philosophy a matter of argument or of insight?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 3
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Causality; Do We Think in Words?; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6
Word count: 237

EXACT ANSWER
Philosophy is a matter of both, but not in the way most people think. Insight generates; logic justifies. They are not rivals but stages.

I have argued that "it is through logic that we discover and it is through logic that we prove." Pascal was wrong to split them. "For there is no discovery without justification. An unjustified intuition isn't a discovery at all."

This is the crux. An insight that cannot be justified is not knowledge—it is luck. "And if an unjustified intuition happens to be right, it's a matter of luck." Most theoretical innovations are not lucky. "While some non-trivial theoretical innovations may be made through luck, most of them are not."

So where does insight fit? It fits as the raw material that logic then processes. "Proof is the identification of the logic embodied in discovery." The insight is not opposed to logic; it is logic in embryonic form, waiting to be articulated.

But I must be honest about logic's limits. "Logic and rigor only go so far. They're no substitute for insight or creativity—especially not in fields such as ethics, politics, and religion." Here insight leads and logic follows. "Logic and rigor have only a secondary function. They're helpful in evaluating insights already generated. But they're useless when it comes to generating them."

The answer, then, is that philosophy requires both, but in a specific order. Insight discovers; logic proves. Neither alone suffices.

Kuczynski 101 — PASS
Question: Are properties in space-time?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 15
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Causality; Part II; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?
Word count: 279

EXACT ANSWER
No. Properties are not in space-time. This is not a subtle point—it is a truism, and the denial of it collapses into incoherence.

My argument runs like this. "Everything that is in space-time is an instance of at least one property, and properties are not themselves in space-time." I like to play tennis. I have the property of liking to play tennis. I am in space-time; that property is not. "No matter how thoroughly one searches the universe, one will never encounter the property of liking to play tennis. One will, at most, encounter its instances."

Consider intelligence. "Instances of intelligence are in space-time. Einstein was in space-time; so was Keynes. But intelligence itself is not in space-time." Someone might object that a property is just an aggregate of its instances. That fails. "Consider the property of having a perfectly triangular shape. Nothing has this property. Are we to say that it doesn't exist?" If we did, we would be saying that "since there are no instances of the property of triangularity, that property doesn't exist."

The same holds for possibilities. "The possibility of your going to law school is not in space-time. So that possibility, being outside of space-time and thus being without location, is nowhere."

This is why nominalism fails. Properties cannot be reduced to spatiotemporal entities, and they cannot be reduced to words either, since "words are themselves universals."

So the answer is unambiguous. "To say that properties exist is simply to say that there are 'ways' things can be." And a way something can be "is simply a possibility as to how it can be, and such a possibility obviously isn't a constituent of space-time."

Kuczynski 102 — PASS
Question: Is the property of being a rock identical with the set of rocks?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 17
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Part II; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Causality
Word count: 295

EXACT ANSWER
No. The property of being a rock is not identical with the set of rocks, and the argument for this is decisive.

A set is a mathematical entity. It has no location and is defined entirely by its formal properties. As I put it, "sets are abstract objects. They don't have space-time coordinates." The set of rocks is not some big rock, nor is it "some big object consisting of rocks separated by stretches of empty space."

The reason is the axiom of extensionality. "A set's membership is frozen—frozen, indeed, in two senses. First, it's temporally frozen. Sets don't gain members and they don't lose them. Second, it's modally frozen." If a set's actual members are x1...xn, it couldn't possibly exist without having exactly those members.

Now consider the property of being a rock. If you destroy half the rocks in the world, you have changed the set of rocks. But you have not changed what it takes to be a rock. "To be a rock, a thing must still have a certain microstructure, or whatnot." The property survives the destruction of its instances; the set does not.

Therefore, by Leibniz's Law, they cannot be the same thing. As I wrote: "that scattered object, if it even exists, cannot be identified with the property of being a rock."

There is a further confusion lurking here. Some anti-Platonists claim properties just are scattered objects—the property of being a rock being some sprawling thing composed of all rocks. I reject this outright: "There are no scattered objects. The very concept of such a thing is an incoherent one."

And even granting them for the sake of argument, the identification fails. Properties are not sets, not scattered objects, not spatiotemporal entities of any kind. They are Platonic entities.

Kuczynski 103 — PASS
Question: Are there scattered objects?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 13
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Part II; Causality; Do We Think in Words?; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible
Word count: 275

EXACT ANSWER
No. There are no scattered objects. The very concept of such a thing is an incoherent one.

Consider what a scattered object is supposed to be. Ordinary objects are "geographically and dynamically cohesive." My backpack is the model here: "If you move one of the straps ten feet across the room, you have moved the whole bag across the room." Its parts occupy "one, fairly compact, relatively continuous region of space-time."

Now take all the rocks in the universe. "Those rocks clearly don't constitute a dynamically or geographically integrated unit." If they constitute anything, it is a "scattered object" — one that "lacks the cohesiveness and dynamic integrity of ordinary objects."

But the concept collapses. "If spatially disjoint entities are to constitute a single spatiotemporal object, their interactions must be characterized by a certain regularity and predictability." Whether the world's rocks satisfy this "cannot be known without doing empirical research." So we cannot even say whether such an object exists.

And even granting it, it cannot be a property. Let R be the scattered object of all rocks. "If you destroy half of the rocks in the world, you have changed the just-mentioned scattered object. But you haven't changed the conditions that a thing must satisfy to be a rock." By Leibniz's Law, R is not the property of being a rock.

The same reasoning applies to persons. Replace "set" with "scattered object consisting of all and only human beings," and the argument shows the property of being a person is not that object either.

So the anti-Platonist's escape route fails. Sets are Platonic entities; scattered objects are incoherent. Neither identifies properties with anything spatiotemporal.

Question: Does the Third Man Argument refute Platonism?
Answer type: indirect
Direct evidence count: 0
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 251

EXACT ANSWER
The Third Man Argument does not refute Platonism, because it attacks a version of the theory of Forms that no careful Platonist need accept. The regress only gets going if one treats a Form as just another particular of the same kind as the things that participate in it. But that is a mistake.

My own work bears on the machinery here. I have argued that "word-types are properties" and that "word-tokens are instances of properties." That distinction matters. A Form is not a token alongside the tokens; it is the type, the property itself. The regress trades on conflating the two.

I have also insisted that "awareness of objects does not constitute knowledge; knowledge consists of truths about objects." So the Platonist is not committed to knowing Forms the way we know rocks and trees. The Third Man assumes a naive ontology of self-predication and non-identity that the theory need not endorse.

Further, my arguments against Lewis are instructive. I hold that "there is no reason, apart from Lewis's analysis, to believe that there are other worlds," and that "there is no reason at all to posit their existence." The same parsimony applies to the infinite hierarchy of Forms the Third Man generates. We have no independent reason to posit it.

So the argument shows at most that a crude Platonism fails. It does not touch a theory that distinguishes types from tokens and refuses self-predication. The regress is a symptom of bad ontology, not a refutation of the Forms.

Kuczynski 105 — PASS
Question: Given that properties have no causal powers, do they explain anything?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 13
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Causality; Part II
Word count: 277

EXACT ANSWER
Properties lack causal powers, but this is no reason to think that "properties are explanatory deadwood or, therefore, that there's no good reason to believe them to exist."

The argument from causal impotence runs like this: "Properties lack causal powers. For this reason, they can serve no explanatory function. To explain something is to show how it came about. Being causally impotent, properties can't make anything come about. Therefore, there is no reason to posit them."

I grant the premise. "Properties do indeed lack causal powers. Causes are necessarily in space and time. To be a cause is to induce change. Changes and their causes are ipso facto in space-time."

But the conclusion doesn't follow. The argument assumes all explanation is causal. It isn't. "Not all explanation is causal explanation. Some explanation is what we call analytic or conceptual."

Consider the set-theoretic case. "There are as many even numbers as there are whole numbers." Why? "Even though the even numbers are a subset of the whole numbers, it is possible to put the two sets of numbers into a one-one correspondence." This "explanation is not causal. It explains a truth not by identifying its causal antecedents, but by delineating the structures of concepts."

The same holds for knowledge. "Why can't someone know something without having any form of awareness?" Because "knowing something involves having a true belief, and a belief is a form of awareness." This "identifies conditions that are conceptually, not causally, necessary conditions for knowledge."

So properties explain plenty. They explain by conceptual necessity, not causal production. "Like this explanation, Plato's theory isn't a causal theory, and it's therefore irrelevant that properties aren't in space-time."

Kuczynski 106 — PASS
Question: Are there uninstantiated properties?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 20
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Part II; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Do We Think in Words?
Word count: 286

EXACT ANSWER
Yes. Uninstantiated properties exist, and denying them is incoherent.

My argument is straightforward. "Properties can be thought of as conditions. The property of being a pink elephant is a condition a thing must fulfill in order to be a pink elephant." Conditions need not be fulfilled to exist. Consider Mary's demand: "he's a genius who is always friendly and never sleeps and always dotes on her and has a billion dollars. That condition isn't fulfilled by anyone. But the condition exists."

From this it follows directly: "given that there are unfulfilled conditions, it follows that there are uninstantiated properties." The property of being a pink elephant is the cleanest case. "The property of being a pink elephant exists, but is currently uninstantiated."

This has a crucial consequence for identity. Properties are not identical with their instances. "If there were to come into being a single pink elephant, which promptly died, the property wouldn't go out of existence. It would still be around. But if it were identical with instances, then it would go out of existence the moment its one instance did."

The same reasoning applies to higher-order properties. "The property of being a square circle has the property of being uninstantiated." And "the property of being a golden mountain does not have that property, since there are no instances of it. It thus has the property of being uninstantiated."

Frege's insight seals it. "The expressions 'exist' and 'doesn't exist' refer to higher-order properties." So "even prime numbers greater than two don't exist" means "the property of being an even number greater than two is un-instantiated."

Uninstantiated properties are simply unfulfilled conditions. Nothing mysterious. Nothing spooky. Just ways things could be that nothing happens to be.

Kuczynski 107 — PASS
Question: Is nominalism coherent?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 6
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Causality; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Part II; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Do We Think in Words?; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means
Word count: 282

EXACT ANSWER
No. Nominalism is not merely false—it is incoherent.

The nominalist holds that properties are identical with words, and therefore that properties are not spatiotemporal. But this position collapses on itself, because "words and linguistic expressions generally are themselves universals or properties."

Consider a simple test. How many words appear below?

"snow"
"snow"
"snow"

The answer is three instances of one word. "There are three s tokens of one word-type." No single utterance of "snow" is identical with the word itself. "It's not as though the word-type 'snow' will disappear when the inscriptions of it in the line above this one are destroyed."

So the word-type is a universal. It is a property of certain ink-deposits and bursts of noise, and those deposits are instances of that property. The nominalist who tries to replace the property of being a rock with the word "rock" has, in doing so, "still conceded the truth of Platonism."

This is why I say the position is not just mistaken but self-undermining. It uses universals to deny universals.

And the deeper point stands independently. Given that "Sally and Fred are both intelligent," it follows that "there exists some property P such that Fred is an instance of P and Sally is an instance of P." Instances of intelligence are in space-time—Einstein was, Keynes was. But intelligence itself is not.

Could the property be an aggregate of its instances? No. "Consider the property of having a perfectly triangular shape. Nothing has this property." To deny its existence because it has no instances is absurd—it amounts to saying there exists a property such that, because nothing has it, it doesn't exist.

Nominalism fails. Properties are real, and they are non-spatiotemporal.

Kuczynski 108 — PASS
Question: Are word-types properties?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 17
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Part II; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Do We Think in Words?
Word count: 245

EXACT ANSWER
Yes. Word-types are properties, and this is not a marginal claim—it is the thesis that breaks the nominalist's back.

Consider three inscriptions of "snow." "There are three instances of one word. To put it another way, there are three s tokens of one word-type." The tokens are physical—ink deposits, bursts of noise. The type is not. "No one utterance of the word 'snow' is identical with that word." Erase every inscription and the word survives.

Why is the type a property? Because "tokens of a type are instances of it. Anything of which there are instances is ipso facto a property." That is the whole argument. The type is what the tokens are instances of, and being an instance-of relation is precisely the property relation.

This is fatal to nominalism. The nominalist wants to identify properties with words, thereby avoiding abstracta. But "words and linguistic expressions generally are themselves universals or properties." He has conceded Platonism to deny it.

The Spanish point seals it. "The Spanish word for rock is 'piedra.' It would be arbitrary to identify that property with the word 'rock' but not with the word 'piedra.'" Since the two words differ, the nominalist must say the property of being a rock is not identical with itself—absurd.

And the metaphysics is independent of us anyway: "A thing's being a rock has nothing to do with words; there were rocks before there were words."

So word-types are properties—non-spatiotemporal, abstract, and instantiated by their tokens.

[Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology] Physiological properties are multiply realizable. More precisely, a given property phi is multiply realizable in so far as it is a physiological property; and so far as that property is not multiply realizable, the reason is that factors having no basis in phi's being a physiological property are preventing phi from being multiply realizable.
[What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?] So propositions are functions, and those functions are individuated by their intensions, not their extensions.

Kuczynski 109 — PASS
Question: What is a proposition?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 20
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Part II; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Causality; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 225

EXACT ANSWER
A proposition is what is meant by an utterance of a sentence. If I point at Smith and say "that man is a scoundrel," the meaning of my utterance is a proposition.

More precisely, propositions are sets of properties. A proposition is true just in case the properties that are members of it are instantiated—so what it is for a proposition to be true is for the members of the set with which it is identical to be jointly instantiated. Roughly, truth is instantiatedness.

Consider "Tommy is smoking." Intuitively, this proposition consists of at least three components: first, something individuative of Tommy; second, the property of smoking; and third, some kind of synthesis of the two. If the proposition is true, then the property of being identical with Tommy is instantiated, and so is the property of smoking.

Propositions are not sentences; propositions are sentence-meanings, not sentences per se. They are not spatiotemporal—the proposition *snow is white* has no location in space or time. And they are not psychological entities; they are mind-independent entities.

This matters because "the believing is mental; the believed is not." When Smith believes that the inventor of bifocals is six-feet tall, his believing is a psychological condition, but the thing believed is not. Propositions are thus "non-derivative bearers of truth and falsity," whereas beliefs and sentences are only derivatively true.

Kuczynski 110 — PASS
Question: What is truth?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 10
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Part II; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?
Word count: 268

EXACT ANSWER
Truth is instantiatedness. A proposition is true just in case the properties that are members of it are instantiated.

By a "proposition," I mean what is meant by an utterance of a sentence. If I point at Smith and say "that man is a scoundrel," the meaning of my utterance is a proposition. And what is that meaning? It is a set of properties.

So consider the proposition: Tommy is smoking. On my account, this proposition is a set of properties—the property of being identical with Tommy, and the property of smoking. The proposition is true just in case those properties are jointly instantiated. "Propositions are sets of properties; and a proposition is true just in case the properties that are members of it are instantiated."

This is why I say, roughly, "truth is instantiatedness." Less roughly, "truth is identical with the property of being a set (of a certain kind) all of whose members are instantiated."

Note what follows. Truth is not a property of sentences in the first instance. "For a sentence to be 'true' is for it to encode a true proposition." The sentence is a human artifact; the truth it encodes is not.

That truth exists independently of us. "After all, the moon was less massive than the Earth before we came along, and it'll be that way after we sign out." The proposition that the moon is less massive than the Earth was true before any of us thought it, and it will remain true after we are gone.

This is the core of my view: "Propositions are properties and truth is instantiatedness."

Kuczynski 111 — PASS
Question: What does Frege's "saturation" actually amount to?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 3
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Part II; Causality; Do We Think in Words?
Word count: 267

EXACT ANSWER
Frege's "saturation" is just a label for the operation, not an explanation of it. As I've argued, "the term 'saturate' is just another label for the operation in question." So while the Fregean statement "1 is the result of Tommy's saturating the concept of smoking" may well be correct, "we don't know what it means."

My theory of propositions as sets of properties gives that meaning. I hold that "1 is a set whose members include the property of being Tommy, the property of smoking, and the property of being a smoking Tommy." Saturation, properly understood, is set-membership: "1 is the result of Tommy's 'saturating' the property/concept of smoking in the sense that 1 is identical with a set S that consists of those three properties."

The general schema is this. "For any proposition X, to say that X is the result of Y's 'saturating' Z (for some Y and Z) is to say that X is a set whose members are the property of being identical with X, and Z itself, and also the property of being identical with something that is identical with X and also has Z."

Why bother with all these properties rather than just identifying the proposition with the property of smoking? Because "if we identify 1 with C, and 1's being true with C's being instantiated, our theory won't accommodate the very reasonable presumption that 1 has discrete parts corresponding to Tommy and to the property of smoking."

So saturation is not a primitive metaphysical glue. It is decomposable into property-instantiation and identity. Frege named the operation; I've given its content.

Kuczynski 112 — PASS
Question: Is Plato a constituent of the proposition that Plato snores?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 2
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Part II; Causality; Do We Think in Words?; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means
Word count: 271

EXACT ANSWER
Plato is not a constituent of the proposition that Plato snores. The argument is decisive:

"Premises: Plato does not exist at this point in time. | If Plato is a necessary constituent of the proposition 'Plato snores,' then the proposition does not exist if Plato does not exist. | The proposition 'Plato snores' does exist. Conclusion: Plato is not a necessary constituent of the proposition 'Plato snores.'"

The reasoning is airtight. If Plato were a constituent of the proposition, the proposition would perish with him. But the proposition survives. Therefore Plato is not its constituent.

What, then, is the constituent? Not the man, but a concept. This is precisely what I argue about indirect reference: "In indirect reference, a proposition has as a constituent not O itself, but rather some concept that O satisfies." The same structure applies here. The proposition contains a concept of Plato, not Plato himself.

This connects to my broader framework. "The objects of knowledge are propositions." And "knowledge requires belief, and belief requires propositions as its objects." If propositions contained Plato himself as a constituent, then knowing anything about Plato would require Plato to be a part of the knowing. But "awareness of objects does not constitute knowledge; knowledge consists of truths about objects." I can know truths about Plato without Plato being a constituent of my knowledge.

The proposition "Plato snores" is a truth or falsehood — it is the kind of thing that stands in logical dependence-relations, since "logical dependence-relations hold among propositions." Plato himself, a man, cannot stand in such relations. Only propositions can. So Plato cannot be a constituent of a proposition.
