Kuczynski 113 — PASS
Question: Is a proposition a set of possible worlds?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 4
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Part II; Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 252

EXACT ANSWER
No. The possible worlds analysis is the most popular approach on the market, and it collapses under its own weight.

According to possible worlds semantics, "a proposition is necessary (possible) if true in all (some) worlds, and a proposition is a function that assigns truths–values to worlds or, alternatively, is a set of worlds (viz. the set of worlds where it is true)." So the proposition *grass is green* "is a function that assigns truth to all the world where grass is green, falsity to worlds where grass is not green."

Here is the fatal problem. Ask what a "world" is. Advocates say "that 'worlds,' as they are using the term, are propositions (or sets of propositions)." But then, as David Lewis himself pointed out, "the PWS slogan that 'a proposition is a set of worlds' becomes 'a proposition is a set of propositions,' which is not only false but viciously regressive."

The same defect infects the functional formulation. "The same thing mutatis mutandis holding of the statement 'a proposition is a function that assigns truth-values to worlds.'" You cannot define propositions in terms of worlds if worlds are themselves propositions.

My own analysis avoids this. A proposition is a set of properties, true just in case all its members are instantiated. This gives the direct-reference theorist exactly what she wants: for some x identical with Plato, the proposition meant by "Plato snores" is true just in case x snores. And it does so without the circularity that sinks possible worlds semantics.

Kuczynski 114 — PASS
Question: Can possible-worlds semantics distinguish 1 + 1 = 2 from triangles have three sides?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 1
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Do We Think in Words?; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6
Word count: 271

EXACT ANSWER
No. That's the fatal defect in possible-worlds semantics.

The class of worlds where 1 + 1 = 2 is identical with the class of worlds triangles have three sides. But those propositions are obviously distinct, that being why you can think the one without thinking the other. There's no intensional fallacy here, since propositions are intensions.

So in its most primitive form, PWS can't distinguish analytically equivalent propositions. That's not a minor bug—it's a structural failure. If your semantics can't tell apart two propositions that any competent thinker can hold separately, your semantics isn't tracking propositions at all. It's tracking something coarser.

The standard patch is to distinguish extensional from intensional views of functions. On the extensional view, F(x) = x + 1 just is the set of pairs <1, 2>, <2, 3>. And on that view, F(x) = x + 1 is identical with F(x) = x + (90 – 89). But the extensionalist view isn't the only one—there's also the intensionalist view. The patch concedes my point: you need intensional structure to distinguish what PWS collapses.

Worse, the whole apparatus is idle. The worlds answer to us, not us to them. Our modal knowledge is the tail that wags the dog, the dog being these other worlds; and from the viewpoint of explaining our modal knowledge, those extra worlds are useless.

What actually does the work? Dependence-relations. The proposition that x is a triangle cannot be true unless the proposition that x has three sides is true. Analytic truths—1 + 1 = 2 among them—express dependence-relations, even when not obviously so. That's the machinery PWS needs and can't supply.

Kuczynski 115 — PASS
Question: Is "this sentence is false" a sentence?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 4
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Part II; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Do We Think in Words?; Causality
Word count: 266

EXACT ANSWER
No. "This sentence is false" is not a sentence. It is a sentence-schema, and the difference matters enormously.

A sentence-schema is an expression that is just like a sentence except that one of the lexical items in it has been removed and replaced with a variable. So "x is tall" is a sentence-schema. The same is true of "this sentence is false." The word "this" has no referent until we supply one. Once we do, the expression either becomes a genuine sentence with a truth-value or it remains a schema.

Russell and Tarski held that there are meaningless bona fide sentences. Their argument was that there are syntactically well-formed sentences that are true if false and false if true and that, consequently, cannot be meaningful without violating the Law of Non-Contradiction. I have argued that Russell et al. were quite wrong. The expressions they were thinking of are either false or they are sentence-schemata, not actual sentences.

Consider what happens when we try to make "this sentence is false" a real sentence. Suppose the occurrence of "this sentence" refers to the sentence "snow is white." Then what is being said is an abbreviation for "The proposition meant by this sentence is false." That is a perfectly ordinary sentence with a truth-value. It is false, because the proposition meant by "snow is white" is true.

The paradox only arises when we refuse to fix the referent. That refusal is what produces the illusion of a meaningful but truth-valueless sentence. There is no such thing. There are only schemata awaiting assignment and sentences that have already received one.

Kuczynski 116 — PASS
Question: Does Russell's paradox refute the Axiom of Comprehension?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 3
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Causality; Do We Think in Words?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means
Word count: 255

EXACT ANSWER
Russell's paradox doesn't merely refute the Axiom of Comprehension—it exposes a structural flaw in any system that permits self-membership. The paradox arises because "the class of all classes that don't belong to themselves is a member of itself entails its own negation, and that the negation of K entails its own negation."

This is fatal. "Since, according to the law of excluded middle (any given proposition is either true or false), either K or its negation is true, it follows that K and its negation are true. But, according to the law of non-contradiction (no proposition is both true and false), this isn't possible."

Russell's own solution was to prohibit self-application entirely. "Russell dealt with this by saying that nothing can be true of itself. Properties cannot be their own instances; statements cannot describe themselves. Thus, AC is ruled out, and so is (i)."

So the Axiom of Comprehension, in its unrestricted form, cannot stand. It must be replaced by a stratified or typed comprehension principle that forbids the offending self-reference.

There is a deeper lesson here about analyticity. I have argued that "analytic truths, even when not obviously so, express dependence-relations." The comprehension axiom was treated as analytic—obviously true—yet it generates contradiction. That shows the axiom was never truly analytic in the robust sense. Genuine analytic truths, like "1+1=2" or "there are infinitely many primes," express dependence-relations that cannot collapse into paradox.

The paradox therefore refutes unrestricted comprehension, not comprehension as such. A restricted version survives—one that respects the dependence-structure of the concepts involved.

Kuczynski 117 — PASS
Question: Is meaning use?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 12
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Part II; Do We Think in Words?
Word count: 255

EXACT ANSWER
Meaning is not use. The doctrine that it is—Wittgenstein's contention, and the core of conceptual role semantics—is incoherent.

The reason is simple. "Expressions have meanings. A meaningless burst of noise isn't an expression." If I cough or guffaw, that noise has no linguistic meaning at all. So there can be no expression-use until there is already expression-meaning. "Since there can be no expression-use until after there is expression-meaning, it makes no sense at all to say that expression-use determines expression-meaning." And what determines cannot be identical with what it determines.

This is why "meaningful expression" is a pleonasm. To be an expression just is to have a meaning. The use comes after.

The decisive point is that meaning guides use. "I know what 'hug' means; I also know what 'discuss' means. That's why, when talking to my students, I say 'I want to discuss the exam,' and not 'I want to hug the exam.' If meaning were use, meaning couldn't guide use. But it obviously does."

When I misspeak—saying "moron" when I meant "genius"—the failure is precisely a failure of meaning to guide use. "To the extent that my uttering those words embodied a knowledge of what they meant—to the extent that meaning did guide use, in other words—I spoke properly."

I grant that use can change meaning. "How a given expression is used may well assign it a new meaning." But there is "all the difference in the world" between causal determination and identity. Use may cause a meaning; it does not constitute one.

Kuczynski 118 — PASS
Question: Does Wittgenstein's rule-following argument show that thinking is not a psychological process?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 9
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Do We Think in Words?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Causality; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6
Word count: 297

EXACT ANSWER
No. Wittgenstein's rule-following argument does not show that thinking is not a psychological process. It is a spurious argument for a false conclusion.

Wittgenstein's idea "that meanings, if grasped, must be interpreted reflects his erroneous belief that, whenever one can't see a consequence of some principle that one grasps, it's because one hasn't adequately interpreted that principle." But this is simply wrong: "principles aren't interpreted. They're grasped. And, if grasped, they guide judgments."

Wittgenstein grants that people think. But because he believes, "totally absurdly, that rule-following and, therefore, thinking aren't psychological acts, he is forced to come up with a different analysis of what thought is." So he concludes that "to think is to manipulate symbols of public languages." This is a non sequitur built on a false premise.

The deeper error is his assumption "that everything there is to know about one's mind is to be known in the same quasi-perceptual, phenomenology-drenched way in which we know of our sensations." That assumption "is blatantly false." I know I believe that 2 + 2 = 4, and I know it directly—not by experiencing some sensation.

Wittgenstein is right that "the sensations and images that pass through one's mind when one is having a given thought do not constitute that thought." But he's wrong to conclude that thinking isn't a psychological process. What he should have concluded is that "not all psychological activity consists of images and sensations."

His view is also "inconsistent with the fact that, unless one can think, one cannot use expressions meaningfully." If I merely bark out sounds with no idea what they mean, I am not using language at all. Speech requires thought guiding it.

So rule-following is not a strictly psychological phenomenon—but thinking is. Wittgenstein conflated the two, and the argument collapses.

Kuczynski 119 — PASS
Question: Is a private language possible?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 7
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Do We Think in Words?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Part II; Causality
Word count: 267

EXACT ANSWER
No. A private language is logically impossible, not merely psychologically difficult to achieve.

Wittgenstein's Private Language Argument holds that "there cannot possibly exist such a thing as a private language." Human beings can devise private codes, he granted. But "any such code must be a translation of an existing public language." It isn't even theoretically possible for there to exist a language that wasn't created by several interacting individuals.

The reason is meaning itself. "There are languages only where there are right and wrong ways to use expressions." A symbol that can't be used wrongly doesn't mean anything. "What makes utterances of 'John is a soccer player' meaningful is that they are used wrongly if John isn't a soccer player." Strip away the possibility of error, and you strip away meaning.

So the private linguist's "Smithese" fails. "Since it is only where several people are using a language that there are right and wrong ways of using its expressions, it is only where there are several people that there are languages: all languages are public."

This has a striking consequence for thought. "Wittgenstein also held that one can't think unless one knows a language." He granted one could have mental states without a language, but "knowledge of a language was a prerequisite for any sort of reasoning." Therefore "one cannot think unless one is embedded in a society of some kind."

The upshot: "It is logically, and not just psychologically, impossible for a human being who isn't either a current or erstwhile member of a society to think." Solitary cognition is a surd, like a square circle.

Kuczynski 120 — PASS
Question: Is "colorless green ideas sleep furiously" meaningless?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 5
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Part II; Do We Think in Words?; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Causality; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6
Word count: 259

EXACT ANSWER
No. "Colorless green ideas sleep furiously" is not meaningless. It is a bona fide sentence of English that expresses a proposition—just a false or vacuously true one.

Chomsky's famous example is supposed to show that a sentence can be grammatical yet meaningless. My reasoning is that this is no good. Depending on how it's interpreted, the sentence "either says (i) that there are dreams that are green and also colorless that sleep furiously, in which case it's false, or it says (ii) that there is nothing that is a colorless green dream that doesn't also sleep furiously, in which case it's vacuously true."

Either way, it says something. It has meaning. It is therefore an expression.

The deeper principle here is that "nothing meaningless is an expression." And since "there would be no languages if there were no expressions," meaninglessness cannot attach to genuine linguistic items.

People confuse two very different failures. Consider the difference between an incoherent statement and a meaningless string. "For a statement to be meaningless is for it to have no meaning. For a statement to be incoherent is for it to have two (or more) opposed meanings." A string like "Frog the marathon pool clearly dabble" has no meaning—it says nothing. But "colorless green ideas sleep furiously" is not in that category. It is a meaningful sentence expressing a proposition "that, for whatever reason, aren't worth affirming."

So the sentence is odd, absurd, false. But it is not meaningless. Absurdity is not the same as meaninglessness, and conflating them has led many authors astray.

Kuczynski 121 — PASS
Question: Do we think in words?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 16
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Do We Think in Words?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Causality; Part II; Why Does Alcoholics Anonymous Work?; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible
Word count: 264

EXACT ANSWER
No. We do not think in language.

I distinguish two versions of the thesis that we do. Version #1 holds that "English speakers think in English; Albanian speakers think in Albanian; etc." Version #2 holds that "we think in an innately known code, a 'language of thought.'" Both are false.

Against Version #1: "We can obviously have thoughts that we are incapable of putting into words." When we struggle to find the right words, "thinking is often a prerequisite to using language, which in turn shows that at least some thinking is non-linguistic." And "people who speak different languages can have the same thoughts"—monolingual Spanish and English speakers both believe 1 + 1 = 2, yet use different sentences to express it.

Against Version #2: "We often think in images (visual and auditory), and the contents of these images seem to have a structure that is fundamentally different from the structure of any sentence." Sentences are "digital" structures; sense-perceptions are "analogue" structures, "characterized by a kind of seamlessness that sharply distinguishes them from sentences." Moreover, "it is viciously circular to hold that we think in an innately known code," since understanding any language requires grasping its rules.

Why does it feel as though we think in words? Because "knowledge of language enormously enhances at least some of our cognitive capabilities." When I think, "my thoughts often take the form of a voice." But this is a tool, not the substance of thought.

My conclusion: "we don't think in language, even though, undeniably, knowledge of language enormously enhances at least some of our cognitive capabilities."

Kuczynski 122 — PASS
Question: Is there a language of thought?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 6
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Do We Think in Words?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Part II; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible
Word count: 243

EXACT ANSWER
No. We do not think in an innate language or code, and we do not think in a public language either.

My view is that "whatever one can grasp through language, one must be able to grasp independently of language." This is counterintuitive, I grant. But I came to it only after trying to defend the negation and finding it impossible.

Consider the sixth reason. "Understanding sentences involves thought." To understand "if snow is cold, then snow is not hot," you must pair the sentence with the right meaning—and that pairing is not itself a sentence flashing through your mind. If I hear a language I don't understand, the sounds may echo later, but I grasp nothing. So understanding a sentence differs from its mere occurrence in consciousness.

Consider the fifth reason. "People who speak different languages can have the same thoughts." A monolingual Spanish speaker and a monolingual English speaker both believe 1 + 1 = 2, yet they use different sentences. Thinking that truth cannot be identical with thinking a sentence of either language.

And consider the book analogy. If nobody understands the sentences supposedly identical with their thoughts, "those sentences aren't really functioning as sentences anymore." They function like a copy of War and Peace hurled at a roommate—a weapon, not a text.

Language enormously enhances cognition. But enhancement is not identity. The icon on your desktop represents electrical activity it only schematically resembles. So too with words and thought.

Kuczynski 123 — PASS
Question: Is Grice right that sentence meaning derives from speaker meaning?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 16
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Part II; Do We Think in Words?; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Causality
Word count: 243

EXACT ANSWER
No. Grice is wrong, and the error runs deep.

His core claim is that "literal meaning is to be understood in terms of speaker's meaning." I deny this outright. "Literal meaning is isn't identical with speaker's meaning and isn't to be understood in terms of it. It's the other way around."

Consider compositionality. If Grice were right, the meaning of "Smith is now living in France" "would be fixed by the intentions people have in using it. But its meaning is not fixed by those intentions. It is fixed by the meanings of its parts." In fact, "Grice's view is inherently incapable of accommodating the fact meaning is compositional."

Then there are subsentential expressions. "Grice's theory fails to deal with the fact that the meaning of a subsentential expression isn't something that could be possibly be meant." What does "or" mean? Whatever it is, "it cannot, at least not by itself, be what a person means."

And the fatal blow: semantic rules are normative. "Unlike scientific laws, semantic rules are normative." If you say "Smith is male" intending to affirm Smith is female, "you've done something wrong." But if literal meaning just were speaker's meaning, "speaker's meaning wouldn't be accountable to existing semantic rules. Since it is, Grice is wrong."

Wittgenstein's version fares no better. His claim that "meaning is use" "isn't even roughly true."

The order of explanation runs the other way: speaker's meaning is accountable to literal meaning, not the reverse.

REPRESENTATIVE SOURCE-LINKED QUOTATIONS

[Part II] CRS is incoherent for reasons other than the one just given. According to that doctrine, what a sentence means is determined by what people infer from it and what people infer it from.

Kuczynski 124 — PASS
Question: Is conceptual role semantics tenable?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 4
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Part II; Causality; Do We Think in Words?; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?
Word count: 305

EXACT ANSWER
No. Conceptual role semantics is incoherent, and it fails for reasons that go to the heart of what meaning is.

The doctrine holds that "for an expression to have a given meaning is simply for it to be used in a certain way." But this gets the order of explanation backwards. An expression must already have a meaning before it can be used to mean anything. As I put it, "E isn't an expression and, therefore, isn't an expression to be used until it has a meaning." You cannot constitute meaning out of use, because use presupposes meaning.

The second failure is worse. CRS says "what a sentence means is determined by what people infer from it and what people infer it from." This inverts the actual dependence. We infer "an even number is less than five" from "two is less than five" *because* the latter already has a given meaning. CRS says the inference is what confers the meaning. That is backwards.

Consider a test case. "If we learn tomorrow that, contrary to what we previously thought, Aristotle wrote several plays, we'll infer 'somebody who wrote several plays wrote the Nichomachean Ethics' from 'Aristotle wrote the Nichomachean Ethics.'" But it does not follow that "Aristotle wrote the Nichomachean Ethics" would have undergone some change in its semantic meaning. The meaning is stable; the inferences shift.

The same brittleness afflicts functionalist cousins of CRS. If meaning is exhausted by causal or inferential role, then "no two people can believe that 1 + 1 = 2 or that Mongolia is in Asia." Smith the physicist and Jones the layman have wildly different roles for "snow is white" — yet they believe the same thing. Since that is obviously false, so is the view that generates it.

Meaning is not use. It is what makes use possible.

Kuczynski 125 — PASS
Question: What do semantic rules assign meanings to?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 20
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Part II; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Do We Think in Words?; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6
Word count: 271

EXACT ANSWER
Semantic rules assign meanings to properties, not to expressions. This is the central correction I make against the standard view.

The standard view holds that "a semantic rule can't be defined as a rule that assigns a meaning to an expression." Why? Because "expressions aren't assigned meanings. They already have them and don't need to be assigned them." Something is an expression only once it already carries meaning.

So what does a semantic rule operate on? "Thus, semantic rules assign meanings to non-expressions." Specifically, they assign meanings to properties of physical objects. As I put it: "semantic rules assign meanings to properties of physical objects—to morphological or acoustical properties (in other words, to properties that a things has in virtue of having a certain shape or sounding a certain way)."

Consider my example of "Barack Obama." There is a semantic rule that assigns a meaning to the property of having a morphology similar to that ink deposit. The meaning assigned to that property is itself a semantic rule—one that assigns Barack Obama to each instance of the property.

This yields a two-level structure. "There are those that assign meanings to properties, and there are those that assign meanings to instances of those properties." The first-level rule (R1) assigns a rule (R2) to a property; R2 then assigns meanings to instances. And crucially, "the meanings that R2 assigns to those tokens are not themselves rules; they are propositions—they are things that are true or false."

So: rules assign meanings to properties; those meanings are themselves rules; those rules assign propositions to property-instances. Language, on my account, is "a set of such rules."

Kuczynski 126 — PASS
Question: Do definite descriptions refer to anything?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 19
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Part II; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Causality; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Do We Think in Words?; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible
Word count: 323

EXACT ANSWER
No. Definite descriptions are not referring terms. No definite description refers to anything.

This is the core of my position. "The inventor of Velcro" doesn't refer to anyone or anything. "The inventor of Velcro is seven-feet tall" doesn't attribute the property of being 7-feet tall to anyone. The meaning of "the inventor of Velcro" isn't given by saying who it refers to, but by saying what whole sentences containing it mean.

The reason is straightforward. Consider a world just like ours where people use the same expressions in accordance with the same rules, but where Bob invents Velcro and is under 7-feet tall. In that world, "the inventor of Velcro has psi" is false, even though the sentence has the very same semantics it has in our world. So there is no individual x such that knowing the semantics of "the inventor of Velcro" is knowing that it refers to x.

What follows is that definite descriptions must be defined contextually. As I put it, "for any property phi, ‹the phi› is defined, not denotatively, but contextually—that is, by saying what whole sentences containing it mean." The rule is: "‹the phi has psi› is true if there exists something uniquely having phi, and any such thing has psi."

This is Russell's insight, and it is correct. "The inventor of bifocals snored" is true iff exactly one thing invented bifocals, and any such snored. That shows definite descriptions are quantifiers, not singular terms. They encode existence-claims rather than picking out objects.

The apparent reference is an illusion of grammatical form. "The fountain of youth exists" looks like it attributes existence to some fountain, but reparsed it becomes "the property of being a fountain of youth is uniquely instantiated." Likewise, "the monster under little Timmy's bed doesn't exist" is true precisely because the description refers to nothing—what's true is that the property of being such a monster isn't instantiated.

So: no reference. Only contextual definition.

Kuczynski 127 — PASS
Question: Does Frege's sense/reference distinction survive scrutiny?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 4
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Part II; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Do We Think in Words?; Causality; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism
Word count: 263

EXACT ANSWER
No. Frege's distinction between sense and reference is not a genuine discovery about language—it is a distortion.

I have argued that "Frege's distinction between 'sense' and 'reference' is an incoherent way of describing the distinction between semantics and pre-semantics." What Frege calls the "sense" of a name is supposed to be some property uniquely instantiated by its referent. But this is false. "One's knowing what 'London' refers to consists in there being a property phi—it doesn't matter which one—such that one knows that phi is uniquely instantiated and that 'London' refers to any instance of it." There is no single property that does this work.

The deeper problem is structural. If Frege's analysis of proper names were correct, then a sentence of the form ‹N has psi› would be true just in case some property phi is uniquely instantiated and any such instance has psi. But that is an existential generalization. So "if Frege's analysis of proper names is right, they are semantically indistinguishable from existential quantifiers and, therefore, are such quantifiers." Yet Frege insists names are referring terms. His position is therefore that names "both are and are not quantifiers," which is incoherent.

His notion of indirect reference collapses for the same reason. "Frege's position is that names refer indirectly. In other words, they refer through the mediation of a sense, and that sense is what makes it into the propositions meant by sentences containing those names." But "indirect reference" is really just quantification. The referent never makes it into the proposition at all.

What survives is only the pre-semantic/semantic distinction, mislabeled.

Kuczynski 128 — PASS
Question: Are there any intensional contexts?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 13
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Part II; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Do We Think in Words?; Causality
Word count: 288

EXACT ANSWER
No. There are no intensional contexts. All contexts are substitution-tolerant.

The appearance of breakdown is exactly that—appearance. When two expressions that seem to refer to the same individual cannot be inter-substituted, they actually refer to different propositions. That is the whole of my argument.

Consider the classic case. From the fact that believing that belief x = belief x does not entail believing that belief x = pattern of neural stimulation y, it does not follow that x ≠ y. The apparent violation of Leibniz's Law dissolves once we see what is really being affirmed.

Take sentences like "it is necessarily the case that any woman who is prettier than every other woman is prettier than every other woman" and "it is necessarily the case that any woman who is prettier than every other woman is also more evil than every other person." The first attributes the property of being necessarily true to one proposition; the second expresses that same property to some other proposition. Since those propositions are distinct, the fact that the one proposition is necessarily true doesn't entail that the same is true of the other. There is no violation of Leibniz's Law.

So I say: "there are no intensional contexts. (In other words, all contexts are substitution-tolerant.)"

The term remains useful only as shorthand. "An 'intensional context' in which expressions that otherwise refer to individuals (e.g., 'Benjamin Franklin') refer to propositions." An expression occurring in such a context does so intensionally; otherwise extensionally.

The deeper point: Leibniz's Law is identical with the obviously correct principle that nothing can fail to have a property that it has. There are no actual exceptions to it. What look like exceptions are misreadings of what the sentences mean.

Kuczynski 129 — PASS
Question: Does Quine's case against modal notions succeed?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 1
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Causality; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Part II; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Do We Think in Words?; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6
Word count: 331

EXACT ANSWER
Quine's case fails. His argument against modal notions rests on a conflation of necessity *de dicto* and necessity *de re*, and once that conflation is exposed, the alleged incoherence dissolves.

His argument runs: "If the concepts expressed by 'necessary' and 'possible' are meaningful, then FB expresses a truth and BF expresses a falsehood." From this, together with "Leibniz's Law holds" and "FB is a necessary truth," he draws the conclusion that "the assumption that 'necessary' and 'possible' express coherent concepts is wrong, making all statements about possibility or necessity either meaningless or false."

That conclusion does not follow. The argument trades on treating the number 9 as if it were a *thing* whose modal properties could be counted independently of how it is specified. But "the number of planets" and "9" pick out the same object under different guises, and necessity attaches to the guise, not the bare object. Leibniz's Law governs objects, not modes of presentation.

The deeper error is Quine's verificationism. He demands that modal claims be reducible to non-modal ones or else be dismissed as "meaningless." But that demand is itself a modal-free dogma, and it proves too much — by the same standard, causal claims would collapse, since "e is the cause of e*" cannot be paraphrased as "If e hadn't happened, then e* wouldn't have happened" without loss. As I've argued, that counterfactual "is not always a consequence of 'e is the cause of e*'" — it "fails to be such a consequence whenever e is but one of many would-be causes of e*."

The lesson generalizes. Confirmation itself is non-monotonic: "Given only that P confirms Q and that R is true, it doesn't follow that P and R jointly confirm Q." And "confirmation does not necessarily warrant inference" — P may confirm Q without Q being inferable from P. These are modal and intensional phenomena Quine's extensionalism cannot capture.

So no, his case does not succeed. It presupposes the very reduction it claims to demonstrate.

Kuczynski 130 — PASS
Question: Is a tautology an analytic truth?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 3
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Causality; Do We Think in Words?; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Part II
Word count: 264

EXACT ANSWER
A tautology is an analytic truth, but not all analytic truths are tautologies. The relationship is one of species to genus.

My position is precise: "A tautology is a definitional truth." That is the core of it. When I say "'A bachelor is an unmarried man' is a tautology," I mean it holds "because it is a definitional truth." The predicate unpacks what the subject already contains.

But analyticity is broader. As I've argued, "An analytic truth is one that holds entirely in virtue of its own content, for example: cubes are three-dimensional figures." And crucially: "A truth is analytic if, given only what it says about the world, it could not possibly fail to be true."

So the genus is analyticity — truth in virtue of content alone. The tautology is one species of this. Every tautology is analytic, but the converse fails. Consider "There are infinitely many primes." This is analytic on my account, yet it is not a definitional truth in the way "a bachelor is an unmarried man" is. It is not a tautology.

I also distinguish analyticity from formality. "A formal truth is one that holds entirely in virtue of its formal properties, equivalently, one whose form is not instantiated by any falsehood." Formal truth and analytic truth overlap but are not identical.

The key move is this: analytic truths, even when not obviously so, express dependence-relations. "Analytic truths, which involve dependence-relations, are known through conceptual analysis rather than sensory observation." Tautologies are the most transparent instance of this — the dependence-relation is laid bare in the definition itself.

Kuczynski 131 — FAIL
Question: Did Gödel refute the analyticity of mathematics?
Answer type: indirect
Direct evidence count: 0
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Do We Think in Words?; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism
Word count: 235
Failure reason: The diagnostic does not accept fluent output based on indirect or absent source material.

EXACT ANSWER
No. Gödel's incompleteness theorems do not refute the analyticity of mathematics. They refute a specific thesis about provability, not the thesis that mathematical truths are analytic.

My position is that analytic truths express dependence-relations. Consider my own examples: "If P, then either P or Q," "There are infinitely many primes," "1+1=2," "1+1≠3." These are analytic, and they "express dependence-relations." Gödel's results concern which such truths are formally derivable from a given axiom system—not whether they hold by conceptual necessity.

The key distinction is this: "Analytic knowledge is always knowledge of dependence-relations." That is a claim about the *nature* of analytic knowledge, not about its *provability*. Gödel showed that in any consistent, sufficiently strong formal system, some truths are unprovable within it. He did not show that those truths fail to express dependence-relations.

Furthermore, "some dependence-relations are known, not through sensory observation, but through conceptual analysis." This is exactly the route by which we grasp the Gödel sentence itself. We see that it must be true—by reasoning about the structure of the system, not by deriving it within the system.

So the validity of non-empirical knowledge "does not depend on the veracity of sensory input, but on the soundness of reasoning." Gödel's theorem is a triumph of that reasoning, not a refutation of analyticity.

In short: Gödel refutes Hilbert's program, not the analyticity of mathematics. The two are routinely conflated, and the conflation is a mistake.

Kuczynski 132 — PASS
Question: Is formal truth a property of sentences or a relation between sentences and axiom-sets?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 7
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Part II; Causality; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 266

EXACT ANSWER
I have held two positions on this, and they are not the same.

In one framework, formal truth is a property of sentences. "Formal truth is a property of sentences. A sentence is formally true if every sentence having the same form is true." On this view, "if Bill is tall, then it is not the case that it is not the case that Bill is tall" is formally true because every sentence of that form is true. The property attaches to the sentence itself, by virtue of its syntax.

In another framework, I reframe it relationally. "A statement S is formally true if and only if there exists a truth-preserving recursive logic L such that S ∈ L." Here formal truth is not intrinsic but "a relationship between a statement and a truth-preserving recursive system."

These are genuinely different claims. The first is about sentences and their forms. The second is about membership in a recursive logic.

The relational conception carries a striking consequence: "The predicate 'formally true' is not recursively enumerable." If we could enumerate all formally true statements, we could enumerate the recursive logics themselves—which is impossible. So "there is no algorithm that can list all formal truths."

I also distinguish sentence-analyticity from proposition-analyticity. "Propositions don't have syntax. Syntax is a property of complex expressions." Formal truth, strictly, belongs to sentences—indeed to sentence-tokens, since "it's sentence-tokens, not sentences per se, that are either true or false to begin with."

So: as a property, formal truth is sentential. As a relation, it is membership in a recursive logic. I have not fully reconciled these.

Kuczynski 133 — PASS
Question: Is logic about sentences or about propositions?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 12
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Part II; Causality; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Do We Think in Words?; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6
Word count: 271

EXACT ANSWER
Logic is about propositions, never sentences. Sentences are the vehicles; propositions are what they encode. My position is unambiguous: "it is always propositions, and never sentences, that are logically true."

Consider a sentence like "If a given thing is round, then that thing is not a square." The sentence itself is a human artifact. What's logically true is the proposition it expresses. As I put it, "A proposition is logically true if the laws of logic prohibit its negation from being true." The laws of logic don't govern ink marks or phonemes—they govern what those marks mean.

This distinction matters because it dissolves a whole family of errors. When someone calls a sentence "logically true," they mean "given what it is that it means, (4) must be true." But that's just to say "the proposition that (4) couldn't be false, given what it is that it means" is what's really being described.

The same point applies to truth generally. "For a sentence to be 'true' is for it to encode a true proposition." The sentence is true derivatively. The proposition is true in the primary sense: "for a proposition to be true is for it to fit the facts."

And what are propositions? "They're properties." A proposition's being true is its being instantiated. So logic tracks properties and their instantiation, not strings of symbols.

This is why I insist that "philosophy is the analysis of propositions," not sentences. Wittgenstein's error was precisely to deny propositions exist and then treat philosophy as sentence-analysis. But "the proposition meant by that sentence can be grasped without speaking English"—which shows the proposition isn't the sentence.

Kuczynski 134 — PASS
Question: What is a priori knowledge knowledge of?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 3
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Do We Think in Words?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Part II
Word count: 279

EXACT ANSWER
A priori knowledge is knowledge of what is constitutive of our cognitive machinery. It is not knowledge of this or that empirical fact. It is knowledge of the structural conditions under which any empirical fact could be known at all.

I define it plainly: "A priori knowledge is knowledge that is constitutive of our cognitive machinery; it's knowledge that is hardwired into us and that we therefore don't acquire." This is why it is not derived from sense-perception. "A posteriori knowledge is knowledge that is not a priori."

Contrast this with empirical knowledge, which "is based at least partly on the testimony of the senses." Not all knowledge is empirical. Some is analytic—"knowledge that is arrived at strictly through the analysis of concepts." Consider 1+1=2. "To know that is it true, one doesn't do empirical work; one doesn't perform experiments or make observations. 1+1=2 is thus a priori."

Now the crucial Kantian point. For Kant, "a priority is a property of our knowledge of propositions." When he calls a proposition a priori, "he is really making a statement about our knowledge of those propositions." A proposition is a priori "not in virtue of its intrinsic or strictly logical properties, but in virtue of facts about how one comes to know it." The consequence: "a given proposition could, in principle, be a priori for one creature and a posteriori for another."

So a priori knowledge is knowledge of the architecture of cognition itself—the hardwired framework that makes experience possible. It is not a species of observation. It is the precondition of observation.

This is why empiricism fails. "If all knowledge were observation-based, knowledge of that very fact couldn't be observation-based."

Kuczynski 135 — PASS
Question: What are the two roles of sense-experience in cognition?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 5
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Do We Think in Words?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means
Word count: 282

EXACT ANSWER
Sense-perception plays two fundamentally different roles in cognition, and confusing them is the deepest error of empiricism.

The first is the **information-transmitting role**. Here the senses actually tell you something about the external world that you could not have known otherwise. As I put it: "If I see Jim playing soccer, my visual perception adds to my knowledge by transmitting to me the correct message that Jim is playing soccer." This is genuine information transfer—"information about the external world is being transmitted to you through your senses."

The second is the **ratiocination-activating role**. Here the senses do not transmit new information; they merely trigger a purely rational process that was already available to the mind. My formulation: "In other cases, sense-perception merely activates some purely ratiocinative process."

The distinction matters enormously. "The ratiocination-activating role of sense-perceptions must be distinguished from its information-transmitting role." Why? Because "empiricism, the doctrine that all knowledge is derived from the senses, is based on a failure to make this distinction."

Consider what perception presupposes. To perceive anything at all, "we be able to represent it as having a location (relative to us) in space and time, that we be able to represent it as having a certain shape, state of motion, color, etc." But "what we don't learn through it are the concepts—space, time, motion, shape, color, etc.—out of which sense-perceptions are constructed." Those concepts "must be in the mind prior to sense-perception, as a necessary precondition for it."

So the empiricist conflates two things: the senses as conduits of worldly information, and the senses as mere triggers for conceptual machinery the mind already possesses. Only the first role supports the empiricist thesis. The second undermines it.

Kuczynski 136 — PASS
Question: Is mathematical knowledge perceptual?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 9
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Do We Think in Words?; Causality; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 255

EXACT ANSWER
No. Mathematical knowledge is not perceptual, and treating it as such is a category error.

The core of my argument is this: "nothing can sense-perceive anything that doesn't affect it." Perception requires causal contact. Light-rays bounce off a book and disturb your eyes; that is how you see it. But the fact that 1 + 1 = 2 does not bounce off anything. It does not disturb your retinas.

This is why I regard the perceptual model of mathematical knowledge as "absurd in the extreme." The contrast is decisive. "Were mass-energy distributed differently, there wouldn't be a book in front of you. But 1+1 would equal 2 no matter how mass-energy were distributed." The mathematical fact is invariant across every possible physical arrangement. The perceptual fact is not.

So the mathematical fact "says nothing about how mass-energy is distributed, and it therefore says nothing about the spatiotemporal world." What follows is unavoidable: "The fact it describes must therefore be non-spatiotemporal." You cannot perceive what is not in space-time.

Contrast this with genuine perceptual knowledge. "My visual perception of the dog in front of me is a case of objectual awareness, as is my awareness of the tightness of my shoes." These are objectual—direct contact with spatiotemporal particulars. Mathematical knowledge is propositional, not objectual.

I do hold that "there are two kinds of awareness: propositional and objectual." But only the objectual kind is perceptual. Mathematical knowledge is propositional awareness of a non-spatiotemporal fact, and it is acquired "directly or indirectly" like any other propositional knowledge—never perceptually.

Kuczynski 137 — PASS
Question: Is perceptual content ever singular?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 6
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Part II; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Do We Think in Words?; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Causality
Word count: 245

EXACT ANSWER
No. Perceptual content is purely descriptive—it is always general, never singular.

My view is that "perception is purely descriptive. For you to perceive an object is for you to be apprised (in a certain way) of an existence-claim that it uniquely satisfies." The content of your perception of Larry, for instance, is given by an existence-claim: "there exists, over in that place at the present time, instances of such and such properties."

This is the crux. You do not see Larry *and* his properties as two separate items. "Your seeing Larry consists in your seeing those property-instances—in your seeing that such and such properties are instantiated." There is no additional singular element layered on top.

Consider what a singular content would even require. It would mean "Pat's being represented to you as a featureless lump, a blank undifferentiated entity, with various property-instances piled on top of it." But "the very idea of a thing's being perceptually represented as a featureless blank is a non-starter."

So the object enters the picture only as the unique satisfier of a descriptive claim. "Given that Larry, and Larry alone, satisfies that existence-claim, he is the object of your perception." Singularity is a fact about what satisfies the content—not a feature of the content itself.

Hence: "there is nothing to seeing (or otherwise sense-perceiving) an object other than seeing (same qualification) the property-instances associated with it." The content stays general; the object is picked out only derivatively, by unique satisfaction.

Kuczynski 138 — PASS
Question: Is Searle right that all mentality is conscious?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 1
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Do We Think in Words?; Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible
Word count: 242

EXACT ANSWER
No. Searle is wrong that all mentality is conscious, and my argument against him turns on a distinction he collapses: the difference between objectual and propositional awareness.

My framework is this. There are two kinds of awareness. "My visual perception of the dog in front of me is a case of objectual awareness, as is my awareness of the tightness of my shoes." Contrast that with knowing that there is a dog before me, or knowing that my shoes are uncomfortably tight—these are propositional. "Knowledge is proposition-awareness, distinct from objectual awareness."

Now apply this to Searle. He wants consciousness to be the mark of the mental. But awareness of objects is not itself knowledge, and it is not itself a proposition. "Awareness of objects does not constitute knowledge; knowledge consists of truths about objects." So we already have mental phenomena—objectual awareness—that are not reducible to the propositional register Searle privileges.

Searle's deeper error is inferential. He reasons from behavior to mind, and I reject that move outright. "Behavior alone cannot be definitive proof of thinking." If behavior underdetermines thought, then consciousness cannot be read off behavior either—and the category of the mental cannot be policed by what is consciously reportable.

So my position: mentality is broader than consciousness. Knowledge is "a conceptualization of my awareness of that state of affairs," and that awareness can be objectual, not merely conscious-propositional. Searle conflates the two and thereby loses the objectual half of mental life.

Kuczynski 139 — PASS
Question: Is Hume's analysis of causation correct?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 10
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means
Word count: 270

EXACT ANSWER
No. Hume's analysis of causation is false, and I can demonstrate this with three decisive problems.

First, it cannot distinguish actual causation from pseudo-causation. Consider Fido, the earthquake-detecting dog. "Hume's analysis entails that Fido's antics causes the earthquake to strike." The antics immediately precede the earthquake, are adjacent to it, and such antics are always adjacent to an ensuing earthquake. All three of Hume's conditions are satisfied—yet the dog clearly did not cause the quake. "Hume's analysis cannot distinguish epiphenomenal causation from actual causation."

Second, the analysis has the absurd consequence that any two spatiotemporally adjacent events are causally related. "Given any two spatiotemporally adjacent events x and y, a similar argument shows that, if Hume's analysis is right, x caused y." Sally hugs Bob right before his heart attack; Hume's machinery makes the hug the cause. The fix—invoking "relevant" categories—fails, because "we can't select the relevant categories until we have the very knowledge that Hume's analysis is supposed to give us."

Third, the analysis is viciously circular. "According to Hume, x is a cause of y only if x and y are space-time neighbors." But space and time are themselves understood causally: "Order in time is thus to be understood in causal terms." So Hume analyzes causality in terms of itself.

The root error is his assumption that "changes consist of events." The truth: "They don't." The world has an analogue, not a digital structure. "It is only with considerable artifice that ME is represented as consisting of some event x and some adjacent event y." Anyone witnessing genuine causation "knows that he is witnessing an instance of continuity."

Kuczynski 140 — PASS
Question: Is constant conjunction or continuity the mark of causation?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 11
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence
Word count: 270

EXACT ANSWER
Continuity is the mark of causation. Constant conjunction is a symptom, not the thing itself.

Hume's mistake was to build causality out of mere succession. As I argue, "Hume's conception of causality involves a falsely 'digital' conception of spatiotemporal reality." On his view, "each region of space and of time is a distinct box that can be filled with a state of affairs," and "if the contents of one of those boxes are replaced or annihilated, that has no ramifications as far as the other boxes are concerned." That is permutation-friendliness, and permutation-friendliness just *is* the absence of causal connection.

The real mark is continuity. "Persistence is a causal phenomenon. Spatio-temporal continuity is a form of persistence. Consequently, continuity is a causal phenomenon." This is why "Causation is bound up with continuity – with the very features of reality that resist the sort of digitization associated with sentences."

Constant conjunctions are merely clues. They "tip off us to continuities, to causal mechanisms. but it's the mechanism, the continuity, that is the sine qua non of causality." That is precisely why there are "confluences of events that are not related as cause and effect but that, if HA were right, would be so related."

The empiricist is blind here. "To the extent that an investigator's methodology is that of an empiricist, he is blind to anything that isn't either depicted or itself a depiction. The invisible is, for him, truly invisible." Hence Hume and his heirs "deny the existence of causes."

We do not infer causes from regularities. "First we know what causes what. Only then do we look for regularities."

Kuczynski 141 — PASS
Question: Are events constituents of the world?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 6
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Part II; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means
Word count: 241

EXACT ANSWER
No. Events are not constituents of the world. They are nominalizations of truths.

The spatiotemporal world obviously undergoes change, and any such change is an event. But that does not make events building blocks. "Events are discrete, isolable entities" — that is the assumption I reject. The truth is that "the spatiotemporal world doesn't consist of them."

Here is the argument. "The world consists of facts, not of truths." Truths hold in virtue of facts, but they are not identical with them. An event is just the nominalization of a truth: "The event consisting of Smith's killing Brown is the nominalization of the truth that Smith killed Brown."

Consider Smith's stroke. Let E be that event, E* the biological event, and the physical displacement beneath it. If E and E* were both constituents of the external world, they would be spatiotemporally coincident. That entails that "some region of space-time isn't self-identical." That is absurd. So "events aren't constituents of the external world."

This is no loss. It is a truism — a corollary of the fact that "true propositions (truths) are distinct from the facts in virtue of which they hold."

The world is analogue, not digital. A pig thrown from a rooftop splatters; the process "can't be atomized." It "isn't a sequence of events." The redistributions of mass-energy that constitute change "do not have a digital structure."

So: events are how we describe change, not what change is made of.

Kuczynski 142 — PASS
Question: Is the deductive-nomological model of explanation correct?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 6
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Causality; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; Part II; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means
Word count: 259

EXACT ANSWER
No. The deductive-nomological model is viciously circular and is therefore a failure.

Hempel and Hume have it backwards. They believe that "laws are logically prior to events" and that "it is on the basis of their knowledge of laws that people explain events." But it's the other way around. "People already have explanations—albeit low-level, low-resolution ones—of the phenomena; and on that basis they posit the existence of laws." Hypotheses concerning laws are distillations of existing, low-level explanations. So the DN model explains the explanandum by appeal to laws that are themselves derived from the very explanations they are supposed to ground. That is circularity, not explanation.

What actually underlies the search for answers is a single principle: "causal anomalies must be minimized." Everything will be explained when and only when it is known, for any given state of affairs, what caused that state of affairs to obtain. "If you know all the causes, you know all the explanations."

The DN theorist will object that one can know what killed Tim—he ate fish—without knowing how. But this objection fails. "How-knowledge is high-resolution what-knowledge." Not knowing the "how" consists in not knowing the specific mechanisms involved; and that consists in not knowing the "what."

And the elimination of causal anomalies consists in the elimination of discontinuities. That is the real work of explanation—not subsumption under law.

The psychologist and the physicist are doing the same thing. "The physicist is looking for causal mechanisms and so is the psychologist." DN obscures this by pretending explanation is deduction from law. It is not.

Kuczynski 143 — PASS
Question: Is probabilistic causation ontological or merely epistemic?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 2
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology
Word count: 280

EXACT ANSWER
Probabilistic causation is epistemically valid but not ontologically fundamental. The probability belongs to our statements, not to the world itself.

As I've argued, "Probability is a property of statements, not of states of affairs. It's a property of statements to the effect that a certain hypothesis is given a certain amount of support by a certain body of data." This is the crux. When I say a radioactive atom has a 50% chance of decaying, I am not describing a feature of the atom. I am describing the support my evidence gives to a hypothesis about the atom.

The ontological picture is starker still. "A complete description of the universe would contain no probability statements. Given any statement S (that isn't a probability statement), such a description would contain either S or not-S." God's-eye view admits no probabilities. Every event either occurs or does not.

Yet this does not eliminate probabilistic causation from science. "Most laws hold only probabilistically." And "two indistinguishable situations could have different outcomes due to quantum events." So "there is epistemic validity to probabilistic causation in scientific explanations."

The reconciliation is this: causal relations "can be known only through one's senses... and through real-time awareness of one's own psychological processes." Knowledge of them "is therefore empirical." Our empirical access is inherently probabilistic—not because the world is indeterminate at bottom, but because our evidence underdetermines which outcome obtains.

The epistemic function of natural laws is "to enable scientists to predict and explain behaviors across various contexts." Probabilistic laws do this. They are tools for navigating a world whose complete description contains no probabilities at all.

So: epistemic, not ontological. The indeterminacy is in us, not in being.

Kuczynski 144 — PASS
Question: What is wrong with grue?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 14
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Causality; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Part II; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8
Word count: 243

EXACT ANSWER
The problem with grue isn't that it's a strange predicate. It's that it picks out an "explanatorily hollow" property. That's the whole diagnosis.

Goodman's puzzle shows that "all green emeralds examined before the present are similar to blue emeralds examined in the future in that they're all 'grue.'" So the data confirm green-after-2010 and blue-after-2010 equally. But this only looks like a crisis if you think induction has a "strictly observational basis." It doesn't.

As I put it, "induction does not have strictly observational basis. From a strictly observational standpoint, it's no less correct to describe an emerald examined in 2009 as 'grue' than it is to describe it as 'green.'" Observation alone can't tell you which similarity counts.

What tells you is explanatory embeddedness. "The supposition that objects don't change color... is deeply embedded in scientific theory and also in the commonsense underpinning of scientific theory." Green tracks a stable property—wavelength. Grue is "gerrymandered," defined by an arbitrary time t. It "doesn't correspond to wavelength."

So the fix is this: "We know that terms like 'grue' and 'carbivore' pick out explanatorily hollow properties, and that's why we don't base our driving habits on our beliefs about the dietary habits of dinosaurs." We know what to infer "only insofar as we know what kinds of similarity count."

Grue isn't a color at all—"it's a color-related property," like "squiangle" is shape-related. The predicate is fine as a predicate. It's just not a projectible one.

Kuczynski 145 — PASS
Question: Is induction justified?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 17
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Why Does Alcoholics Anonymous Work?; Causality; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Do We Think in Words?; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Part II
Word count: 262

EXACT ANSWER
Induction is justified—but not by the standard Hume imposed. Hume's riddle was a pseudo-problem, generated by a false equation of rationality with deduction.

The old view ran: "Rationality = deduction; induction ≠ deduction; therefore induction needs justification; no justification exists; therefore induction is irrational." I reject the premise. "Rationality = pattern recognition," and "induction IS pattern recognition." Pattern recognition is basic—"it's not justified by something else, it's the foundation." Asking why pattern recognition is rational is like asking why seeing is visual. It is constitutive of rational thought.

So the circularity objection dissolves. Hume said you cannot use induction to justify induction. Correct—because induction doesn't need justification by something else. It is self-correcting and truth-tracking: "When patterns mislead, we recognize that too (anomaly detection)." It is also more fundamental than deduction, since "even applying deductive rules requires recognizing patterns."

I also deny that we actually reason by induction by enumeration. "All cases of induction by inference, when legitimate, are parasitic on cases of inference to the best explanation." Hume attacked a form of inference we barely use.

Where does the justification live? Not in our propositional reports. "The justification for our inductions lies in the smooth curves of experience, and not in the jagged edges of our descriptions thereof." Our perceptions are our only source of information, but "the content of a perception doesn't decompose in the same way as the content of the propositions that we would typically use to report those perceptions."

Hume was right that induction is basic to cognition. He was wrong to think that makes it non-rational.

Kuczynski 146 — PASS
Question: Is behaviorism anything other than empiricism?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 1
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Causality; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism
Word count: 194

EXACT ANSWER
Behaviorism is nothing other than empiricism. They are the same doctrine under two names.

My argument is direct. "Behaviorism is empiricism." And empiricism, stated plainly, is the thesis that "it's only through sense-perception that one learns." That is the whole of it.

This has a consequence that empiricists rarely confront. If all learning runs through the senses, then "ab initio the mind is a blank slate." Locke named this condition with the term "tabula rasa," and he was right to do so—it is the inevitable result of the empiricist premise.

So the equivalence holds: "This in turn is tantamount to saying that it is only through sense-perception that the mind learns. And this is nothing other than behaviorism."

Now consider procedural knowledge—knowledge-how. The behaviorist cannot say we learn a skill through a single perception. So he must say "that it is through operant conditioning that we acquire procedural knowledge."

Take the word "fire." How do you learn what it means? The behaviorist answers: "Through sense-perception... you see fire while hearing utterances of the word 'fire.'"

That is empiricism applied to language. Same doctrine, same mechanism, same blank slate. There is no daylight between them.

Kuczynski 147 — PASS
Question: Is Lewisian functionalism a form of behaviorism?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 1
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Causality; Part II; Do We Think in Words?; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means
Word count: 281

EXACT ANSWER
No. Functionalism is not behaviorism, and the difference is precisely what makes it a distinct position.

The behaviorist identifies mental states with dispositions understood in strictly behavioral terms. As I put it, "behaviorism identifies mental states with dispositions that can be understood in strictly behavioral terms." That is the fatal flaw. It forces the absurd result that "a person who had no linguistic knowledge would react by saying '2' to an utterance of 'what is 1 + 1?'"

Functionalism avoids this. "Functionalism doesn't run into this problem." Why? Because "unlike behaviorism, functionalism can (supposedly) accommodate the fact that among the causes and effects of a mental entity are other mental entities." The functionalist allows that a belief that snow is white is caused by perceptions of white snow and causes further beliefs — a belief that snow is not green. That is a mental-to-mental causal chain, which behaviorism cannot countenance.

So the functionalist's core claim is: "for any mental type M, mental entities are among the characteristic causes and effects of instances of that type." And more strongly: "for any mental category M, there is some causal role C such that x falls into M if and only if x has C."

But here is the problem I flag. "For something to be a pain is for it to feel a certain way—its causal role is secondary." Functionalism defines the mental wholly by causal role, and that is exactly where it fails. The qualitative feel drops out.

So no — functionalism is not behaviorism. But it inherits behaviorism's deepest mistake: it treats the mental as exhaustively characterizable by its functional relations, ignoring what it is like to be in the state.

Kuczynski 148 — PASS
Question: Is psychology reducible to physics?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 12
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology   Volume 8; Causality
Word count: 303

EXACT ANSWER
No. Psychology is not reducible to physics, and there are two distinct senses in which this is true.

First, psychology is irreducible "in the generic sense in which biology and every other physical science is irreducible to physics." Biological phenomena are identical with atomic interactions, yet "there would be no way to translate a biological statement (e.g. 'Smith is now breathing') into a statement about atoms bouncing off of one another." The same holds for psychology: "psychology talk isn't physics talk (or chemistry talk or biology talk), even though psychological events are physical events."

Second, there is a deeper irreducibility. "Epistemically speaking, physics and physiology model the same facts," so the two can be reconciled. "But psychology and physics don't converge on any one set of facts. What they're studying is the same. How they study it is different."

This is why reductive materialism fails. "If materialism were right, then if I knew what physical concepts were instantiated in R, I could literally compute what mental concepts were instantiated in R." But no such computation is possible. Physical knowledge "wouldn't even provide a decent inductive basis for inferring what mental concepts were instantiated in R."

The datum that there are psychological data cannot be dismissed. "It is not his job to prejudge the significance of that data. A scientist's suspicion that there is no physics-friendly way to model psychological data is not a good reason to deny the existence of such data."

The relevance of behavior to psychology is contingent on its being "driven by forces that are correctly described by truths... that are either known (or to be known) introspectively." Strip that away and the behavior "ipso facto ceases to be of any concern to psychology."

So: psychological events are physical events, but psychology is not reducible to physics—neither generically nor epistemically.

[Causality] We don’t observe electrons or quarks, but we have good reason to believe them to exist. How are causal ties different? Given that it’s methodologically permissible to posit unobservable viruses and particles, why isn’t it equally permissible to posit unobservable causal ties?
[Causality] But this means that, if functionalism is correct, then the mental does nothing; it has no causal powers at all.
[Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology] Two microphysically identical situations (or universes) cannot be macrophysically different.

Kuczynski 149 — PASS
Question: Did Berkeley anticipate Sellars on the myth of the given?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 6
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Berkeley and Contemporary Anti foundationalism; Russell's Improvements on Frege's Work   Chapter 6; What Are Propositions and What Is Truth?; Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Causality; Part II; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible
Word count: 272

EXACT ANSWER
Yes. Two hundred years before Sellars, Berkeley destroyed the myth of the given—and did so more thoroughly.

I argue that "in An Essay Towards a New Theory of Vision (1709), George Berkeley made essentially the same points that Sellars would make, over two hundred years later, in Empiricism and the Philosophy of Mind." Moreover, "Berkeley's attack on the given is more perspicuous, more radical, and more cogent than Sellars' version of it."

The structure of the argument is identical. Sellars showed that a sensory episode carries no determinate message unless placed in a context of background knowledge. Berkeley showed the same thing about distance-perception: "In the absence of background empirical knowledge, our sensory episodes become indeterminate to the point of meaninglessness – to the point of having no representational content."

So no sensory experience is foundational. "The senses tell us about the world only through the 'mediation of various past experiences'." Knowledge arises from "coherencies obtaining among sensory experiences; thus it isn't given through isolated sensory experiences; and thus, for Berkeley, empirical knowledge has no foundation."

Berkeley's version is superior in two respects. First, he generalizes: he "explicitly shows how anti-foundationalism applies to a wide range of contexts," whereas Sellars "discusses only very special contexts." Second, Berkeley supplies "a non-metaphorical way of interpreting some of the metaphors that dominate contemporary anti-foundationalism"—the "arc," the "web."

Sellars distinguished two myths: that the given is epistemic, and that it is representational. Berkeley attacks both. He denies that what is given "constitutes knowledge," and he denies that it even "tells us anything, whether true or false."

The revolution usually credited to Sellars was, in substance, Berkeley's.

Kuczynski 150 — PASS
Question: Are emotions beliefs?
Answer type: direct_aligned
Direct evidence count: 14
Representative quotation count: 20
Named works: Empiricism and the Foundations of Psychology; Chapter 27   How Is Rationalization Possible; Part II; Libet’s Experiment   Why It Matters and What It Means
Word count: 254

EXACT ANSWER
Emotions are beliefs. That is my position, and it is the exact inversion of Hume's.

Hume held that "emotions can be healthy or unhealthy, but they cannot be true or false." On his view, "emotions are neither true nor false, neither accurate nor inaccurate." He granted that "emotions presuppose beliefs; but emotions aren't themselves beliefs." I reject this entirely. "Hume's view, we will now see, is totally false. Emotions are true or false. The reason is that, counterintuitive though it may seem, emotions are beliefs."

Consider fear. "To fear her coming is for you to believe that her coming would frustrate some desire of yours." Strip away the belief that something you want is jeopardized, and fear evaporates. You could believe she is coming, but you could not fear it.

So I generalize: "Emotions, then, are beliefs about the prospects of gratifying desires that one has. If the belief is that the prospects are good, the emotion is a positive one (e.g., jubilation, relief). If the belief is that those prospects are bad, it's a negative one (e.g., anger, remorse)."

This is why emotions admit of truth and falsity. Your outrage at Smith is "identical with your belief that Smith's behavior thwarted your desire for a relationship in which certain rules of decency were observed." If Smith did no such thing, your outrage is simply mistaken.

The counterintuitive sting dissolves once you see that "emotions, though beliefs, are not discursive beliefs." They are egocentric beliefs about your own desires—no less truth-apt for being so.
